the same pair was run there — one arm, twice, in one dispatch (`43557304930`, `select-mixed`,
`deepseek-chat`, served as `deepseek-flash` on all 1,532 questions):

| reading | Mini-Dev (496) | dev (1,532) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| accuracy | 58.06% | **62.86%** |
| the same arm again | 62.30% | **63.12%** |
| A/A score delta | **+4.23pp** (11 : 32, p = 0.0019) | **+0.26pp** (45 : 49, p = 0.757) |
| A/A ceiling delta | +2.62pp | **−0.33pp** (42 : 37) |
| paired MDE — the resolution | 3.70pp | **1.77pp** |
| ceiling MDE | — | 1.63pp |
| discordant share | 8.67% | 6.14% |
| distinct result sets per question | 1.34 | 1.30 |
| questions with one result set | 66.9% | **74.2%** |
| selection loss | 7.3% | 5.6% |
| pool ceiling | 69.2% | 68.47% |

Two predictions were registered before the dispatch and they land differently, which is the point
of registering them:

- **The ceiling delta lands inside the ±1.0pp band** the lottery predicted for this n (−0.33pp).
- **The resolution came in at 1.77pp, not the 2.0–2.3pp predicted.** The prediction scaled 3.7pp by
  1/√n and held the *discordant share* fixed, and the share is the other half of the arithmetic:
  it is 6.14% on dev against 8.67% on Mini-Dev. A design's resolution is `(1.96 + 0.84)·√(share/n)`,
  so a split that also disagrees less often is better than 1/√n twice over. The estimate was wrong
  in the direction that costs nothing, and the formula is now the stated one rather than a scaling
  rule.

**The 4.23 points did not reproduce.** At three times the questions the same pair separates by
0.26pp with p = 0.76. That is the strongest available evidence for the reading above: the Mini-Dev
delta was a draw from a distribution whose tail the 496-question design can reach, not a harness
that is noisy by four points. It also means the honest summary of `43535849969` is not "our
instrument is broken" but "a 496-question A/A can wander that far, which is why it is not the split
to decide anything on".

**What it unlocks.** A mechanism worth 2pp is now measurable with two arms on dev for 1,532 × 4
calls. That is the same bill as the Mini-Dev runs that could not resolve it, and it is the only
change in this document that alters what the next round can claim.

#### The instrument's first external failure, found on the artifact it was pointed at

`select-mixed` draws three candidates and keeps three, so on dev there is no pool wider than the
draw and the lottery band is a constant zero. The verdict printed at that artifact was **"the A/A
ceiling delta of −0.3pp is 0.3pp beyond the ±0.0pp the offered pool can produce, so the draw
distribution itself moved"** — a claim about a moved distribution produced from no evidence at all,
because a zero band makes every delta "beyond" it. The reading was caught within a minute of the
artifact landing, which is what a verdict sentence is for, and the third state is now explicit:

| kind | condition | what it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `inside` | the graded delta is inside the band | the pair read the draw |
| `beyond` | it is outside the band | the draw distribution moved |
| `unpriced` | the widest pool is exactly the draw | nothing about composition can be separated; only the pair's own interval grades a delta |
| `unmeasured` | the run carried no A/A | no pair to grade |

So a dev dispatch that wants its band priced has to include a wider arm in the same run — the
dispatch after this one carries `select-mixed-rule-spread3` beside `select-mixed` for exactly that
reason, and `--arm` on the instrument names which arm supplies the universe.

### Text2Vis: the cue table, scored against the one corpus that labels a chart

The chart half of the product ships a deterministic decision — `readCues` reads the question and
ranks the marks that can carry it — and until now nothing external had ever scored it. Text2Vis
states, per row, a question and the chart type its authors judged correct, so the cue half can be
scored with **no model call, no database and no renderer**:

```
pnpm bench:text2vis:rule                 # download once, score, print
pnpm bench:text2vis:rule --artifact out/text2vis-rule.json
```

The unit is a **family**, because the corpus writes `Bar Chart` and the contract writes `bar`; the
mapping is a table, and a label it has no family for is **excluded from the score and named in the
log** rather than folded into `bar`. Three numbers are always printed together, because any one of
them alone is a number about nothing:

| reading | what it is for |
| --- | --- |
| top-1 | the leading mark carries the labelled family |
| shortlist | some recommended mark does — a different claim, reported separately |
| baseline: always *X*, always bar | the two constants a cue table has to beat |

Two widenings are argued rather than convenient: a `line` answers for an `area` because an area chart
is that line filled, and a `bar` does **not** answer for a `histogram` — a histogram is one measure
binned, and folding them together would hide the finding the confusion table exists to surface.
What this does not measure is stated in the module: encoding (which fields, which aggregate), the
recommender's data-shape half, and whether a label is one annotator's judgement.

#### The first reading of the cue table, and the three defects it names

`text2vis-rule` ran for the first time in CI (`43545023250`, the corpus downloaded over the network,
not from a cache), on the whole corpus: **1,985 rows**, of which **1,469** carry a label this build
has a family for. No model call, no database, no renderer.

| reading | value | what it is compared against |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| top-1 | **37.37%** (549) | **always bar: 28.52%** — the constant a cue table has to beat |
| shortlist | 68.01% (999) | a different claim: the family is in the recommended set |
| declined | 0 | every question in this corpus fires at least one cue |
| cue path, p50 / p95 / max | **0.11 / 0.16 / 5.59 ms** | per question, over 1,985 questions |

So the table beats the constant by **8.85 points**, and the shortlist says the *right answer is
usually one of the marks it names* — the loss is in the ordering, not in the vocabulary. The cost is
what a rule is supposed to cost: a fifth of a millisecond per question, four orders of magnitude
inside the one-second budget the chart path is held to.

The confusion table is where the work is, and it names three defects rather than a score:

| label in the corpus | rows | top-1 | what the table answered instead |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Line | 391 | 54.48% | pie (81), heatmap (63) |
| **Bar** | **357** | **12.32%** | **pie (164)**, heatmap (61), line (54) |
| Area | 137 | 42.34% | line (58), heatmap (38) |
| Pie | 113 | 78.76% | pie (89) |
| Scatter | 93 | 31.18% | scatter (29), line (25) |
| **Histogram** | **90** | **0.00%** | **boxplot (53)**, pie (24) |
| Boxplot | 89 | 51.69% | boxplot (46) |
| Donut | 69 | 81.16% | pie (56) |
| Stacked Bar | 56 | 12.50% | **pie (30)** |
| Heatmap | 20 | 5.00% | line (8), scatter (5) |
| Funnel | 11 | 0.00% | **pie (11)** |
| Bubble | 10 | 10.00% | bar (5) |

1. **The `share` cue leads with `pie`, and the corpus draws bars.** 164 bar questions and 30 stacked
   bars were answered `pie` — **194 rows, 13.2% of the scored population**, which is where most of the
   8.85-point gap to a *perfect* ordering lives. The table's own justification for pie-leading was
   never measured; it is now.
2. **`histogram` is unreachable by construction.** The contract has 22 series types and none of them
   is a histogram, so the honest product answer to a histogram question is a binned bar — but the
   `distribution` cue prefers `boxplot`, and 90 rows score zero. This is the case the family table
   deliberately *kept* visible instead of folding `bar` over `histogram`; the reading is the argument
   for changing the cue, not for changing the table.
3. **Two labels the build could not name are worth naming.** `Barh` (the corpus's horizontal bar) is
   the same decision as a bar, and it is now mapped. `Dot`, `Dot Plot`, `Choropleth Map`, `Subplot`,
   `Treemap`, `Waterfall` and one empty label stay unmapped and are **printed with the rows they
   account for**, because "516 rows are unmapped" and a list of eight names do not tell a reader which
   one to fix first.

The next reading is one change: `share → ['bar', 'pie']`, with the bar registered in advance —
top-1 ≥ 45.0% and `Bar` top-1 ≥ 60.0%, on the same corpus, with the same two baselines printed
alongside. A change to the cue table that does not clear its own baseline is not a change.

#### The sweep: four cue tables, one run, and the bar none of them clears

`share → ['bar', 'pie']` was registered with two numbers attached — top-1 ≥ 45.0% and `Bar` top-1 ≥
60.0% — and the reading that decides it now costs nothing to take: a table is scored in a fifth of a
millisecond, so the arm prices the shipped table and every table this build can construct on the same
rows, in one run over the same 1,470 scored questions. The denominator moved from the 1,469 of the
first reading because `Barh` is now mapped, and the shipped table reads 37.35% against the 37.37% it
read on 1,469 — the same **549** hits, so the two readings are the same reading.

| table | top-1 | Δ vs shipped | `bar` family | `pie` family | `histogram` | shortlist |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `shipped` | **37.35%** (549) | — | 51/420 (12.14%) | 145/182 | 0/90 | 1,000 |
| `bar-share` | 40.82% (600) | +3.47pp | **247/420 (58.81%)** | **0/182** | 0/90 | 1,000 |
| `histogram` | 39.46% (580) | +2.11pp | 51/420 | 145/182 | **31/90 (34.44%)** | 1,031 |
| `bar-share+histogram` | **42.93%** (631) | **+5.58pp** | 247/420 (58.81%) | 0/182 | 31/90 | 1,031 |

Three things this table says that a single number could not.

**The mechanism is exactly the size the corpus said it was, and the cost is the one nobody priced.**
The `bar` family is 420 questions and the shipped table answers 51 of them; flipping the cue answers
**247**, which is the 196 rows the previous round counted as bars answered `pie`. The price is
**all 145** of the pie rows that family had: `share` now leads with a bar for every question that
fires it, and the 182 pie-and-donut questions are inside that set. The gain was predicted to the row
and the loss was not priced at all, which is exactly why the bar was registered at 45.0% and not at
"better than before".

**The histogram cue is a real but smaller fix, and it is scoped.** It recovers **31 of 90** histogram
questions (0.00% → 34.44%), lifts the shortlist from 1,000 to 1,031, and leaves `boxplot` at 47 of 90
and every other family where it was — because a question that says "histogram" does not say
"boxplot". The other 59 histogram rows never use the word, and that is the finding: the label is an
annotator's choice of *shape*, and 59 of them ask for a distribution in words a cue table cannot
separate from a boxplot's.

**None of the three registered bars is cleared.** 40.82% against the required 45.0%, `Bar` 58.81%
against 60.0%, `Histogram` 34.44% against 40.0%. The combined table reaches **42.93%**, which is
+5.58pp on the shipped table — an exact, census-wide gain, since the corpus is not a sample and this
delta carries no sampling noise at all — and still 2.07pp short of the number registered before the
run.

**So the shipped table does not change.** A pre-registration that is missed by two points and then
adopted anyway is not a pre-registration; it is a note taken after the fact, and the next change would
be measured against a bar that had already been moved once. What the sweep buys is the diagnosis:
the loss is not in the ordering, it is in the *cue*. `share` is one phrase covering two pictures, and
196 + 145 = 341 of the corpus's questions are the evidence that it cannot be one line. The next
experiment is a discriminator inside `share` — pie when the question names a whole it is a part of,
bar when it names categories to compare — registered before it is run, with the two numbers this
sweep fixes as its floor: top-1 ≥ 45.0% **and** `pie` no lower than the 145 the shipped table keeps.

#### The discriminator inside `share`, priced at two widths — and both of them miss

The criterion above was registered with two numbers: top-1 ≥ 45.0% and `pie` no lower than 145. The
discriminator was registered at **two widths** before either ran, so that which one ships is a
reading rather than a choice made while looking at the result:

- `share-by` — a share word immediately followed by the dimension it splits on (`share by`,
  `breakdown across`, `percentage per`).
- `share-by-any` — the same signal with a measure between the words, so "the share of revenue by
  region", the corpus's most natural way to ask for a comparison, is also a bar.

Both carry a single bar as their only mark, and both are inserted ahead of `share`, because the
leading mark is the first mark of the first fired cue. One dispatch of the rule arm prices all six
tables on the same 1,470 scored questions, no model call (`43591108214`):

| table | top-1 | Δ vs shipped | `bar` | `pie` | `histogram` | shortlist |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `shipped` | 549 (37.35%) | — | 51/420 | 145/182 | 0/90 | 1,000 |
| `bar-share` | 600 (40.82%) | +51 | 247/420 | 0/182 | 0/90 | 1,000 |
| `histogram` | 580 (39.46%) | +31 | 51/420 | 145/182 | 31/90 | 1,031 |
| `bar-share+histogram` | **631 (42.93%)** | +82 | 247/420 | 0/182 | 31/90 | 1,031 |
| **`share-by`** | 554 (37.69%) | **+5** | 61/420 | 140/182 | 0/90 | 1,000 |
| **`share-by-any`** | 599 (40.75%) | **+50** | 246/420 | **0/182** | 0/90 | 1,000 |
| `share-by+histogram` | 585 (39.80%) | +36 | 61/420 | 140/182 | 31/90 | 1,031 |
| `share-by-any+histogram` | 630 (42.86%) | +81 | 246/420 | 0/182 | 31/90 | 1,031 |

**Both widths miss, and they miss in opposite directions, which is the finding.**

`share-by` moves **ten** rows and loses **five**: the phrase is rare in this corpus. Ten rows out of
420 bar questions say "share by" with nothing in between, so the narrow reading of the signal is
almost never the corpus's way of asking, and its 37.69% is a measurement of that rarity rather than
of the idea. It also fails the second clause — `pie` 140 against the required 145 — which is the one
number a discriminator must not spend.

`share-by-any` moves **195** rows and loses **all 145**: every single pie question in the corpus
contains a share word and a `by` somewhere after it. It lands at 40.75% with `pie` 0/182, which is
`bar-share` (40.82%, `pie` 0/182) reproduced to within one row. Two different mechanisms producing
the same table is not a coincidence to be explained away: at this width the "discriminator" *is* the
blunt flip, because the phrase it keys on is present in the questions it was meant to exclude.

**So the distinction is not in the words around `share`.** That is what a cue table can see, and it
cannot see it, at either width. The honest statement of the position:

| family | n | shipped top-1 | reading |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `pie` | 182 | 145 (79.7%) | the one family the shipped table answers well |
| `bar` | 420 | 51 (12.1%) | the largest family in the corpus and the worst served |
| `line` | 394 | 216 (54.8%) | |
| `area` | 138 | 59 (42.8%) | |
| `scatter` | 104 | 30 (28.8%) | |
| `histogram` | 90 | 0 (0.0%) | the cue names no binned measure |
| `boxplot` | 90 | 47 (52.2%) | |
| `heatmap` | 20 | 1 (5.0%) | the `matrix` cue fires on `by … and …` and almost nothing else |
| `funnel` / `violin` / `candlestick` / `radar` | 32 | 0 | four families with no cue that reaches them |

The confusion table says where the mass is. The shipped table answers `pie` for **529** of the 1,470
scored questions and only **145** of them are pies: `bar → pie` is 196 rows, `line → pie` 81,
`area → pie` 35, `histogram → pie` 24, and 48 more from five smaller families. The cue is not a shape
word at all — "what percentage of orders…" asks for a **number**, and the corpus's annotators drew a
bar for most of those. That is why every table that leads `share` with a bar lands within a row of
every other one: the choice is not between two pictures inside a cue, it is between a cue that
over-claims and a cue that over-claims less.

**The shipped table does not change, and the cue-only path is now closed as a lever.** Three
different tables — the blunt flip, the wide discriminator, and the two of them plus the histogram cue
— land at 40.75%, 40.82% and 42.93%, inside 2.2pp of each other while differing by 195 rows. A
mechanism that produces the same score three ways is at its ceiling, and the ceiling is 42.93% against
a registered 45.0%.

What the next experiment has to be is therefore not a fourth phrase. The corpus ships the reference
`code` for every row, so the *shape of the answer* — how many categories the statement groups by,
whether the measure is a part of a stated total — is recoverable without a model. That is a
**profile** decision rather than a lexical one, it is what `recommendChart(profile, question)` already
does in the product, and the rule arm has only ever scored the cue half of it. Registering it here:
score the full recommender on the same 1,470 rows, cue-only as the control, and require top-1 ≥
45.0% with `pie` not below 145 before the shipped path changes.

#### What the 515 excluded rows are, and the correction that makes

The block now prints the rows behind each unmapped label, and the second run (`43546926456`) is what
that was for. The 515 excluded rows are not a long tail of odd spellings:

| label | rows | why it is excluded |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `Subplot` | **200** | a **layout**, not a mark: the reference is a multi-panel figure, and a `ChartIR` is one plot |
| `Waterfall` | 108 | a real chart type with no member in the contract's 22 series types |
| `Treemap` | 92 | in the contract, but not among the marks the recommender chooses between (it needs a hierarchy the result set does not carry) |
| `Dot` | 81 | a lollipop/dot plot; the contract has no such series |
| `Dot Plot` | 15 | the same, spelled differently — which is why the table matches on families rather than on strings |
| `Choropleth Map` | 14 | a map, which needs geometry rather than rows |
| `<empty>` | 5 | rows whose authors left the column blank |

So **13.5% of this corpus is a multi-panel figure or a chart the contract cannot represent**, and the
37.4% is the agreement on the 74% that remains. That is the bound on how far this number generalizes,
and it belongs beside the score rather than under it.

The same run also corrects a claim made one paragraph too early: mapping `Barh` moved **one row**
(1,469 → 1,470 scored, top-1 unchanged at 549). The label was worth naming — it is a bar — but it was
worth one row, and the reason it looked more important is that the first version of this block printed
eight labels without saying how many rows each accounted for. **A list of labels is not a priority
order; that was the defect, and it was in the instrument rather than in the table.**

### The largest bucket was counting spellings: a quarter of `predicate` was one condition written two ways

`bench:bird:gap:values` splits the `values` bucket — the statement ran, the width matched, the
numbers did not — into the fix each case asks for. On the dev split it named `predicate` as the
largest rung at **100 of 365** cases (27.4%), and the fix that rung names is *condition coverage*:
write the conditions the question implies. Before spending a run on that, three cases were read
line by line, and all three were the same statement as the gold with the join written the other
way round:

```
gold  ... from schools as t1 inner join frpm as t2 on t1.cdscode = t2.cdscode
pred  ... from frpm join schools on frpm.cdscode = schools.cdscode

gold  select count(t1.account_id) ... where t1.balance < 0
pred  select count(distinct t.account_id) ... where t.balance < 0
```

`a.id = b.id` and `b.id = a.id` are one condition. The ladder compared the atom lists as text, so
they were two, and the case was filed under a rung whose fix could not have changed the answer.
Three spellings account for the error: an equality written in the other direction, a column with
its table qualifier dropped in front of a literal (`charternum is not null` against
`schools.charternum is not null`), and an `in` list in another order.

`predicateKeys` now compares conditions as keys. It canonicalizes direction (`a > b` is `b < a`),
drops the qualifier when the other side is a value, and reads an `in` list as a set. It keeps the
qualifier when **both** sides are columns, because stripping it there would make every join equal
to every other join, and it keeps `between`'s bounds in order, because swapping them is a
different question. A literal that contains the word — `status = 'like new'` — is still an
equality; the operator is read outside quotes.

The same 365 cases, before and after:

| rung | before | after | the fix it names |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `filter-wide` | 78 | **78** | the filter is too weak, or a join multiplied rows |
| `predicate` | 100 | **70** | condition coverage |
| `tables` | 62 | 62 | join selection |
| `filter-narrow` | 54 | 54 | a predicate matched nothing |
| `literal-missing` | 34 | 34 | a value the question named is not in the statement |
| `aggregate` | 16 | **27** | which function answers the question |
| `projection` | 12 | **23** | which columns, in what order |
| `literal-case` | 5 | 5 | the value is in another case |
| `window` | 2 | **5** | which window of the same rows |
| `grain` | 0 | **4** | the aggregation level |
| `unclassified` | 2 | **3** | nothing the shape can name |

Thirty cases moved, and the correction changes the order of the work: the largest rung is no
longer `predicate` but `filter-wide`, and `aggregate` + `projection` together went from 28 to 50
cases. Those name a different mechanism than condition coverage — one of them is arithmetic over
the right rows, the other is which column holds the answer — and neither had been visible while a
quarter of the bucket sat one rung too early.

Two things this does **not** fix. A join whose conditions are written as `a = b and c = d` against
`c = d and a = b` still compares equal (the set is sorted), which is correct, but a join that
writes the pair in a subquery and the gold outside it still lands in `tables`. And the rungs are
still counted over cases whose candidate set held no answer: 118 of the no-answer cases sit
outside the `values` scope and are not in this table at all.

### The free selectors, exhaustively: 64.20% is the ceiling, and the paid one is worse than three of the four

`select-mixed-rule` ships `shortest` — the candidate with the fewest characters of SQL — and it
replaced a model call on the strength of a reading, not a preference. The question this round asked
is whether `shortest` is the *best* call-free rule or only the first one that happened to be tried.
Four signals that had never been priced were added to the offline device, all of them functions of
data already in the artifact's candidate records, so the whole scan spends no model call:

| rule | what it reads | correct | accuracy |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| `oracle` *(not a rule)* | any candidate correct | 1,049 | 68.65% |
| **`complex`** | fewest structural units — tables + subqueries, then `and`/`or`, then aggregates and `case`; length breaks ties | **981** | **64.20%** |
| `shortest` *(shipped)* | fewest characters | 976 | 63.87% |
| `struct` | the most common structure — tables, aggregates, `group by`, `over`, `limit`, `distinct` — then shortest inside it | 967 | 63.29% |
| `nomultiline` | fewest newlines, then length | 967 | 63.29% |
| `model` *(the paid selector)* | the LLM's own choice | 963 | 63.02% |
| `short-tie-modal` | shortest, and when two are the same length the result set most candidates agree on | 952 | 62.30% |

Three of the four new signals **lose to a character count**, and the shipped rule is beaten by 5
cases only when the count is replaced by a structural one. The paid selector is beaten by three of
the five call-free rules. That is the same finding the shipping decision rested on, now with the
rest of the space filled in: **on this pool, reading the statements buys about a point over reading
the results, and nothing buys the 4.78 points to the ceiling.**

Two readings this table needs, because both are ways it could be quoted wrongly:

- **Every column above is measured under one judge.** The five free rules are priced with the
  artifact's stored `correct` flags, which the run wrote with `judgeOfficial`; nothing here
  re-executes. The `shortest` row reads 63.87% here against `bench:bird:consensus`'s **64.56%** on
  the same artifact, and the 0.69pp between them is not a disagreement — it is the candidate that
  returned nothing, which the consensus device rules out before ranking and this scan does not. The
  comparison inside the table is between rules, and it is measured on one judge.
- **The ceiling moved between two runs of the same pool.** `oracle` is 68.65% here and the shipped
  arm's artifact recorded **66.91%** on 1,532 questions. Same three prompts, same temperature, a
  different draw. So the "2.94pp the selector loses" that this table's last column implies is
  itself a difference between two draws, not a stable property — which is the second reason not to
  read any of these rows as a gain until a run reproduces it.

#### The signal that was calibrated before it was priced, and did not survive

The idea worth stating is the one that failed cleanly. A question that asks "how many" is answered
by one row of one column; a candidate that returns forty rows is wrong for a reason no majority of
identical mistakes will reveal, and the shape costs nothing to read because the candidate has
already been executed. The rule would be: keep the candidates whose result shape matches the
question's intent, then take the shortest.

It was calibrated against the golds first, and that is what refused it: of the 519 dev questions
this phrasing matches, only **460 (88.63%)** have a 1×1 gold. Eleven percent of the population the
rule would act on does not obey the rule. Applied to the pool it then changed **nothing** — 976
before, 976 after — because on a "how many" question the shortest statement is usually the
aggregated one already. A rule that is wrong on 11% of its own population and never changes an
answer is not underpowered; it is not a rule.

### `count(distinct)` is not a defect the product can see: 36 wins against 23 losses

The `values` bucket is 365 of the split's 569 failures, and 27 of those sit one rung above the
literal: the aggregate is wrong, not the condition. Reading them produced a direction — **13 of 14
`distinct` cases were the model adding one**, `count(distinct t.account_id)` where the gold counts
plain rows — and a rule that follows from the engine rather than from a judgement: remove the word.

`drop-count-distinct` is now in the rewrite catalogue, priced by re-execution with `judgeOfficial`
on `select-mixed`'s 1,532 dev questions:

| | value |
|---|---:|
| fired | 162 (10.6% of selected statements count distinct rows) |
| won | 36 |
| lost | **23** |
| broken | 0 |
| **net** | **+0.85pp** (+13 cases) |
| exact McNemar | p = 0.1175 |
| resolves | 1.4pp |

**The gain is below this instrument's own resolution, so the rule is not adopted.** What makes it
worth writing down is the structure of the loss, which is not noise:

| group | count | gold contains `count(distinct …)` | what removing the word does |
|---|---:|---|---|
| won | 36 | **0 of 36** | the over-count was the failure |
| lost | 23 | **23 of 23** | the under-count becomes the failure |

Every case the rule loses is a case where the gold counts distinct rows. It is the same statement
as the prediction — same tables, same conditions, same join direction — and the only difference is
the word. So the rule is not repairing a mistake; it is **taking a side on a convention BIRD does
not apply consistently**. Some of its annotators counted rows and some counted entities, and 33 of
the 1,532 golds contain a `count(distinct …)` at all.

That is the honest form of the finding: the `distinct` direction is a real 59-case disagreement
(36 + 23) that no product can adjudicate without the answer. It is kept in the catalogue as the
ablation reference for the `values` rung — the same role `drop-limit-on-count` plays for caps at 1
win against 19 losses.

### The same two points for a tenth of the prompt: `samples-wide-link` on dev

The section above ends with a budget rather than a verdict: the competitor's value block buys
+2.02pp for +74.9% of the prompt, which no product ships. The block's cost is not its bracket but
**the number of columns that carry one** — the sampler, the order, the values and the call count are
identical whether one column carries a bracket or eighty. So the next dispatch held all of that fixed
and changed only the set: MAC-SQL's rule, applied to the columns the prompt's **own hint** already
names.

That rule is not a fitted allow-list. `buildAskMessages` renders `Likely columns: t.c, …` as the first
line of the user message, so the block lands on columns the model is already pointed at, and both the
hint and the block are read from the question and the schema. The oracle version of the same idea —
the columns the gold statement filters on — has been in the table for rounds as a ceiling; this is the
first runnable member of the family.

One dispatch (`43591209696`), the dev split, both arms inside one artifact, one call each:

| arm | passed | accuracy | prompt tokens | prompt chars | calls |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `inline+evidence` | 937 / 1,532 | 61.16% | 676 | 2,781 | 1.00 |
| `inline+evidence+samples-wide-link` | **960 / 1,532** | **62.66%** | **738** | 2,965 | 1.00 |
| difference | +23 | **+1.50pp** | **+9.17%** | +6.62% | 0 |

| quantity | value |
|---|---:|
| right only with the block | 52 |
| right only without it | 29 |
| net | **+23 cases** |
| exact McNemar (two-sided) | **p = 0.0140** |
| disagreement share | 5.29% |
| instrument resolution `R = 2.8·√(share/n)` | 1.64pp |

**The registered bar was two numbers, and both were cleared.** `≥ +1.5pp` — met at +1.50pp — and
`≤ +25%` prompt tokens — met at +9.17%. The oracle for the same family (`samples-gold`) sits in the
table as the ceiling; this is within half a point of the wide block's +2.02pp at **an eighth of its
cost**, which is the trade the family needed.

**A delta at the bar has to be read with its resolution, not instead of it.** `R` is 1.64pp, so the
*magnitude* here is not resolved — this run can say the sign is positive (52:29, p = 0.0140) and
cannot say whether the true gain is 1.0pp or 2.5pp. The reason to believe it is not a draw that moved
is the bucket reading below, which is the same instrument that names the fix, run on both arms of the
same artifact (zero model calls, one oracle query per case):

| bucket | `inline+evidence` | `samples-wide-link` | `samples-wide` (last round) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `literal-case` | 13 (3.0%) | **1 (0.2%)** | 1 (0.2%) |
| `literal-missing` | 42 (9.6%) | 39 (9.2%) | 34 (8.1%) |
| `filter-narrow` | 74 (16.9%) | 62 (14.6%) | 60 (14.4%) |
| `filter-wide` | 94 (21.5%) | 95 (22.4%) | 94 (22.5%) |
| `tables` | 76 (17.4%) | 81 (19.1%) | 79 (18.9%) |
| `predicate` | 71 (16.2%) | 73 (17.2%) | 71 (17.0%) |
| `aggregate` | 35 (8.0%) | 35 (8.3%) | 41 (9.8%) |
| `projection` | 21 (4.8%) | 29 (6.8%) | 30 (7.2%) |
| in-scope failures | 435 of 591 | 422 of 560 | 418 of 560 |

Twelve of the thirteen case-mismatched literals become one, with a block an eighth the size of the
block that bought the same twelve. That is the mechanism arriving at the same place from a much
smaller card, and it is why the gain is attributable rather than merely significant.

**The two instruments agree exactly**, which is the other half of the claim. `bench:bird:card`
recomputes the prompt from the schema, the pinned definitions and the same narrowing rule, and prints
**2,965 characters and 738 tokens** for the arm — the numbers the endpoint billed, to the unit. That
agreement is what a card instrument is for: it priced these arms as their parents for four rounds
because it rendered a card the run never sent, and the rule it needed was shared rather than copied.

**Adoption is open, and deliberately.** The arm this product ships is `select-mixed-rule` — three
candidates, one rule, 63.97% on dev — and a block on one call is not a block on three: the same
+9.17% would be paid on every candidate, and the selector would see a pool drawn from a different
card. Registering that test now: `select-mixed-rule` against `select-mixed-rule` with the narrowed
block on every candidate, on dev, requiring **≥ +1.0pp** (a third of this arm's gain, because a pool's
ceiling moves less than one draw's accuracy) with the token increase on the artifact's own meter.

### What is left, and why it is a composition and not a lever

The gap to the strongest training-free system is now attributable, and the attribution says the
remaining work is a *pipeline*, not a prompt:

| quantity | value | where it comes from |
|---|---:|---|
| shipped arm, dev | **63.97%** | `select-mixed-rule`, 3.00 calls, 3,137 prompt tokens |
| its pool's ceiling | 66.91% | same artifact |
| the same pool, another draw | 68.65% | this round's re-read of `43557304930` |
| MAC-SQL, our harness, our model, dev | **67.89%** | 1,040/1,532 |
| MAC-SQL, our harness, our model, Mini-Dev | 65.12% | — |
| our single best single-call arm, Mini-Dev | **59.44%** | `metadata+evidence` |

The last two rows are the ones that move the plan. MAC-SQL's pipeline is **5.7 points above our
best single-call arm on the split where both were measured**, and every one of its parts has been
priced here separately: value examples (`values`, 56.63%), their dense schema description
(`dense.ts`), their refiner (`inline+repair`, +0.41pp at 1.02 calls), their decomposer (−1.1pp).
**The composition has never been priced as one arm.** Nothing in this document measures
`values` + `repairs` + their dense card together, which is what their `MAC-SQL` actually runs, and
that is the next dispatch rather than another rule.

### The competitor's value block is worth two points, not 5.7: `samples-wide` on dev

The section above ends with a claim that had never been tested: the 5.7-point gap between MAC-SQL's
pipeline and this repository's best single-call arm is a *composition*. The first block of that
composition is now priced. It is their value-example rule, ported with the quirks kept
(`eval/bird/value-examples.ts`, cross-checked against `core/agents.py` at sha `31a9df5e` over three
databases and 87 columns with zero disagreements): six most-frequent values of every non-key column,
a numeric column dropped above ten distinct values, a text column dropped whole when any stored value
is longer than 50 characters or is a URL or an email, a date collapsed to one example, and `NULL`
emitted first when the column stores one.

One dispatch, `43579551678`, the dev split, the same endpoint and the same model, one call per
question and nothing else changed:

| arm | passed | accuracy | prompt tokens | prompt chars | calls |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `inline+evidence` | 941 / 1,532 | 61.42% | 676 | 2,781 | 1.00 |
| `inline+evidence+samples-wide` | **972 / 1,532** | **63.45%** | **1,182** | 3,950 | 1.00 |
| difference | +31 | **+2.02pp** | **+74.9%** | +42.0% | 0 |

Both arms ran inside one artifact, so the delta is a paired reading on the same 1,532 rows and not a
subtraction across two runs:

| quantity | value |
|---|---:|
| right only under the value block | 69 |
| right only without it | **38** |
| net | **+31 cases** |
| exact McNemar (two-sided) | **p = 0.0035** |
| disagreement share | 6.98% |
| instrument resolution `R = 2.8·√(share/n)` | **1.89pp** |

**The delta is beyond the instrument's own resolution and the direction is registered**, so the
mechanism is real: showing a column's stored spellings buys about two points on the split a
leaderboard is compared against. It is not, however, the 5.7 points, and the remainder is therefore
not in this block.

Three readings decide what happens next, and only one of them says yes.

**The accuracy bar was cleared as a delta and missed as a level.** The criterion registered before
the dispatch was `≥ 63.5%` — the historical `inline+evidence` reading of 61.16% plus the split's
2.3pp resolution. The block landed at 63.45%, five hundredths of a point short. The reason is not the
block: the parent re-measured **61.42%** in this run, 0.26pp above its own historical value, so the
level the criterion was written against moved. The delta, which is the quantity that survives a
move, is +2.02pp against a 1.89pp floor. Both numbers are recorded because a pre-registered level
that is missed *and* a pre-registered delta that is cleared is a state a reader has to be told about
rather than resolved by whoever is reporting it.

**The cost bar was not cleared, and it is not close.** The block adds **74.9%** to the prompt — three
times the 25% the plan allowed — for a 42% increase in characters. The gap between those two numbers
is itself a finding: the block tokenizes at 3.34 characters per token against the card's 4.11, because
it is a list of short quoted values separated by punctuation, and a budget computed in characters
would under-count it by a fifth. A gain priced in accuracy and not in tokens is half a reading.

**The bucket the block is aimed at fell, which is the mechanism's fingerprint.** The same instrument
that names the missing fix, run on both arms of the same artifact (zero model calls, one oracle query
per case):

| bucket | `inline+evidence` | `samples-wide` | reading |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `literal-case` | 11 (2.5%) | **1 (0.2%)** | the block's own claim: a stored spelling is now on the card |
| `literal-missing` | 42 (9.7%) | 34 (8.1%) | a literal the card never held |
| `filter-narrow` | 78 (18.0%) | 60 (14.4%) | |
| `filter-wide` | 89 (20.6%) | 94 (22.5%) | |
| `tables` | 77 (17.8%) | 79 (18.9%) | |
| `predicate` | 65 (15.0%) | 71 (17.0%) | |
| `aggregate` | 37 (8.5%) | 41 (9.8%) | |
| `projection` | 21 (4.8%) | 30 (7.2%) | |
| in-scope failures | 433 | 418 | of 591 and 560 |

Eleven case-mismatched literals became one. That is what a block of stored spellings is for, and it
is the reason the accuracy gain is credible rather than a draw that moved. The buckets that *rose* are
all in the third family — what the statement computed, not what it read — and they rose as shares of a
smaller population: `aggregate` + `projection` are 58 of 433 (13.4%) before and 71 of 418 (17.0%)
after. **The next lever is generation-side, and this run makes that quantitative rather than a hunch.**

The gain is also not concentrated in the easy stratum, which is the other way a prompt change can look
real and be worthless:

| difficulty | `inline+evidence` | `samples-wide` | delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| simple (925) | 619 (66.9%) | 628 (67.9%) | +1.0pp |
| moderate (463) | 248 (53.6%) | 262 (56.6%) | +3.0pp |
| challenging (144) | 74 (51.4%) | 82 (56.9%) | **+5.6pp** |

**Verdict: not adopted as it stands.** A +2.02pp gain that costs 75% more prompt is not a trade a
product ships when the same budget buys a candidate; the arm stays in the table as the priced ceiling
of the value family, the way `samples-gold` is the ceiling of the column-sampling family. What the
result licenses is a **narrow** block: the same rule restricted to the columns a question can plausibly
filter on, which is the one form in which the mechanism can survive its own cost.

### Where the gap stands after the block

The table the previous section left open, with the row this dispatch adds:

| quantity | value | where it comes from |
|---|---:|---|
| shipped arm, dev | **63.97%** | `select-mixed-rule`, 3.00 calls, 3,137 prompt tokens |
| its pool's ceiling | 66.91% | same artifact |
| the same pool, another draw | 68.65% | this round's re-read of `43557304930` |
| the competitor's value block, alone | 63.45% | `samples-wide`, 1 call, 1,182 tokens |
| **the same block on the hint's columns** | **62.66%** | `samples-wide-link`, 1 call, **738 tokens** |
| MAC-SQL, our harness, our model, dev | **67.89%** | 1,040/1,532 |
| MAC-SQL, our harness, our model, Mini-Dev | 65.12% | — |
| our single best single-call arm, Mini-Dev | **59.44%** | `metadata+evidence` |

The block is 1.50 of the 5.7 points at a price a product can carry (738 tokens against the parent's
676, and against the wide block's 1,182), so the composition is real, its first term is smaller than
the gap, and the term is now affordable. A second term has to be found in the harness rather than in
the card: their selector reads *their* card, their refiner runs on top of it, and the part this
repository has never reproduced is the pipeline that puts their description, their examples and their
refiner in one arm — with the narrowed block on every candidate, which is the adoption test registered
above and read in the next section, where it fails.

## The block paid three times, and the control that was already in the artifact

**Registration.** `select-mixed-rule-narrow` is `select-mixed-rule` with one field added:
`sourceSamples: { samples: 'example', sampleColumns: 'link' }`, which rides every candidate's card
instead of the arm's own. The arm's `notes`, `evidence`, `repairs`, `linking`, `definitions`, `vote`,
`selectRule` and `mixed` list are the parent's; the block is the whole diff. Registered before the
dispatch: accuracy **at least +1.0pp** against the parent on the same 1,532 questions, `calls.mean`
unchanged at 3.00, prompt tokens read from the artifact's own column rather than from the
single-prompt arm's +9.17%, and a delta inside the split's resolution (1.64pp on this pair's
disagreement rate) read as **the block does not survive being paid per candidate**. One dispatch,
`43606308056`, dev, 1,532 scored questions, both arms in the same artifact against the same judge.

| quantity | `select-mixed-rule` | `-narrow` | delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| passed | 993 (**64.82%**) | 1,001 (**65.34%**) | **+0.52pp** |
| pool ceiling (`candidateRecall`) | 1,053 (68.73%) | 1,057 (68.99%) | +0.26pp |
| strict (no duplicate credit) | 919 | 924 | +5 |
| selection loss (ceiling − passed) | 60 | 56 | −4 |
| calls a question | 3.00 | 3.00 | 0 |
| prompt characters a question | 7,261 | 7,435 | +2.4% |
| prompt tokens a call | 3,137 | 3,327 | +6.1% |
| cached prompt tokens a call | 2,558 (81.5%) | 2,137 (64.2%) | **−16.5%** |
| **charged prompt tokens a call** | **835** | **1,404** | **+68.1%** |
| questions carrying a block | 0 | 1,173 (76.6%) | — |
| columns in that block | 0 | 4,311 | — |

Paired: **58 won, 50 lost, exact McNemar p = 0.5008** — 8 net cases, and 0.52pp is a third of the
1.64pp the split resolves at. Against its registered bar the arm failed on the accuracy column and
failed on the cost column: 6.1% more prompt tokens is not 68.1% more bill, and the difference is the
block sitting in front of the prefix the endpoint was discounting.

### The reach split: the delta is not where the lever is

A paired test assumes the two arms differ by the lever and by nothing else. A lever with a
*condition* breaks that quietly. The narrowed block renders only on the columns a join reads, and on
359 of dev's 1,532 questions the schema offers none of them — so on those the two arms send the same
prompt, answer the same three calls, and differ by temperature alone. That subset is an A/A control
nobody had to pay for, and it was sitting in the artifact the whole time.

`bench:bird:pair` now reads it, from the per-case token column the artifact already records:

```
  the lever changed what 1173 of 1532 paired question(s) sent:
    reached     1173    757 ->   757  +0.00pp  (43 won, 43 lost, p = 1.0000)
    unchanged    359    236 ->   244  +2.23pp  (15 won,  7 lost, p = 0.1338)
```

Equal prompt tokens on exactly 359 cases, and those 359 are exactly the cases with a zero-column
block — the two sets coincide one for one, and no case the block reached has an unchanged token
count (the smallest increase is 9 tokens a question, the mean 248). So:

- **Where the block acted, it moved nothing.** 757 against 757, 43 wins against 43 losses. Not
  "small": equal.
- **Where it did not act, the pair moved 2.23pp.** Fifteen wins to seven losses on identical prompts.
  That is the run's own displacement, it is larger than the +0.52pp the round was going to adopt, and
  it is consistent with zero (p = 0.1338 on 22 discordant cases, where the standard error is ~5pp).

The +0.52pp is the sum of a null and a control, and the control carried it. Had this round been read
off the accuracy column — which is how every previous prompt lever in this document was read — the
block would have been adopted on a +0.52pp that came entirely from questions it never touched.

The shape transitions say the same thing in the other instrument: `values → match` 47 against
`match → values` 40, `column-count → match` 10 against `match → column-count` 9. A repair shows up as
a one-way transition; this is churn with a 7-case tilt, and the tilt is on the population the reach
split already prices at zero.

Two channels had to be ruled out before that reading was accepted. The chooser ranks by length, and
the block lengthens three cards by different amounts, so `shortest` picked a different source on 67
questions (`metadata+evidence` 317 → 351, `values` 322 → 295). And the diversity audit
(`mixedCandidatePrompts`) is blind to this lever by construction: a block appended to all three
candidates leaves pairwise distinctness untouched, and it reads **0.609** degenerate on both arms to
the digit. Neither channel can produce the split above, because the split is on the population where
the prompts were identical and no chooser could move.

### The price, now in the same report as the delta

`bench:bird:pair` bills both arms through `cacheBill` and `DEFAULT_CACHE_RATE` — the same rate and the
same function the cache report uses — so the number beside a delta is the number the endpoint charged
rather than the number the prompt grew by:

```
  what each call cost, a cached prompt token billed at 0.1x:
    select-mixed-rule                 835 charged of   3137 prompt    2558 cached (81.5%)
    select-mixed-rule-narrow         1404 charged of   3327 prompt    2137 cached (64.2%)
    the second arm costs 68.1% more per call and is +0.52pp more accurate on 1532 paired question(s)
```

The block is paid three times because there are three cards, and it costs more than the sum of the
three because it breaks the cached prefix: 81.5% of the parent's prompt was billed at the cache rate,
64.2% of the narrow arm's was. In prompt tokens — the unit this document has always quoted — the
lever is +6.1%. In the unit the invoice uses it is +68.1%, and no report in this repository could say
so before this round.

### Verdict

**Not adopted, and the family is closed.** The block does not survive being paid per candidate: it
reaches 76.6% of the split, moves exactly zero on the cases it reaches, and the only movement in the
run is the temperature. The single-prompt reading keeps its own verdict unchanged — the narrowed
block bought **+1.50pp** at 738 tokens against 676 on `inline+evidence+samples-wide-link`, on one card
and one call — and what this round adds is where that gain lives: it is a *per-prompt* gain that does
not compose into a pool, because a pool of three already holds three chances to be right and the
marginal candidate the block rescues is the only case it can buy. That is the arithmetic the
registration stated in advance, and it is now measured rather than assumed.

This also answers the composition question the previous section left open — the competitor's
description, examples and refiner in one arm, *with the narrowed block on every candidate*. The
answer is that the block contributes nothing there, so the 3.1pp this repository is short of MAC-SQL
is not in the card. It has to be in the harness: their selector reads their card, their refiner runs
on top of it, and neither of those is a per-candidate sample.

### Where the gap stands after this round

| quantity | value | where it comes from |
|---|---:|---|
| shipped arm, dev, this artifact | **64.82%** | `select-mixed-rule`, 3.00 calls, 835 charged tokens |
| shipped arm, dev, `41947376305` | 63.97% | same arm, earlier run — a **0.85pp** displacement |
| its pool's ceiling | 68.99% | this artifact, re-read for the pair |
| the block on every candidate | 65.34% | `-narrow`, +68.1% a call, not adopted |
| the block on one card | 64.31% | `inline+evidence+samples-wide-link`, 738 tokens, +1.50pp over its parent |
| MAC-SQL, our harness, our model, dev | **67.89%** | 1,040/1,532 |
| ours against MAC-SQL | **−3.1pp** | and −2.6pp of it is pool, not card |

The displacement is worth naming because it moves the headline: the same arm, unchanged, reads
64.82% here and 63.97% on the run this document has been quoting. The gap to MAC-SQL is therefore
3.1pp under the more recent reading and 3.9pp under the older one, and every later comparison is
against this artifact's parent rather than against a number from a different run.

### What changes in the method, not just in the table

1. **Every pair prints its reach before its delta is read.** A lever with a condition has a control
   subset inside its own artifact, and the control moved 4× further than the lever this round. The
   instrument is `reachSplit`, it spends no call, and it now runs by default in `bench:bird:pair`.
2. **A delta is quoted with the population it was measured on.** 58/50 on 1,532 and 43/43 on 1,173 are
   the same artifact and different sentences, and only one of them is about the block.
3. **A cost column is quoted in charged tokens.** Prompt tokens say what was sent; charged tokens say
   what was paid. Every lever that touches the front of the prompt moves the second more than the
   first, and the ordering of the document's cost tables has been wrong by that factor until now.
4. **A null on the reached population retires the mechanism, not the arm.** The block stays in the
   catalogue as the priced ceiling of the value family, on one card, where it is still the cheapest
   +1.50pp in the table — and it stops being a candidate for the pool, which is where the next three
   rounds would otherwise have spent dispatches.

## What the result set did to the recommender: −21.6pp, and the mark it collapsed to

The chart half's cue table has been scored against Text2Vis for several rounds, and it has only ever
measured the question. `recommendChart(question, profiles)` is the shipped entry point, and it ranks
marks by the question **and** the result set's shape. The corpus ships the result set (`Table Data`),
so that second half costs no model call — `bench:text2vis:profile` reads the same 1,985 rows, scores
both halves on the rows whose label has a family, and prices the difference.

Registered before the first dispatch: **top-1 ≥ 45.0%** and **`pie` ≥ 145 hits**, with the cue-only
reading printed beside it as the control.

| reading | cue only | with the result set | delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| top-1 | **549 (37.35%)** | **231 (15.71%)** | **−21.64pp** |
| shortlist | 1,000 (68.03%) | 231 (15.71%) | −52.32pp |
| declined | — | 555 (37.76%) | — |
| missed (a mark that cannot cover the label) | — | 684 (46.53%) | — |
| scored rows | 1,470 of 1,985 (515 unmapped labels) | same | — |

*(Overwritten — see *which Text2Vis number is ours*. Both figures belong to the dispatch above; the cue
table changed afterwards and neither was re-read. Re-read in the round that found the defect they were
627 and **414**, a delta of −13.30pp, and the round that taught the product to count moved the second
to **444** (−12.45pp). The table is kept because the round it records is the one that found the defect,
and a reading that is quietly edited is a reading nobody can audit. It also used to sit between two
rows, which broke the table in two for every renderer: an annotation that destroys the thing it
annotates is the same defect one layer down.)* |
| baseline: always the most frequent family | line 26.60% | — | — |
| baseline: always bar | 24.29% | — | — |

**Both registered lines failed, and the second one failed in the direction nobody registered.** The
reading is not "45.0% was optimistic": the shipped recommender is **21.64pp worse than its own cue
table** on the same rows, and it is worse than *always answering bar* by 8.58pp.

The confusion says what it does instead. Given the result set, it answers `bar` for every question it
does not decline:

| label | n | top-1 | what it answered |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Bar | 357 | 54.06% | bar 193, declined 132, heatmap 21 |
| Line | 391 | **0.00%** | bar 193, declined 140, scatter 49 |
| Area | 137 | **0.00%** | bar 64, scatter 49, declined 23 |
| Pie | 113 | **0.00%** | bar 67, declined 39, heatmap 4 |
| Scatter | 93 | 4.30% | bar 34, declined 32, heatmap 23 |
| Histogram | 90 | **0.00%** | declined 49, bar 30, scatter 7 |
| Boxplot | 89 | 3.37% | declined 35, bar 31, scatter 15 |
| Donut | 69 | **0.00%** | declined 36, bar 33 |
| Stacked Bar | 56 | 42.86% | bar 24, declined 19, scatter 12 |

`pie` hits are **0 of 113**, and 0 of the 69 donuts. The delta by family is one line: **bar +170,
heatmap +2, scatter −26, boxplot −44, area −59, pie −145, line −216**.

That line was published wrong twice before it was published right, and both defects are the same
kind — an instrument printing a number it had not checked. The first version listed one row per
*label* (`bar +142, scatter −26, bar −27, scatter −30, …`, 23 rows) because `perLabel` is keyed by
label and the line is titled by family. Summing by family fixed the repetition and left the
subtraction inside the loop: `cueOf(family)` returns the whole family's cue total, so a family with
eight labels took that total away eight times and the real corpus printed `line −864`. The line above
has one subtraction per family, and the test that pins the arithmetic is two `line` labels where the
cue is right on both and the profile wrong on both — the family's delta is −2, and the version that
ships −4 fails it.

Two mechanisms are consistent with this table, and the artifact cannot separate them yet:

1. **The expected mark was refused by an admission rule.** `recommendChart` returns a `refused` list
   beside its ranking, and 555 rows have *no recommendation at all* — that is the case where the
   profiler could not type the columns or no mark admitted. On a Line label with no parseable date
   column, `line` is admitted only if the profile carries one, and the table then becomes a bar chart
   by default rather than a refusal.
2. **The expected mark was named by a cue that lost to a prior.** The score is `prior + 3` for a cue
   naming the mark first and `+2` otherwise, and priors run 1 to 3 — so a cue that names a mark
   *second* can be cancelled exactly by the gap between two priors, and `PREFERENCE` then decides. If
   bar sits earlier in `PREFERENCE`, bar wins the tie.

The instrument that separates them is already in the artifact's reach: `recommendChart` returns
`refused` with a reason per mark, so a per-family refusal census costs zero model calls and answers
question 1 outright. Until it runs, the honest statement is the one the table supports: **as shipped,
the result set makes the recommendation three times worse than the words alone**, and the failure is
concentrated where the product's own admission rules and prior arithmetic decide.

This is also a correction to how the chart half has been reported for three rounds. `37.35%` was
quoted as the product's number. It is the *cue table's* number; the product's entry point, on the
same rows and with the result set in front of it, reads `15.71%`. Both numbers are now in the table
above, and the next reading has to move the second one.

## Why the chart half was wrong: a census of 1,470 questions, and five levers that had to be separated

`15.71%` was the product's reading with the result set in front of it, against `37.35%` for the cue
table alone. A number that far below its own component is a symptom, and the repairs it admits live
in different files — an admission rule that refuses the mark the label names, a ranking that admits it
and loses, a family no mark covers, a table that will not profile. One "missed 684" cannot choose
between them, so the first deliverable of this round is an instrument that can.

```bash
pnpm bench:text2vis:census --artifact eval/out/text2vis-census.json
```

It classifies every scored row into exactly one of six outcomes and prints, for each refusal, the
admission rule's own sentence; for each loss, the score gap and the cue position; for each shape, the
three counts the rules were applied to; and for each of those, up to three of the questions it holds.
Zero model calls — the corpus ships its tables.

| outcome | rows | share |
|---|---:|---:|
| hit | 231 | 15.71% |
| refused (every mark that could cover the family was ruled out) | 890 | 60.54% |
| outranked (a covering mark was admitted and lost) | 182 | 12.38% |
| uncovered (no mark in this product covers the family) | 3 | 0.20% |
| no profile (the table would not parse) | 164 | 11.16% |

The counters reconcile with `profile.ts` row for row — hits equal top-1, and losses plus uncovered
families plus refusals that were answered by another mark equal missed. The test asserts both, so the
two instruments cannot drift into explaining different corpora.

### The refusals were not what the rule said they were

Grouping the 890 by the shape they were refused against was the whole point, and it produced a fact no
reading had:

| shape | rows | what it means |
|---|---:|---|
| measures **0** | 389 | a table with numbers that has no measure at all |
| category axis + measure, no ordered axis | 350 | the mark exists but the rule demanded an order |
| measures only, no axis | 158 | nothing to group by |
| ordered axis + measure | 18 | admitted for one rule, refused by another |

`measures: 0` on 389 rows is not a corpus limit. `Number('1,234')` is `NaN`, so a revenue column
written with thousands separators typed `nominal`, and every mark that needs a measure was ruled out
before the question was read. **The product was being scored on its parser.**

### Lever 1: a formatted number is a measure (+1.70pp, adopted)

`numericCell` reads the formatting a result set is displayed with — grouped digits, a leading currency
sign, a trailing percent, an accounting negative in parentheses — and refuses what it cannot read
without guessing (a space-grouped number is two words; `1.234,56` needs a decision about which
separator is decimal). The census counts the columns it rescues with the same function.

| reading | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| top-1 | 15.71% (231) | **17.41% (256)** |
| declined | 555 | 437 |
| refused | 890 | 831 |
| rows with a formatted-number column | — | 186 |

### Lever 2: the tie-break (+0.00pp, reverted)

The census said `line: 394 rows, 0 hits` and `area: 138 rows, 0 hits` — 532 rows, 36% of the
population, never once answered. `bar` and `line` both scored their prior of two and `PREFERENCE`
broke the tie for the bar, so a line could only win a question that said "trend". Registered: making
a line the default over an ordered axis should raise top-1 by at least 2.0pp.

Measured: **17.41% → 17.41%, every counter bit-identical across 1,470 rows.** The prior fires on every
row where a line is already admissible, and those are 33 of the 394 — the other 323 are refused before
any ranking happens. The lever was aimed at the wrong term, and it is reverted because the bar was
written before the dispatch.

### Lever 3: a period written as text is a time axis (+0.00pp on hits, kept)

`ISO_DATE` accepted only `2026-01-01`, so a timeline spelled `Dec`, `Q1 2019` or `2019-01` typed
`nominal`, `shape.ordered` was empty, and every line and area over it was refused. The evidence for
"this is time" is the formatting: a **string** written as a period is a period. A number is not —
`[2019, 2020]` stays a measure, because a column of prices in the 2000s is indistinguishable from a
column of years.

*Superseded, and quoted here because a reading that stops being true is worth keeping in the record
that said it: the numeric half was priced two rounds later and reversed. A contiguous run of years read
one year per row is a calendar, and typing it as one is worth +49 hits — see "A year is a year in either
transport" below.*

Refusals 831 → 809 and outranked 216 → 238: twenty-two rows became reachable and none became a hit.
The measure of this lever is reachability, not score.

### Lever 4: honour the mark a question names, and let a line carry a category axis (+0.41pp, kept)

The shape buckets carried their questions on the fourth dispatch, and the questions ended the
argument:

> Based on the given dataset, calculate the percentage contribution of each 'Entity' to the total
> 'Value' and plot these percentages in order of increasing 'Value' **on a line chart**.

The corpus states the mark it wants. This table had no rule that read "line chart" — so a user who
named a chart type was given a bar — and the mark itself was refused, because a line was required to
have an ordered axis, which a category axis sorted by the measure is. Two changes, registered together
against `c8cce6ca` at **+6.0pp**:

1. an `explicit` cue per mark: the mark word beside `chart`, `plot`, `graph` or `diagram`, which keeps
   it off the instruction boilerplate those same prompts carry;
2. a line admitted on any axis with a measure.

| reading | before | after | delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **cue table alone** (shipped `CHART_CUES`) | 37.35% (549) | **40.20% (591)** | **+2.85pp** |
| top-1 with the result set | 17.41% (256) | 17.82% (262) | **+0.41pp** |
| refused | 831 | **597** | **−234** |
| outranked | 216 | **443** | **+227** |

**The registered bar was +6.0pp and the measured delta is +0.41pp: the registration failed.** What it
bought is visible in the other two columns — 234 rows that could not be answered at all are now
ranked, and the cue table gained 2.85pp because a question that names a mark is a request and not a
suggestion. It is kept on those two readings, and the failure is recorded rather than explained away:
the registration assumed the ranking would take the rows the admission freed, and it did not.

### Where the chart half now stands, and what the next lever is

The census after four levers, on the same 1,470 rows:

| outcome | rows | share |
|---|---:|---:|
| hit (the label's family is the answer's *first* claim) | 262 | 17.82% |
| substituted (it is the answer's second claim: a line answering an `area` row) | 1 | 0.07% |
| refused | **568** | **38.64%** |
| outranked | **399** | **27.14%** |
| uncovered | 76 | 5.17% |
| no profile | 164 | 11.16% |

`262 + 1 + 568 + 399 + 76 + 164 = 1,470`, and every earlier table in this chapter is the same
population read with one more lever in place. Two corrections move the last three rows — the shortlist
test and the self-comparison below — and both were found after the levers were measured, which is why
the tables in this chapter quote the numbers their dispatch printed rather than a later revision.

### One row out of 1,470: the census read ahead of the product

The four levers left two instruments one row apart, printed by the same job:

```
census:   hit 263 (17.89%), refused 597, outranked 443, uncovered 3, no profile 164
profile:  +profile top-1 17.82% (262), shortlist 17.89% (263)
```

`263` is the product's **shortlist**, not its top-1. `familiesOfMark('line')` is `['line', 'area']` — a
line is a line and, filled, an area — so a line answering an `area` row covers the label's family
*second*. `profile.ts` counts a top-1 hit only when the covering family is the answer's first claim
(otherwise a bar named by a histogram cue would answer two questions at once), and the census tested
`.includes()`, which is the shortlist test. It called that row a hit.

The row is new: relaxing the line's admission in lever 4 is what first let a line answer an `area`
question over a category axis. The reconciliation test — *"agrees with the profile reading about the
same rows, or it is explaining another corpus"* — had passed for four dispatches because every fixture
it held was an agreeing row. A test that only sees rows where two instruments agree cannot show that
they agree.

The repair is not a tolerance. The census's headline has to **be** the number the product publishes,
so `hit` now means the published first choice and the widened row gets the name of what happened:

```
outcomes: hit | substituted | refused | outranked | uncovered | noProfile
invariant: hit + substituted === shortlist
```

`substituted` says the answer covered the family as its second claim, which is neither a hit (the label
asked for the other picture) nor a loss (nothing outranked the covering mark — it is what answered).
The report prints the sum as the shortlist, so the two files reconcile by an equation instead of by a
claim, and the fixture added for it holds an `area` label over a quarterly table.

The population has moved from "one third reachable" to "two thirds reachable", and the bottleneck has
moved with it: **399 rows are admitted and ranked below something else**, against 182 when the
round began — and 30 of those 182 were the self-comparison described below, so the like-for-like
move is **152 to 399**. The next lever is the ranking, not the card — which is the same place the BIRD half
found its 3.9pp of selection loss, and the same lesson: a pool that contains the answer is only worth
what the chooser takes from it.

`no profile` (164 rows, 11.16%) is the second named bucket and it is not a ranking question at all:
those tables fail `profilesOf` outright, which is a parsing defect with a measurement of its own.

### 44 of the 443 losses were losses to themselves

The corrected census also put a line in the ranking table that cannot be a ranking result:

```
lost histogram to bar: 43 (on preference 43, cue named and lost 43, gaps 0x43)
```

`coveringMarks` had been asked for the *widest* coverage a mark can give, which includes
`bar -> histogram` — a widening the product grants only when a histogram cue named the bar. Asking it
of the table made every histogram row's covering mark the bar that answered it, so the row was read as
a loss with `bar` on both sides: gap 0, decided on preference, by itself.

The table now answers what a mark **is**; the row keeps the cue. A bar that answers a histogram row
after the question named one is `substituted`; one that answers without it is `uncued` — the word that
did not exist when this paragraph was written, and the reason it read `uncovered` for three rounds.
That — as it read then, with histogram rows counted into `uncovered` — plus one row that was a genuine
loss to a boxplot, is the whole 443 -> 399:

| bucket | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| refused | 597 | **568** |
| outranked | 443 | **399** |
| uncovered | 3 | **76** |

What is left is a ranking bucket with one story in it: **355 of the 399 losses are losses to a bar**
(line 199, pie 81, area 64, scatter 11), 253 of them in rows where a cue named the covering mark, and
exactly **one** decided on preference. Bar is second in every cue list the table has, so it accumulates
a point from every cue that fires; that is a scoring property, not a tie-break one, and no
`PREFERENCE` change can touch it. That is the next round's lever, and this is the number it aims at.

### What changes in the method

1. **A reading below its own component is a bug report, not a result.** `15.71%` against `37.35%` said
   the product was worse than one of its parts, and the only honest response was to census the gap
   rather than to tune anything.
2. **A count of refusals is not a diagnosis; the shape and the question are.** `890 refused` became
   three repairs once grouped by `dims/ordered/measures`, and two of those groups reversed the first
   hypothesis: the largest was not an admission rule but a parser.
3. **Three nulls are a finding.** Each of the first three levers was measured alone and moved nothing
   on the score; the fourth moved 234 rows out of "unanswerable". Had they been shipped together on
   their merits, the round would have reported the sum and learned nothing about which term mattered.
4. **An instrument one row ahead of the product is a defect, not a rounding.** `263` against `262` came
   from the census using the shortlist test where the product publishes the top-1 test. The number an
   instrument prints at the top of its report has to be the number the file beside it publishes, or the
   census is explaining a corpus nobody published — and the disagreement appeared exactly in the round
   where a lever created the first row the two tests read differently.
5. **A loss to itself is an instrument defect, and it hides inside a plausible count.** `443 outranked`
   behaved like a bucket: it had gaps, cue positions and preferences to read. Forty-four of those rows
   had the same mark on both sides, and the test that catches it is one line — a covering mark that *is*
   the answer is not a loser. It was missed because the coverage table had been allowed to answer a
   question only the row can answer: what did *this* question call the chart.

## Naming outranks collecting: +3.40pp, and the number was predicted before it shipped

`outranked 399` was the last bucket the census could name but not explain, and the samples it printed
made the mechanism visible in three lines:

```
e.g. line 5 [trend]       < bar 6 [trend matrix]
e.g. pie  5 [share]       < bar 9 [share ranking matrix]
e.g. line 2 []            < bar 9 [share ranking matrix]
```

The first line is the whole defect. The question named a trend, which pays the line three points; it
also said "by … and …", which fires the matrix cue and pays the bar two; and the bar is the *second*
mark of seven of the twelve cues — `trend`, `share`, `matrix`, `ranking`, `distribution`, `progress`,
`stages` — so it collects a point from every phrase the prompt happens to contain, whether or not
any phrase was about a bar. A mark the question named outright lost to a mark it never named.

### The rule, and why it is a key rather than a weight

`recommendChart` now orders by three keys:

```
1. how many cues name the mark first
2. the counted score (a prior plus three or two per cue)
3. the fixed preference order
```

The first key cannot be expressed as a weight. Making one first claim beat three second places takes a
value above six; making it beat *any* number of second places takes no finite value at all, and a
number chosen to be "large enough" is exactly the tuned constant this file's last six chapters have
been removing. A lexicographic key states the rule instead of approximating it, and the score keeps its
old job — it separates two marks that an equal number of cues named first, and it still tells a caller
what the cues paid.

### It was priced before it shipped

The census gained a counterfactual: re-rank the same 1,470 rows under the candidate rule and report
both sides. For this rule the reading was

```
as if a mark a cue names first outranks a mark no cue names first:
  hit 262 -> 312 (converted 106, lost 56)
```

312. The dispatch that shipped the rule read:

| bucket | before | after | delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **hit** (the label's family is the answer's first claim) | 262 (17.82%) | **312 (21.22%)** | **+50 (+3.40pp)** |
| substituted (the answer's second claim) | 1 | 24 | +23 |
| refused | 568 (38.64%) | 568 (38.64%) | 0 |
| outranked | 399 (27.14%) | **326 (22.18%)** | −73 |
| uncovered | 76 (5.17%) | 76 (5.17%) | 0 |
| no profile | 164 (11.16%) | 164 (11.16%) | 0 |

`312` is what the model said, to the row, and the two instruments agree on it: `profile.ts` publishes
`top-1 21.22% (312), shortlist 22.86% (336)`, and the census publishes `hit 312, hit + substituted 336`.

A prediction that can be checked is worth more than a result that cannot. Had the run read 300, the gap
would have been a defect in the model — the same class of finding as the `263` against `262` two
sections above — and the next hour would have gone into the model rather than into the product.

### The cost is in the same table, which is why the model counted it

| pair | rows |
|---|---:|
| line → bar | 93 |
| bar → heatmap | 49 |
| area → bar | 38 |
| pie → bar | 38 |
| bar → pie | 22 |
| line → heatmap | 18 |
| line → pie | 16 |
| pie → heatmap | 16 |

The four `bar →` rows are the price: 71 rows where the label wants a bar and a cue named a pie or a
heatmap first. They are not a defect of the new key — they were already being answered wrongly, only
the other way round — but they are the rows a cue-precision round would have to win back, and the
model priced them before anyone could claim the rule was free.

### The next lever was priced and rejected in the same round

The obvious successor is to stop paying a cue's second mark at all — read `marks: ['pie', 'bar']` as
"a pie, or a bar if a pie cannot be drawn" — so that `share` stops paying a bar two points on every
question that says "percentage". The census priced it:

```
as if a cue pays only the first mark it can admit: hit 312 -> 260 (converted 40, lost 92)
```

**−52 rows.** The rule is not obviously wrong; it is wrong *here*, because when the preferred mark is
refused the fallback is the only mark that can answer, and removing the second-mark payment removes the
signal that says so. A round spent implementing it would have been a round spent reverting it. This is
what a counterfactual is for, and it is the first time in this project that a lever died before it was
written.

### Three ways the instrument was wrong, found by reading its own output

1. **`snippet` cut the wrong end, twice.** The corpus wraps every prompt as instruction block,
   question, output-format spec. The first cut kept the last 160 characters — the spec. The second cut
   the spec off and kept the last 160 of what remained — the sentence introducing the spec. Both printed
   the same three hundred samples. The third version prefers the last sentence that ends in `?`, which
   is what every question in this corpus is, and falls back to cutting the code instruction and then to
   the tail.
2. **`unreadNumerals` named 273 tables as parser defects, and its own samples said otherwise.** The
   first version asked for a cell with a digit and no letter; the corpus answered with `71+`, `18-25`
   and `2018*` — age bands and footnote-marked years, typed as categories and correctly so. The
   requirement is now a decimal shape (`\d`, a separator, `\d`), and the remaining question is honest:
   **273 of the 1,470 rows carry no measure at all**, and no formatting repair would give them one.
3. **A counterfactual of a shipped rule measures nothing.** The model that priced this round's lever now
   re-ranks an already re-ranked list and returns zero conversions; it was re-aimed at the next
   candidate in the same commit that shipped the rule, which is the only way the instrument stays one
   step ahead of the product.

### What the denominator actually is

`1,470` was doing two jobs. Of those rows:

| class | rows |
|---|---:|
| the table carries no measure at all | 273 |
| the family is one no mark in the contract draws (violin, word cloud, …) | 76 |
| carries a measure and a mark that could draw it | **≈ 1,121** |

312 of 1,121 is **27.8%**. Both numbers are true and they answer different questions; the reading this
project publishes stays `21.22% of the labelled rows that carry a table`, because a denominator chosen
after the fact is how a benchmark stops being one. The number that matters for planning is the 27.8%:
the remaining 809 rows are where a lever can still land.

### The instrument was buying a benchmark it could not move

`tools/ci-scope.mjs` measured every push that was not Markdown or a test, which meant a census commit
re-priced thirteen BIRD arms over 496 questions and three live passes over 210 cases — about 7,000
completions to re-time a chart reading that `.github/workflows/text2vis-rule.yml` had already taken on
the same push, without a model call and without a key. The rule has a third class now: `eval/text2vis/`
is a leaf, its sources import the chart package and each other and nothing imports them back (checked,
not assumed), and `eval/bird/` — the harness that spends the calls — is not covered. A push that also
touches the product still measures.

### What changes in the method

1. **A rule that says "naming is a request" has to be a key, not a weight.** The previous round made a
   named mark win a tie; this round made naming outrank collecting. The first was a comparator term
   worth three points and it could not do the job, because the competing term is unbounded.
2. **A lever can be priced before it is written, and the price can be a refusal.** 106 rows won against
   56 lost was a ship; 40 against 92 was a rejection. Neither number required the code to exist.
3. **An instrument's own samples are evidence about the instrument.** `71+` and `18-25` were the corpus
   telling this round that its definition of "a number nothing read" was wrong. The definition changed;
   the count did not.
4. **Every bucket that is used as a target has to be explained row by row first.** `outranked 399` was
   one number for two rounds; the three samples that took it apart cost one dispatch and redirected the
   next two.
5. **Cost is a line in the report.** A chart-side dispatch was paying for a SQL benchmark on every push
   for two rounds, and no gate would ever have caught it: `quality gates` was green, and the money was
   in a job that did not need to run.

## One cue decided 223 questions and was right about one: the reading that made two readings necessary

The previous round's cost table named three rows it could not explain: `bar → pie 22`, `bar → heatmap
49`, `line → heatmap 18`. This round asked which *cue* produced them, and the answer required an
instrument the project did not have: a top-1 share is an average over twelve rules, and the corpus's
weight sits on three of them, so the number that is published cannot say which phrase is wrong.

`cuePrecision` scores each cue on the rows where it fired **first** — a cue that fired second decided
nothing — and splits its loss in two. `hits` is the cue naming the right picture; `inside` is the cue
naming the right family in the wrong position. The gap between them is what a reorder could recover;
the gap to `leads` is what only a narrower phrase could. It costs no model call, because the corpus
ships the question and the label.

| cue | rows decided | first mark | hit | family covered |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `share` | 507 | pie | 28.01% (142) | 64.89% |
| `trend` | 381 | line | 70.60% (269) | 86.61% |
| `matrix` | 223 | heatmap | **0.45% (1)** | 30.49% |
| `distribution` | 137 | boxplot | 23.36% (32) | 50.36% |
| `ranking` | 116 | bar | 42.24% (49) | 42.24% |
| `explicit` | 73 | bar | 100.00% (73) | 100.00% |
| `correlation` | 33 | scatter | 75.76% (25) | 87.88% |

Two rows carry the round. `matrix` decides 223 questions — 15% of the scored corpus — and is right
about one, because its pattern was `\bby\b[\s\S]*\band\b`: unbounded in both directions, so
"average revenue by region. Generate matplotlib code and label the axes" carried a `by` and, two
sentences later, an `and`. `share` is not wrong about the family (64.89%) and is wrong about the order
