as a hit, and the reading would go up by 32 rows while the product drew nothing it had not drawn
before. That is scoreboard, not capability, so **the derivation of `scatter` is retired**, and this
table is the reason.

The second retirement is the pie cap. Five Donut rows and one Pie row are refused for carrying 16 to
20 slices against a limit of 12, and folding them to *top 11 plus Other* is a standard picture. The
corpus prices the alternative: lifting the cap changes **23 rows**, because every question that says
"percentage" then prefers a pie — 21 of them labelled Line, Area or Stacked Bar. Product top-1 falls
689 → 678 on the shortlist test, shipped rises 934 → 938 on the same. Four rows on the shipped column
for eleven on the product's own is not a trade this project takes, so the cap stays an admission rule.

What is left of the whole 109-row bill, measured rather than imagined: **candlestick 3 rows**, where a
table holds four numbers per row and no date, and the row's own order is the axis. Nothing else in the
table is a derivation; everything else is a table that does not hold the picture the question named.

### `limit` is a limit on the picture, and a matrix has columns

The third defect is in the library, and no label can see it. `toChartIR`'s `limit` sliced **rows**:

```ts
toChartIR('Revenue by region and quarter', grid, { limit: 4 });
// before: 4 cells, so the second column is half drawn
// after:  one whole column (3 cells), because a cell missing to the limit is
//         indistinguishable from a cell missing from the query
```

A row limit is a limit on a picture when the picture is a sequence: cut a line at row 500 and you get
a shorter line. A matrix is not a sequence. Cutting it inside a column leaves a lane that reads as
missing data, and "this cell has no value" is the one reading a heatmap exists to give. The unit is
therefore the column — whole ones kept in the order they first appear, the first that does not fit
dropped rather than started — and the rows keep the order they arrived in, because the limit is about
how much of the matrix is drawn and not about how it is read.

`matrixFieldOf` decides what a matrix is from the **encoding**, not from the mark's name: neither axis
may be a measure. The first version asked for `nominal` twice, and the corpus's heatmaps put `quarter`
and `year` on the second axis, so every one of them would have kept being cut inside a column — the
defect was found by the test written to prevent it, on its first run. A limit below one column keeps
no column, and that is a refusal (`NL2C_E_INVALID_INPUT`) naming the column and both numbers, not an
empty chart.

The default path is untouched: `limit` defaults to 5,000 and no table in this corpus is that tall, so
the shipped reading does not move. The fix is verified where it lives — `wholeColumns` on a five-cell
grid, and three `toChartIR` cases: a heatmap at a limit of four, at six, and a bar at two, which keeps
the row limit it always had.

## The candlestick's axis was never a calendar

The refusal bill that closed the last round priced every remaining debt at its ceiling, and exactly
one family came out honest: `candlestick`, 3 rows, "a derivation could win: at most 3". Those three
rows are a week written `Day 1 … Day 7`, four numbers per row, one row per period. The profiler types
that column `nominal` — `Day 7` is not a date, and reading it as one would be a fiction — so the mark
was refused for a missing date axis, and the table drew a line or a bar instead.

A candlestick does not read a calendar. It reads **a sequence**: one row per period, four numbers, and
the order the rows arrive in. A date column is one spelling of that claim; a label column with as many
distinct values as there are rows is the other. `Shape.sequence` is that second spelling, and it is
deliberately narrow: one axis column only (two dimensions state a grid, not a sequence) and every
value distinct (a repeated label describes two series interleaved in one column of candles). It also
requires the caller to state the row count, because twelve periods and twelve thousand sales profile
the same, and "one value per row" is a claim about the rows.

```ts
// before: a candlestick on `Day 1 … Day 7` was refused before the question was read
shape.measures.length >= 4 && shape.ordered.length >= 1
// after: an axis that orders the rows, which a date is one spelling of and a label per row another
shape.measures.length >= 4 && (shape.ordered.length >= 1 || shape.sequence !== undefined)
```

The shipped reading pays for it in full: **807 → 810**, exactly the bill's three rows, all three drawn
as the model named them. `not-admitted` falls 109 → 106, the rows the table answers 142 → 139, and
`decided` does not move at all.

The rule arm cannot see the change, and that is worth stating rather than hiding: `profileAnswer`
prices the product from profiles alone — no row count — so its top-1 stays 614 with the same shortlist
and the same 28 declines. An instrument that reads shape without rows cannot see a rule about rows.
The floor is therefore registered on `shipped`, the number a caller receives, and the obligation this
creates is written down: whoever teaches `profileAnswer` to carry the row count will move eight rows
(two gained, two lost, four drawn differently) and will need to re-register this floor on the answers,
not on the count.

Eight rows in all answered differently, and the four that gained or lost cancel: two `Bar` tables now
draw candles because their question named the OHLC cue, and the scoreboard reads them as a wash. That
is the trade the bill predicted, and the reason the bill is what decides which derivations are worth
building — a capability that gains three and costs three is still right to build when the three it
gains are the three the question asked for, and wrong when it is a renaming.

## Ninety rows with no picture: what a histogram is, when the grammar has no word for it

The refusal bill closed the last round with one family it could not price: `histogram`, 90 rows,
"nothing: the label never asked for it" for eight of the sixteen other families and a *gap in the
contract* for this one. The census had been saying the same thing in a different column for four
rounds — `histogram` was on its "labels no mark can lead with" list, beside `area` and `violin`.

That list was wrong in one word. A histogram is not a mark this grammar lacks; it is **a bar with the
measure binned**, which is what the corpus's own reference code does:

```python
plt.hist(all_values, bins=20)     # the label says "create a histogram with bins of width 20%"
```

ECharts has no histogram series either — you bin the data and draw bars. So the capability was never a
new mark. It is a **data rewrite**, the same class of transformation as the melt in `melt.ts`: the
numbers are pooled, counted into equal-width bins, and the counts become the rows. Nothing downstream
learns an aggregate, and the contract does not change.

The 90 rows say why it matters. None of them could be reached: `familiesOfMark('bar', 'histogram')`
widened the bar to answer for the family, but the hit test reads the *first* family, so a bar answer
scored as a bar — 0.00% for four rounds with the widening in place. And the pictures were not
histograms either: `Characteristic | 2016 | 2017` was drawn as a grouped bar of the period columns when
the question asked for the distribution of all the cells together.

### What gets pooled, and how many bins

| decision | rule | why |
|---|---|---|
| which columns | every `quantitative` column | a measure is a measure; a label column contributes nothing |
| when none is typed that way | columns that hold numbers and are not `temporal` | a column of one repeated number is typed `ordinal`, and three sevens still have a distribution |
| never pooled | `temporal` columns | the years are the axis the table runs along, not a distribution of anything |
| how many bins | Sturges — `ceil(log2 n) + 1` — clamped to `[5, 12]` and to the distinct values | four bins hide the shape; twelve is where this product's own tick-crowding logic starts; two values are not five bins with three empty ones |
| the last bin | closed at both ends | the maximum has to land in a bin, and `floor` of the top edge is one past the last one |
| a table wide in time | the melt's single `value` column | five entities over three years is fifteen numbers written sideways |

The reading is gated on the **question**: a table of five numbers has as many readings as it has marks,
and the pooled distribution is only the one that was asked for in words.

### The family claim had to move with the picture

`familiesOfMark('bar', 'histogram')` was `['bar', 'histogram']`. That was the honest order while a bar
on a histogram question was a grouped bar of the columns — the mark answered for the family in the
shortlist and not in the chart. Now the bars are over the bins, so the list is `['histogram', 'bar']`,
and the two changes had to ship together: the ordering alone would have been a claim about a picture
that did not exist, and the reading alone would have changed the picture without changing the score.

The same fact reached one more reader, and finding it was the round's second defect. `markAnswer` —
the function every scorer uses to say what a model's answer covers — did not read the question:

```ts
// before: a bar answer to a histogram question scored as a bar
familiesOfMark(choice)
// after: the same chart the caller receives, scored as the chart it is
familiesOfMark(choice, familyCue(cueKinds(asked)))
```

The 11-mark roster has no `histogram` in it, so `bar` is the only answer a model can give to a
histogram question. Scoring it as wrong was a defect of the instrument, not a reading of the product.
`route.ts` had the same defect in its own construction (`families: [left]`), which is why the router's
disagreement count fell from 248 to 236 without a single answer changing.

### The readings

| reading | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| `profile` top-1 / shortlist / declined | 614 / 718 / 28 | **664 / 744 / 27** |
| `deepseek-chat\|mark` / `deepseek-reasoner\|mark` | 861 / 875 | **889 / 892** |
| arbitration `product` / `model-holds` / ceiling | 614 / 863 / 970 | **664 / 891 / 1,020** |
| ship `decided` / `shipped` | 863 / 810 | **891 / 843** |
| duel `chat` / `reasoner` / `cue-led` (shipped) | 810 / 821 / 831 | **843 / 849 / 865** |
| prior `chat` / `cue-gate` / `table-agrees` | 810 / 818 / 816 | **843 / 851 / 847** |
| cost | — | **¥0** (answers already on disk) |

Two numbers in that table are worth reading twice.

**The ceiling rose by 50, and by all 50 at once.** The union of the two answers is what could be
recovered with the key in hand, and it rose by the full size of the capability — because the rows it
wins are rows *neither* system answered before. The rule path had no histogram mark and the model had
no histogram word in its roster. These were rows where agreeing could only ever mean agreeing on a
wrong answer.

**The strong-against-weak gap on the mark scale collapsed from 14 rows to 3**, while the label scale
kept its 61. The chat arm gained 28 histogram rows and the reasoning arm 17: on these questions the
thinking arm talks itself into `boxplot` or `line`, both of which are refused or drawn as something
else, while the plain answer `bar` is exactly what the reading needs. That is not noise and it is not a
regression — it is the first measurement in this repository where deliberation *costs* rows, and it
sharpens the claim the two scales exist to make: deliberation buys vocabulary, and this family is
answered with a word the vocabulary already had.

## The widening that looked free cost sixteen rows, and the instrument was mine

The last round closed with 50 of the corpus's 90 histogram rows recovered and 40 still unreachable.
All 40 are written in the word `distribution` rather than `histogram`, and the obvious next move is to
read that word as the same instruction. It is not obvious, but it looked *measurable*: an offline probe
priced the widening at **+31 top-1** on 1,470 scored rows, and the price it named — 7 pies — looked like
change.

The shipped instrument said otherwise.

| reading | before | word alone | gated on one measure |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `top1` | 664 | — | **648** |
| `shortlist` | 744 | — | 778 |
| `declined` | 27 | — | 23 |

The gate was the one the probe said was the discriminator: a table with exactly one measure column has
one distribution in it, and a table with two has two — which is why the box plots live on the other
side of it (41 of the corpus's 47 box-plot hits are tables with two or more measures). It was the right
*shape* of idea on the right *discriminator*, and it was still a regression. The row-level diff says
where:

| rows | what happened |
|---:|---|
| +10 | a histogram-labelled `distribution` question, answered `boxplot`, now answered with bins |
| −13 | a bar-labelled `distribution` question the product already answered `bar` — the picture is the same bar, but the *first* family became `histogram` |
| −12 | a pie the corpus labelled `distribution` and the product answered correctly, which the bins reading now pre-empts |
| −1 | a box plot |

### Two blind spots in my own probe, both of the same kind

**It counted the shortlist and called it top-1.** `family in families` is the rule the *shortlist* uses;
top-1 reads `families[0]`. The 13 bar rows were hits before the change and hits after it — the product
answered `bar` both times — and the probe booked them as gains because the families now also contained
`bar`. A widening that changes only the ordering of the family claim is a widening that changes the
score, and the probe could not see it.

**It assumed a rewrite that returns first would return second.** `histogramReading` runs before every
other reading in `toChartIR`, by design: the rows it produces are the picture's, not the table's. The
probe priced the 12 pie rows as if the share reading still had a say. It does not — a question about the
distribution of percentages is a pie to the corpus and a histogram to this reading, and the reading
wins because it is asked first.

Neither blind spot is exotic. Both are the same mistake the repository keeps paying for: **a number has
to be taken from the path that ships**, not from a re-implementation of the path that ships. The
correct version of the probe is the one the gate already runs, and the answer it gave is *do not ship
this*.

The refusal is now a test, with the arithmetic in it:

```ts
it('does not infer a histogram from the word distribution, even over a one-measure table', () => {
  expect(histogramReading('Analyze the distribution of delivery times and identify any outliers', labelled))
    .toBeUndefined();
  expect(toChartIR('Analyze the distribution of delivery times and identify any outliers', labelled).mark)
    .toBe('boxplot');
});
```

### The census caught a real bug on the way past

Running the census after the reverted gate produced a sentence no reading had ever printed:

```
census report: the product sweep reads 661 hits for the shipped table and the census reads 664,
so one of the two is not the product
```

Three rows are both a histogram question and a table wide in time. The product bins them — `toChartIR`
takes the bins first, then the melt — and the *sweep* asked the melt first, so the control candidate
claimed 661 against the classifier's 664. The identity that compares the two is the only reason this
was visible at all; nothing else in the repository reads both numbers.

The repair is an ordering, five lines up:

```ts
// before: the melt was asked first, so a row that is both a histogram and a wide table was a line
const lead = wide !== undefined ? fixedLead : histogramReading(...) ? bins : ranked;
// after: the product's order, which is bins, then melt, then the ranking
const lead = histogramReading(row.prompt, typed, set.columns, candidate.cues) !== undefined
  ? familiesOfMark('bar', 'histogram')
  : wide !== undefined ? familiesOfMark('line') : ranked;
```

and a unit test pins the row the identity stood on: a histogram question over `Country, 2019, 2020,
2021` is a hit, and the control must reproduce the classifier's count on it.

The class of defect is worth naming: the census prices fourteen cue-table ablations *through* a second
code path, so any disagreement between the two is either the sweep lying about a candidate or the
classifier lying about the product. With three rows of the 1,470 lying, every delta in the ablation
table was off by up to three — small enough to read as noise, which is exactly how a broken instrument
survives.

## A 429 is one endpoint's fact, and six callers retrying in lockstep repeat it

The Zhipu key was refilled and the 429s were not a balance problem: a benchmark arm at concurrency 6
refused a burst that the same key answers serially. The provider retried correctly — `429`, `500`,
`502`, `503`, `504`, honouring `Retry-After`, reading the vendor's own body to tell a quota from a
concurrency limit — with one property that a busy endpoint punishes:

```ts
// every caller computed the same delay from the same attempt number
await sleep(retryDelayMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1));
```

Six calls refused in the same instant wait the same 500 ms and arrive together, and the second attempt
meets the limit the first one did. The provider now draws a spread:

```ts
const backoff = (attempt: number): number =>
  retryDelayMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1) * (1 - jitter * random());
```

`retryJitter` is 0.5 by default, so the wait is drawn from `[0.5d, d]` — never earlier than the backoff
promised, never in lockstep — and it is drawn from an injected source, so the test can state the delay
it asserts:

| draw | wait at `retryDelayMs: 100` |
|---|---|
| `0` (the latest arrival) | 100 ms |
| `1` (the earliest) | 50 ms |
| `retryJitter: 0` | 100 ms, then 200 ms — the old timing, exactly |

`Retry-After` is never spread. There the endpoint has stated its own window, and arriving early inside
it is the same lockstep one level down.

### Gates

|---|---|
| `tsc --noEmit` | clean |
| `vitest` with real PostgreSQL and MariaDB | 5,928 passed / 0 skipped (194 files) |
| `packages/ai` | 85 cases, including the spread and the retry that keeps the old timing |
| `eval/bill.ts` branch coverage | 86.2% → 95.8% — three cases: an armless BIRD row, a line with reasoning and cached tokens, a bill with no rows to name |
| census identity | 664 = 664, after three rounds of 661 against 664 |
| census sweep floor | 4 rows recorded; 10 self-test cases, `--census --require` exit 0 |
| `packages/chart` coverage | 100 / 100 / 100 / 100 |
| cost | **¥0** |

## A guard that was computed, asserted, and never printed — and the change it caught on its first run

`ProductVariant.split` has been in the census since the sweep learned to price cue tables: two disjoint
halves of the scored population, fixed before the reading, so that a candidate chosen for winning cannot
also be chosen for fitting. `assertCensusReport` refuses a split that does not add up. The calendar
ablation next door prints its halves — `halves 53/4 and 59/3` — and the thirty-four-table sweep printed
only the total, so the guard existed and no reader ever saw it.

That is the shape of an instrument that does not work: the number was computed, asserted, and withheld,
and every `+7` in the table arrived as a `+7`.

The table now prints the two halves as deltas against the control, and says the word `fitted` when they
disagree in sign:

| table | `hit` | families | halves | |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| `distribution-wide` | 671 | boxplot +17, bar −6, line −2, scatter −2 | **+3 / +4** | consistent |
| `progress-bar-first` | 665 | bar +1 | 0 / +1 | consistent |
| `no-share` | 665 | bar +59, line +16, boxplot +4, funnel +1, pie −79 | **+8 / −7** | fitted |
| `no-ranking` | 669 | pie +39, line +25, boxplot +6, scatter +1, candlestick +1, bar −67 | **+8 / −3** | fitted |

`no-ranking` is the reason to print it. Removing the ranking stage reads **669**, five rows *above* the
shipped table and the highest number on the board — and it is `+8 / −3`: eight rows won on one half of
the corpus and three lost on the other. A reader shown the total has to be told that; a reader shown the
halves has been told it.

### The first reading of this table did not reproduce, and the reason is the table's shape

The two fitted rows above were first written down as `671` and `677`, with halves `+8 / −8` and
`+10 / −4`, in a draft taken while `distribution-wide` was applied to the shipped table. The widening was
then reverted on the ensemble's evidence, and the draft kept its numbers: a re-run of the same instrument
on the tree the draft describes prints **665** and **669** on halves `+8 / −7` and `+8 / −3`, and the
family columns move with them (`no-share` gains a funnel row, `no-ranking` a scatter and a candlestick
row). Every number in the table is priced *against the shipped table*, so reverting one candidate moves
thirty-three totals at once, and a total quoted from the tree before the revert is a sentence about a
tree nobody can check out.

This is the second defect of the same family as the guard itself, and it is worth naming precisely:
the guard was computed and never printed, and this table was printed and never re-taken. Both are
readings that outlive the state they were taken in. The fix is not discipline — the sweep now writes
`eval/out/text2vis-census.json`, `eval/text2vis/baseline.json` records the shipped total, the two gap
counts and the four rows a decision is read off, and `node tools/check-text2vis-baseline.mjs --census --require` refuses a
run whose totals or halves moved:

```
TEXT2VIS CENSUS: the shipped table reads 664 of 1470, at its floor
TEXT2VIS CENSUS: `uncued` reads 40
TEXT2VIS CENSUS: `uncovered` reads 8
TEXT2VIS CENSUS: `distribution-wide` reads 671 (3/4)
TEXT2VIS CENSUS: `no-share` reads 665 (8/-7), fitted
TEXT2VIS CENSUS: `no-ranking` reads 669 (8/-3), fitted
TEXT2VIS CENSUS: `no-histogram` reads 614 (-27/-23)
```

A move is refused with both numbers and the instruction, because the correct response to a moved row is
to re-take it on purpose and raise the floor in the commit that earns it — the same rule the profile and
the render halves already live under. The gate has ten self-test cases, and the one that matters is the
one that is easiest to miss: a total that stands still while its halves trade rows. That is a change the
old table could not have shown at all.

### The +7 that survived the guard and died on the ensemble

`distribution-wide` is the other half of the story. It was the first candidate in this table to clear
both checks: **671** against 664 on the rule arm, and `+3 / +4` — the halves agree, so the gain is not a
property of which rows were drawn.

It was shipped, on that evidence, and then measured again:

| reading | before | widened | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| rule arm `top-1` | 664 | **671** | **+7** |
| `ceiling` (union of the two arms) | 1,020 | **1,014** | **−6** |
| `shipped` (the path the product takes) | 843 | **841** | **−2** |

Same artifact, same rows, one pattern's width. The rule arm gained seven rows and the union of the two
arms *lost* six, which can only happen one way: **the rows a rule wins are mostly rows the model already
had, and the rows a rule loses are rows only the rule held.** A cue change is therefore not priced on the
rule arm, and the widening is reverted — kept as a candidate whose note now carries all three numbers.

The criterion this round pre-registers, and the reason the revert is not a judgement call:

1. **The rule arm is not the product.** The product ships through an arbitration that scores the model's
   recorded answers under the same cue table, so a cue that renames the family a mark claims moves both
   arms at once.
2. **`ceiling` is the honest upper bound and it is a free check.** A change that lowers the union of the
   two answers cannot be a change that helps the ensemble, whatever it does to one arm.
3. **`shipped` is the only number that is about the product**, and it is the last gate, not the first.

### Two other things that were measured and closed

**The 147 rows no mark can lead with are not a capability gap.** 138 of them are labelled `Area Chart`
and 9 `Violin Plot`, and an area chart is a line with the region filled. Two facts settle it: **2 of the
138 area rows name "area" in the question**, so no width of any cue would reach them, and 80 of the 138
is already `substituted` — drawn as a line, which is the covering mark. The corpus is stating an
aesthetic preference, not a picture this grammar cannot draw. A new mark would have to be *inferred*
from the same table and the same question, which is the inference this repository measured and refused
in the previous round.

**`binned 0` is not a counting bug.** The outcome exists for the rows whose label the bins reading
rewrites away, and it reads zero because every row the reading takes is labelled `histogram`: 50 binned,
50 hits. The counter would be a bug if it were reporting a branch nobody reaches, so the branch is
asserted by a unit test that classifies a histogram question over a pie-labelled row instead.

| halved sweep | 34 tables, 2 fitted (`no-share`, `no-ranking`) |
| `packages/chart` coverage | 100 / 100 / 100 / 100 |
| cost | **¥0** |

## Forty rows were a missing word, and the census called them a missing mark

The histogram reading answers 50 of the corpus's 90 histogram rows, and the remaining 40 have been
described in every plan since as "uncovered" — the outcome that means *no mark in this contract covers
this family*. That sentence was wrong, and the census was the thing saying it.

A probe over the 40 rows (`eval/text2vis/misses.mts Histogram`, ¥0) prints them with their outcome and their
words. Every one of the 40 comes back `uncovered`, and one of them reads:

> "Given the dataset of daily trading volumes in millions of shares, determine whether the distribution
> is skewed … identify any outliers using both the Z-score method … and the interquartile range (IQR)
> method."

The product answers that row — with a bar, or with a boxplot — and the corpus calls it a histogram. The
missing thing is the word *histogram*, which the question never says and which the cue table therefore
never fires. That is a **trigger** gap, and `uncovered` is the outcome for a **capability** gap: violin
is the only family no mark leads with whatever the question says.

So the vocabulary gains one word. `cueReachOf(family)` asks `familiesOfMark` over every cue the shipped
table can fire and returns the mark that would lead with the family, plus the cue that does it — the
pair is `bar` + `histogram`, derived rather than named, so a second cue-conditional widening lands in
the same place without a second edit. A row whose family is reachable that way but which never claimed
it is `uncued`; a row whose family is reachable by nothing stays `uncovered`:

| outcome | before | after | what it now means |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `uncovered` | 48 | **8** | no mark leads with this family under any cue — violin, 8 of its 9 rows |
| `uncued` | — | **40** | the family is drawable and this question never named it |
| `hit` | 664 | 664 | unchanged: the split relabels, it does not re-rank |

The number that changes is the one a plan is written from. "40 rows uncovered" reads as a capability to
build; "40 rows uncued" reads as a cue to widen — and the widening that would close them (`distribution`
as a histogram trigger) was measured three rounds ago at **−16** on the same instrument, because it
steals thirteen bars and twelve pies whose questions also say "distribution". The two readings are the
same 40 rows; only one of them tells you what to do next, and it is the one that names the gap correctly.

Tests: the pair is pinned (`cueReachOf('histogram')` → `bar`/`histogram`, `cueReachOf('violin')` →
nothing), the row is pinned (a one-measure histogram question with no cue is `uncued`, carrying the pair),
and the identity that a reader would otherwise re-derive by hand is pinned too — `outranked + uncovered +
uncued + declined === missed`, and `renderable === hit + substituted + refused + outranked + uncued +
uncovered`.

| gate | result |
|---|---|
| `tsc --noEmit` | clean |
| `test/text2vis-census.test.ts` | 117 passed |
| census | 664 hit, **uncued 40**, **uncovered 8**, identity 664 = 664 |
| cost | **¥0** |

## The +7 that the ensemble refused, measured again on a branch so master never carried it

`distribution-wide` — the `distribution` cue widened to the words boxplot questions are written in
("IQR", "interquartile", "outlier", "z-score", "standard deviation", "skew") — has been the only
candidate in the sweep to clear both the rule arm and the two halves: **671** against 664, halves
`+3 / +4`. It was priced on the ensemble once, refused, and kept as a candidate. That reading has now
been re-taken end to end, because a number nobody can re-run is a number a reader has to trust.

The mechanics matter more than the arithmetic. The widening needs the shipped cue table changed, so a
commit carrying it would have put a refused candidate on `master` for the length of a dispatch. Instead
the tree was pushed to a throwaway branch (`probe/distribution-wide`, one commit over master, deleted
after the reading) and `text2vis-llm` was dispatched against it. Same corpus, same answer store — 1,470
cache hits, **¥0** — and the two arms that price the change:

| reading | floor | widened | verdict |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| model arm `deepseek-chat\|mark` | 889 | 889 | unchanged: the answers are the same rows |
| model arm `deepseek-reasoner\|mark` | 892 | 892 | unchanged |
| **`ceiling`** (union of the two answers) | **1,020** | **1,014** | **−6, below the floor** |
| product (rule path) | 664 | 671 | +7, and the reason the run is red |

The gate refused it in the two places that matter, with the sentences it was built to say:

```
TEXT2VIS ARBITRATION: the ceiling fell to 1014 from the recorded 1020; the union is a property of
  the two answers, not of a policy
TEXT2VIS ARBITRATION: the product baseline reads 671 and the floor records 664; the rule path is
  deterministic, so this is a change to the product and not a re-sample
```

**A ceiling is an upper bound on every policy**, so `shipped` cannot rise while it falls: the widened
tree gives up six rows that *either* system used to get right, and buys seven that only the rule arm
gets right — which is the same asymmetry the round that reverted it described, now with a receipt
(run `44847630022`). The candidate stays a candidate, its note carries all three numbers, and the
criterion it had to clear (ceiling ≥ 1,020 **and** shipped ≥ 843) is recorded next to it.

The cost of the change is also on the record now: the widening is 152 bytes of regular expression, and
`packages/chart` reads **41,078 B gzip against a 41,000 B budget** — a change that fails two gates
before it fails a third.

### What the ranking cue actually does, row by row

`no-ranking` reads 669 against 664 and `+8 / −3`, so the guard calls it fitted and the total says
nothing. A probe (`eval/text2vis/ranking-flips.mts no-ranking`) prints the rows that move:

| direction | rows | what moved |
|---|---:|---|
| lost by removing the cue | 98 | every one of them a **bar** the corpus drew as pie (55), line (21), boxplot (18), candlestick (3) |
| won by removing the cue | 76 | the corpus's own family back: pie (41), line (26), boxplot (6), scatter (2), candlestick (1) |

So `ranking` is not a ranking reading at all: it is a **bar-for-superlatives default**. Every "which
country had the highest…" question becomes a bar, which is right 98 times and wrong 76, and the net +22
is why removing it looks like a gain until the halves disagree. The two obvious narrowings are already
on the board and both lose: `share-ranked` (a share word plus a ranking word inside one clause) reads
657, and moving `ranking` in front of `share` reads 664 exactly — no row changes.

The row-level reading suggests the narrowing the sweep has not priced: 39 of the 98 losses are rows
whose superlative is over **time** ("in which year did Italy experience the highest percentage
increase"), answered `bar` where the corpus drew a line or a boxplot. A `ranking` that does not fire
when the only axis is temporal would keep the 98 category superlatives and hand those 39 rows to the
trend and distribution cues. That is a shape condition on a cue rather than a new pattern, it costs ¥0
to price in the sweep, and it is the next candidate this table should carry.

## Which leaderboards this repository is on, and which it is not

A number without its leaderboard is a number nobody can place. This repository has published
readings on two corpora and has been asked, every round, where it stands on five more. The honest
answer is a table with two kinds of row, and until this round that table existed only as paragraphs
spread across this file — which is how "we run BIRD and Text2Vis" and "we cover Text2SQL and Text2Viz"
came to be written as if they were the same sentence.

`eval/benchmarks.ts` holds the table as data. `pnpm bench:coverage` resolves every citation and
refuses: a `measured` row whose number the repository cannot find, an `absent` row with no reason a
reader can act on, and a missing row for a leaderboard the plan names.

| leaderboard | corpus | metrics | status | number |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WikiSQL (test) | 80,654 question/table pairs, single-table | EX | **absent** | — |
| Spider 1.0 dev | 1,034 questions, 20 databases | EM, EX | **absent** | — |
| BIRD Mini-Dev | 498 questions, 11 databases | EX | measured | 56.0 (floor) |
| BIRD dev | 1,532 scored questions | EX | measured | 62.5 (floor) |
| BIRD dev | the same questions | R-VES | **partial** | 56.63 over 600 of 1,532 questions, floor 57.96 |
| Text2Vis | 1,470 scored rows | top-1 | measured | 664 |
| Text2Vis | the same rows | render validity | measured | 1,418 figures |
| nvBench 2.0 | 7,878 queries / 24,076 visualizations | F1@3, F1@5 | **absent** | — |
| VisCodeBench | 2,672 samples (843 / 805 / 1,024) | seven, incl. displayed-data similarity | **absent** | — |

Four of nine carry a number over the denominator their leaderboard reports, and two of those four are
counts rather than accuracies. A fifth — R-VES — carries a number over 600 of its leaderboard's 1,532
questions, which is a real reading and not that row, so the table states the denominator rather than
letting the reader assume one. The other four are not a scandal; they are a to-do list with prices,
which is the only kind of to-do list this document has ever been able to act on.

Two things about the `number` column, both learned by watching it be misquoted. A printed line now
carries the kind of number it printed — `= 62.5 (floor)`, `= 664 (count)`, `= 56.63 (600 of 1532)` —
because a floor is the minimum a rerun may land on, a count is not a percentage, and a rate over a
subset is not a rate over the split. And `BIRD dev` cites the floor (62.5), not the run: the
published reading on that split is **62.34%** in run `41296610389`, and the floor sits 0.16pp *above*
it because the floor was set from an earlier 63.0% reading of the same arm. The gate compares a rerun
against `floor − tolerance`, where the tolerance is no longer one constant: 4pp was measured at
n=239, and at 1,532 questions the same σ-multiple is **1.58pp**, so the 0.16pp is still inside the
band and the number in this table is still the floor. What changed is that a dev run can no longer
lose 3.9pp and pass.

**Why `R-VES` is partial rather than absent or measured.** The metric is implemented and tested
(`eval/bird/ves.ts`): the reward table, the `tau = time(gold) / time(predicted)` ratio, the
median-absolute-deviation trim over repeated timings, and both normalisations the literature uses
(averaged over all questions, and over the valid ones). The reading it now carries is
**56.63%** — arm `select-cross`, the 600-question dev artifact at `eval/out/bird-eval-41453395203.json`
(378 correct of 600, **63.0% EX**), five timings per statement, three full executions of the loop
landing 0.07pp apart (56.58, 56.54 and 56.63). It is `partial` because the leaderboard files
OpenSearch-SQL at 69.36 over all 1,532 questions and 600 of them is a different claim; a rate is
about a set of questions, and this repository has already published one subset reading beside a
full-split reading as if they were ordered. The first number on a metric is worth recording
precisely because it is wrong to compare, and the row says so in the same breath.

**The reading has a floor, and the floor is most of the gap.** `--self-check` runs the same
measurement a second time with every prediction replaced by its gold statement: same case list,
same two-block shape, same trim, and the only difference removed is the one between the statements.
It reads **57.96%**, with 121 of the 378 correct answers in the 0.75 band and **none** in the 1.25
band:

| τ band | reward | floor | reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| at least twice as fast | 1.25 | 0 | 15 |
| at least as fast | 1.00 | 257 | 209 |
| within a factor of two | 0.75 | 121 | 145 |
| between a quarter and a half | 0.50 | 0 | 4 |
| slower than a quarter | 0.25 | 0 | 5 |
| **paid** | | **57.96** | **56.63** |

The 5.04pp the floor costs is arithmetic — 121 × 0.25 / 600 — and it is the reward table's shape
rather than the corpus's. The table steps at τ = 1, paying a quarter of the reward less for a ratio
one percent under parity, and does not step *up* until τ = 2. A stopwatch that cannot resolve
544 microseconds (the corpus median) to better than about one percent therefore lands a statement
that is exactly at par in the lower band half the time, and the top band is too far away to hand
the other half of those cases back. This is not a defect in this harness: the measurement anyone
else's number came from has the same step, which is why the leaderboard's own top row shows 72.28
EX against 69.36 R-VES — 2.92pp of the same tax, paid by a system whose statements are mostly at
par.

**What the previous round said about this gap, and why it was wrong.** The claim was that the 6.2pp
was the joins and subqueries this harness ships that the gold does not. Two measurements refute it.
A per-case cross-tabulation over the 145 statements in the 0.75 band finds **131 with exactly the
gold's number of joins**, 9 with more and 2 fewer; subqueries split 6 / 5; aggregates 4 / 5;
`distinct` 20 / 8; and the median τ of the cases that *do* carry an extra join is 0.86, which is
inside the floor's own spread. And the floor itself puts 121 statements in that band with no
statement difference at all. The arithmetic that made the story look proven — 148 × 0.25 / 600 =
6.2pp — was a correct multiplication of a count that had another explanation. A metric with a step
is a metric that needs an A/A run before any story about its gap, and this one now has one.

The reading is reproducible from the artifact and the cached split, with no model call and no quota:

```
pnpm bench:bird:ves \
  --artifact eval/out/bird-eval-41453395203.json \
  --dataset  eval/.cache/bird/dev/dev_20240627/dev.json \
  --arm      select-cross --repeats 5 \
  --databases eval/.cache/bird/dev/dev_20240627/dev_databases \
  --self-check
```

105 seconds for 12,000 executions, half of them the floor. What it cannot do is produce the
1,532-question number: that needs a
full-dev artifact, the only copies of which live inside GitHub Actions runs, and this project's
sandbox cannot read them — `GET /actions/runs/{id}/logs` and `/actions/artifacts/{id}/zip` both answer
`401` from the signed storage URL. A dispatched dev run therefore produces a number only a browser can
see, which is a defect in the measurement loop rather than in the metric, and it is written down here
instead of being worked around by quoting 600 questions as if they were 1,532.

**Three estimators were measured before the existing one was kept.** The trim is only one way to
summarise five timings, and a reading that is a quarter of the reward away from parity depending on
which summary is used would be a reading about the summary. One collection of ten samples per
statement, split into two halves of five, gives all three on the same machine and the same corpus:

| estimator | A/A floor | reading | A/A median spread |
|---|---|---|---|
| minimum of five | 57.54 | 55.50 | 1.010 |
| median of five | 58.83 | 56.50 | 1.021 |
| MAD-trimmed mean | 58.38 | 56.62 | 1.018 |

The three land inside 1.5pp of each other and the ordering of the two columns does not change, so
the trim stays: it is the one with an argument for why a loaded machine's right tail should be
dropped rather than down-weighted, and it reads highest of the three on the column that is about
statements. What the table does settle is that the gap is not an artefact of the estimator — every
summary loses 1.8 to 2.3pp of reward to the statements and 4.4 to 5.3pp to the table.

One defect had to be fixed before the metric could exist at all, and it was found by writing the
test rather than by writing the run:

> `oracle.py` reported whole milliseconds. Most statements on BIRD finish inside one, so both sides of
> the ratio read `0` and the ratio was `0/0` — a metric that would have paid 1.25 for the resolution
> of its own stopwatch. The oracle now returns `us` from the same stopwatch, `ms` stays whole because
> a timeout budget is written in whole milliseconds, and `timeRatio(0, 0)` is pinned to 1 by a test.

**A peer that cannot resolve a millisecond is refused, not floored.** `us` is optional on the wire,
and the decoder's fallback for a peer that omits it is `ms * 1000` — the coarse clock the field was
added to replace. Applied silently, that fallback is the original defect wearing the fix's name: every
statement that fits inside a millisecond reads the same on both sides, τ = 1, and the reward table
pays its top band for a question nobody timed. The decode now records `usFromMilliseconds`, the timer
answers `us: undefined` when that flag is set, `measureVes` counts the case as `unmeasured` rather than
as fastest, and the fixture for it is a real Python peer that sends `ms` alone.

### The tolerance is per split, and one floor was guarding nothing

`4pp` was the last coordinate of the gate read as a constant. It was measured at **n=239** (ADR-166)
and then applied to every split, so a dev rerun was allowed to fall 4pp below a floor taken on 1,532
questions — where the same σ-multiple is **1.58pp**. The direction of that error matters: a too-loose
threshold does not annoy anyone, it silently passes a regression the split can resolve. The baseline
now records `toleranceAtN: 239` beside `tolerancePp: 4`, and the gate re-expresses the constant at the
split's own sample size:

| split | questions | tolerance the split resolves |
|---|---|---|
| BIRD dev | 1,532 | **1.58pp** |
| BIRD Mini-Dev | 496 | 2.78pp |
| a 600-question subset of dev | 600 vs 1,532 | 2.10pp |

The sample size used is the harmonic mean `2 / (1/n_floor + 1/n_run)` rather than either count alone,
because the comparison is between two proportions — the floor's and the run's — and a run that scores
fewer questions is a noisier side of it. The A/A check reads the same per-split number, which is the
point: 5pp on 1,532 questions is a disagreement between two runs of one arm, and 5pp on 100 questions
is what 100 questions do on their own. A baseline with no `toleranceAtN` still applies its constant,
and the gate prints `uncalibrated` when it does, because the looser direction is the one that has to
be visible.

The same loop had a second gap: an **accuracy** floor on an arm the split does not run was skipped in
silence, while the ceiling-floor loop three lines below refuses exactly that shape. It was live —
`floors.dev` carried `select-prune` at 60.4 from the round the arm became on-demand, and every dev run
since printed nothing about it. The row is deleted and the loop now refuses one, scoped to a split
that declares its arm list: the list is the authority, and a floor outside it is a row to delete or an
arm to declare. Two checks, one lesson — a threshold is a claim about a coordinate, and a claim about
a coordinate that is not the current one is not a check.

### The two normalisations, and which one the leaderboard numbers imply

The leadership guide averages the reward over **all** questions (`100/N · Σ mᵢ·g(τᵢ)`), while one
paper's appendix says `N` is "the number of queries that passed EX". Both cannot be right, and the
leaderboard decides it: OpenSearch-SQL is filed at 72.28 EX and 69.36 R-VES, a ratio of **0.96**,
which is what averaging over all questions produces when a correct statement averages slightly under
1.0 on the reward table. Dividing by the valid count would put R-VES *above* EX for any system whose
correct answers are mostly at par, and no published row does that. `rvesOf` therefore reports `rves`
(the leaderboard's normalisation) and `rvesOfValid` beside it, so the choice is visible in the
artifact rather than buried in an instrument.

Our own ratio is **0.899** (56.63 / 63.0) against the 0.96 the leaderboard's two fields imply for
OpenSearch-SQL. Read as a like-for-like comparison that would be a finding — this harness's correct
statements are slower relative to their gold queries than theirs are — but it is not like-for-like:
600 questions against 1,532, one arm against one system, and two different execution environments.
What the ratio is good for is the direction, and the floor is what makes the direction readable: the
6.37pp between EX and R-VES here decomposes into 5.04pp of table and noise and 1.33pp of statements,
against 2.92pp for the leaderboard's top row. A system that sits 1.33pp under its own floor is a
system whose speed is not the lever it is looking for; a system that sits 3pp under it is.

## The selector's only net contribution is the 16 questions the vote cannot settle

Five selector arms were dispatched over the same 600-question dev pool (`41453395203`) and the
question they were dispatched to answer — which one should ship — was answered by reading their
scores: `select-cross` 378, `select-cross-pooled` 377, `pooled-vote` 380, `pooled-agree` 374,
`pooled-reconcile` 359. Five numbers inside a 2.3pp band, no pair separated by more than the
split's own noise, and the one policy that costs nothing (`pooled-vote`, zero calls a case) sitting
second. `tools/pool-replay.mjs` prices the same question offline from the artifact's own record:

```
node tools/pool-replay.mjs eval/out/bird-eval-41453395203.json --arm select-cross --verify-vote
```

Its first line is the check that makes the rest a measurement: **the replayed modal rule reproduces
`select-cross-pooled-vote` on 600 of 600 cases**. A policy table computed by a rule that cannot
reproduce the arm it models is a table about the tool, and the tool exits non-zero when that line
changes. It also exits **3** when the artifact holds no such arm at all: pointed at `44889941650`,
whose two arms are `select-cross` and `select-cross-tie`, the first version of this check printed
"0 of 0 agree" and exited 0 — a green check that compared nothing, which is the failure mode this
repository refuses everywhere else.

### What the pool looks like, by how many distinct results it returned

| distinct results | cases | pool holds the answer | modal group holds it | of which tied |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 447 | 326 | 326 | 0 |
| 2 | 137 | 80 | 52 | 0 |
| 3 | 16 | 9 | 2 | 16 |

Three facts follow, and the third one is the finding. On the 447 questions whose three candidates
returned the same rows, there is nothing for a selector to decide and 121 of them are wrong — the
three prompts wrote one wrong statement between them, so the loss is **generation diversity**, not
selection. On the 137 two-result questions the modal group holds the answer 52 times against a pool
that holds it 80, which is where a decision has something to win. And on the 16 questions where all
three differ, the vote has **no majority at all**: `majorityResult` returns the earliest group, and
that is arrival order being reported as agreement.

### The policies, and which of them can ship

| policy | correct | accuracy | shippable |
|---|---|---|---|
| `chosen` (what the arm answered) | 378 | 63.00% | yes — one selector call a case |
| `vote` (modal result group) | 380 | 63.33% | yes — no call at all |
| **`vote-unless-tie`** | **383** | **63.83%** | **yes — one call on 16 of 600 cases** |
| `vote-preferred-shape` | 380 | 63.33% | yes — no call |
| `oracle{chosen,vote}` | 396 | 66.00% | no — reads the answer key |

`vote-unless-tie` is worth 5 cases over the selector and 3 over the vote, and it is the only policy
here that is better than both of its parents. The mechanism is not a hybrid: the selector was
**worse** than the vote on every pool that could be decided (`chosen` 378 against `vote` 380) and it
was the only thing that could decide the 16 where the vote could not. So the call is not priced per
question any more, it is priced per *undecidable* question — 16 selection calls instead of 600, and
the 584 it does not make returned nothing a majority could not have returned.

That is what `select-cross-tie` measures (`gate: 'tie'`): the same three cross-model candidates, the
same selector, the same prompt, and the call made only when `majorityResult` reports a tie. Its
protocol is written here before the dispatch, in the form this file uses: the accuracy bar is **at
least 383 of 600** (the replay's own number, which is what the arm exists to reproduce), `calls.mean`
**at or below 3.03** (three generations plus 16 of 600 selections), and `spend.asked` **at or below
0.05 of the cases**. A dispatch that lands below 383 is a statement about the replay's transfer, not
about the vote's arithmetic, and the rows above are then a derivation rather than a reading.

### Two fields the artifact was not recording, and the dispatch each one cost

Replaying a policy needs the information the policy would have had. The record carried each
candidate's statement, its verdict and a fingerprint of its result, and was missing three things:

- `rows` and `columns`, which are what the selector is *shown* (`buildSelectionPrompt` renders
  `result: N rows, M columns`). A rule of the form "prefer the group whose shape matches the
  question" could not be priced from an artifact that recorded neither, which is why
  `vote-preferred-shape` above is only as good as its two parents in this table: the columns it
  reads are there now, and the 600 questions that would price it were scored before they were.
- `chosen`, which says which member became the answer. `winnerSource` names a *source*, and a pool
  whose three candidates come from three sources can be replayed through it only because they happen
  to be distinct; a repair turn can also replace the answer with a statement no candidate holds, and
  then **no** member is marked — a reading, not a gap.

All three are in `cases[].candidates[]` from this round on, and the nine tests in
`test/bird-candidate-failures.test.ts` hold them, including the case where the pool holds one
statement twice and only the earliest copy is marked.

### The measurement loop, which was the actual blocker

None of the above needed a dispatch, and that is the point: the artifact already held the pool. What
did need one — and what had been failing for three rounds — is reading a dispatched run's result.
`GET /actions/runs/{id}/logs` and `/actions/artifacts/{id}/zip` both answer `401` from a signed
storage URL, so a 1,532-question reading existed only for whoever had a browser.

`tools/readback.mjs` writes the reading to `readings/index.json` on a `readback` branch through the
contents API, one entry per workflow, and reads it back through `api.github.com` — the one host this
environment can reach. The channel is exercised end to end in this round: the five-arm artifact above
was published as `bird-dev` and read back identically, and the workflow that produces the next dev
reading publishes it in an `if: always()` step that cannot fail the job.

```
node tools/readback.mjs --publish --out eval/out/bird-eval.json
node tools/readback.mjs --read --slug bird-dev
```

### The 401 was not the artifact, and one header was the whole of it

The paragraph above was wrong about the cause, and the next round proved it in the only way that
counts: by reading two artifacts the previous three rounds had described as unreadable.

`/actions/artifacts/{id}/zip` answers `302` to a storage URL that carries its own signature. Both
`urllib` and `fetch` forward the caller's `Authorization` header across that redirect, and the storage
service refuses a token it did not issue. The signature was valid; the request failed because of a
header the client added on its own. Strip it **on a cross-origin redirect only** and the same URL
answers `200` with the same bytes the Actions page downloads. `tools/fetch-artifact.mjs` is that two
lines plus a zip reader (Node's `unzipSync` is a gzip reader and answers "incorrect header check" to a
real archive), and `test/fetch-artifact.test.ts` holds it against a second HTTP server that refuses
exactly what the storage service refuses:

```
GITHUB_REPOSITORY=AgentiX-E/nl2charts GH_TOKEN=... node tools/fetch-artifact.mjs 44889941650 --out /tmp/run
fetch-artifact: bird-eval.json 3550061 B -> /tmp/run/bird-eval.json
```

The lesson is not the header. It is that "the artifact is unreadable" was a **hypothesis about
somebody else's server** that three rounds of work were built on — the readback channel, its tests,
its workflow step — when the failure was reproducible in four lines with the response in hand. The
readback channel stays, because a reading that survives the artifact's 90-day expiry is worth having;
it is no longer the only route.

## The gate is exact, its price is not, and the bar was derived from another pool

`select-cross-tie` was dispatched on `44889941650` with the protocol written above: accuracy at least
383 of 600, `calls.mean` at or below 3.03, `spend.asked` at or below 0.05.

| reading | bar | what the dispatch returned | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| accuracy | ≥ 383/600 | **388/600 (64.67%)** | held, +5 |
| `calls.mean` | ≤ 3.03 | **3.077** | missed, +0.047 |
| `spend.asked` | ≤ 0.05 (30 cases) | **46/600 (7.67%)** | missed, +2.67pp |
| `selectorRule.decided` | not registered | 554 | — |

Two of three missed, and the reason is the one the pre-registration was least able to see: **the bar
counted ties on the wrong pool, and read the count off one bucket of it.** The 16 was read off
`41453395203`, whose 600 questions produced 593 three-candidate pools, 6 one-candidate pools and **1**
two-candidate pool — so on that pool every tie was a three-way tie by construction, and the two
buckets could not disagree. This run's pool is 589 three-candidate, 8 two-candidate, 3 one-candidate,
and the census reports `tied` **per bucket**: 39 in the three-result bucket and 5 in the two-result one,
where a two-candidate pool that disagrees is a 1-1 tie. The arm paid on 46 cases — **41 three-way ties
and 5 two-way ties** — which is exactly the 46 cases whose pool returned all-distinct fingerprints.

The gate did what it says. The number naming its price was a constant about a different draw, and the
tool that could have said so had already printed it: `census` counts `tied` in every bucket, and
`vote-unless-tie` is priced from the same field. What the pre-registration needed was the census's
**total**, not the bucket that had a story attached to it.

### The comparison it cannot make

`select-cross` scored 383 and `select-cross-tie` 388 in the same run, which reads like +5 for the
gate. It is not, because the two arms drew their own candidates: `candidateRecall` is **427 against
429**. A gate changes which candidate is chosen, never which candidates exist, so the pool difference
is a confound and the +5 is a pool difference and a gate difference added together. The mechanism is
separated from the pool only by reading one pool three ways, which is what the next two arms do.

### What the artifact recorded about its own decision, and what it got wrong

`spend.asked` 46 against `calls.mean` 3.077 is the arithmetic of the same fact (600 × 3 + 46 = 1,846
calls), and it is the first reading where the two agree without my having to derive one from the
other — because this round the published record carries the funnel instead of only the mean:

- `spend` now travels through `tools/readback.mjs`. The pre-registration named it and the first
  publication dropped it, so the criterion had to be checked by hand from the artifact.
- `selectorRule.rules` is new, and it exists because the record **contradicted its own rows**: the
  artifact for this run says `{"rule": "shortest", "decided": 554}` for an arm that declares no
  `selectRule` and whose gate answered by `modal` on all 554 cases. The declaration was published as
  if it were the behaviour. `selectorRuleOf` is now a pure function with five tests, `rule` stays the
  declaration, and `rules` is the census of what the rows name.

## The free rule the pool admits, which the shipping set did not have

Replaying the same 600 cases against the rules that read nothing but the pool turned up one that is
not in `SELECTION_RULES`'s shipping set: **take the modal group, except where it returned a single
row and a candidate outside it returned more rows in at least as many columns.**

| policy | correct | accuracy | calls a case |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vote` (modal result group) | 377 | 62.83% | 0 |
| `chosen` (the selector's answer) | 383 | 63.83% | 1 |
| `vote-unless-tie` (the gate above) | 383 | 63.83% | 0.077 |
| **`wider`** | **385** | **64.17%** | **0** |

It fired on 19 questions, was right on 10, and the vote was right on 2 of those 19 — so the shape of
a result carries information no text-level rule has. The mechanism is specific: a single-row
consensus is what an aggregate answer looks like, and on these 19 questions the answer was a set of
rows that the aggregation had thrown away. It is shipped as `'wider'` in `@agentix-e/nl2charts-ai`.

**The four numbers in that table are wrong, and the correction is the next section.** The vote they
are measured against was counting statements that returned nothing; over the pool that answered, the
same rule scores 387 against a vote of 391. The mechanism above still holds on those 19 questions —
what does not hold is the comparison, and a rule is not worth shipping on an absolute count.
`select-cross-pooled-wider` ran before the correction and is kept as the arm that priced it, its
preregistration is withdrawn, and `select-cross-pooled-wider-tie` was withdrawn before it ran.

Both arms are pooled, so the delta from `vote` is the rule, the delta from `pooled` is the gate, and
the delta from `pooled-vote` is what a call adds where the vote cannot decide — three questions, one
pool, one dispatch, and 0 + 0 + 46 calls against the selector's 600. What that sentence assumed, and
what the next two sections take apart, is that the arm they are differenced against answered the pool
it was given.

### The free signal the pool admitted was not free, and the rule it was paying for

The two preregistrations above were written against a vote that counted empty statements. That is the
kind of premise a preregistration cannot check and a replay can, so the replay was extended and the
bars were re-derived; both changed.

**The vote was taken over the wrong pool.** `modal` filters empty results through `eligibleIndices`;
the vote called `majorityResult` on the raw `considered` list, so two statements that returned nothing
outvoted the one that answered. On this artifact that is 8 questions — `--verify-vote` names them
(`95`, `119`, `577`, `678`, `803`, `1075`, `1314`, `1464`) — and calling empty is a failure, not an
opinion to count. `vote` over the answered candidates:

| policy | correct | accuracy | calls a case |
|---|---|---|---|
| `chosen` (the selector) | 383 | 63.83% | 1 |
| `vote` | 391 | 65.17% | 0 |
| `wider` | 387 | 64.50% | 0 |
| **`vote`, except on ties where the selector decides** | **395** | **65.83%** | **0** |
| `wider`, except on ties where the selector decides | 391 | 65.17% | 0 |
| `oracle{chosen,vote}` | 406 | 67.67% | — |

**`wider` is 4 short of the vote it was supposed to improve.** The +4 that motivated the shape rule
was the bug: `wider` was priced at 385 against a vote of 377, and once the vote stops counting empty
statements the comparison reads 387 against 391. The second pool says the same thing (386 vote, 385
wider), so this is not one sample — the shape rule was never ahead, and the only lever that survived
the correction is the gate. `select-cross-pooled-wider-tie` is **withdrawn** before it ran; `wider`
stays in the table as a priced row and out of the shipping list.

**A second defect, found by checking the rule against the arm.** `--verify-wider` compares the
replayed shape rule with `select-cross-pooled-wider` case by case, and it disagreed on 1 of 600
(`1066`). The cause was not the replay: `rowsKey` collapses duplicate tuples, so two members of one
group can hold the same distinct rows while differing in physical row count — a join fan-out returns
`7` once and six times — and `widerIndex` read the group's shape off its **first** member. 21 of the
600 modal groups have members that disagree this way, and on 3 of them the first member was the
fanned-out one, so the rule skipped the wider candidate it exists to find. A rule over a set may not
depend on arrival order. The group's row count is now the **fewest** any member returned, which is
also its distinct-row count: every member holds the distinct set with multiplicity at least one, so
the thinnest member holds it exactly once. Corrected, the replay reproduces its arm on 600 of 600 and
the score does not move (387 before, 387 after) — an order-independent rule that scores the same is
strictly better than one whose score was luck.

`verifyRule` is now generic for the reason this case gives: the vote was the only policy checked
against its own arm, and the one it was not checking is the one that had drifted.

**The arm to dispatch is the gate, not the shape.** `select-cross-pooled-tie` re-run on the corrected
vote, with the bar written before it runs:

- accuracy **at least 400 of 600**. The floor is arithmetic from two numbers this artifact already
  holds: the corrected vote answers 391 of the cases the gate does not buy, and the gate bought 39
  questions on which it added 13 — and **none of those 39 is one of the 8 the repair recovered**, so
  the two gains are disjoint and compose. 396 was that same arm reading a vote that under-reported
  itself by 8; a run that lands at 396 again means the repair did not reach the pool.
- `spend.asked` **at or below 0.10**: 39 of 600 is 6.50%, and a tie gate's bill is a property of the
  pool, so the bar is written from this census rather than from the 2.7% another pool implied.
- `--verify-vote` must report **600 of 600 agree** on the new artifact. The artifact these numbers
  come from reports 592 of 600, which is correct: it was recorded by the arm before the repair, and a
  check that agreed with it would be a check that certified the bug.
- `selectorRule.rules` must show `modal` on every case the gate held and no rule on the bought ones —
  the split this artifact shows as `{modal: 561}` and 39 unruled.

The 15 cases between 391 and 406 are what a per-question router would have to find, and the question
it answers is no longer "when does shape beat size" — that one is settled, and the answer is never.

### The bar was 400, the arm read 389, and the free rule it was bought for read 391

`44905985381` ran the three arms on the corrected code, 600 dev questions, `deepseek-chat` with
`deepseek-reasoner` as the second source. It is the first artifact this repository has produced whose
vote check passes on its own terms: **`vote` replay 600 of 600 agree**, which was the third bar and the
one that says the repair reached the pool rather than the replay.

| arm | correct | accuracy | calls a case | bought |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `select-cross` (the selector) | 379 | 63.17% | 4 | — |
| `select-cross-pooled-vote` | 387 | 64.50% | 0 | — |
| `select-cross-pooled-tie` | **389** | 64.83% | 0.075 | 45/600 |

**The preregistered bar failed: 389 against 400, eleven short.** The prediction it tested was arithmetic
— the corrected vote answers 391 of the questions the gate does not buy, the gate bought 39 and added 13,
and the two sets were disjoint — and the arithmetic was wrong in its middle term. Over this pool the
vote answers 387, not 391, and the gate adds **2**, not 13:

| policy | correct | calls |
|---|---|---|
| `vote` | 387 | 0 |
| `wider` | 388 | 0 |
| `vote-unless-tie` (free: the recorded choice on a tie) | **391** | 0 |
| `vote` + the gate's paid answer on ties | 389 | 45 |
| `oracle{chosen,vote}` | 404 | — |

Paired against the vote: **3 wins, 1 loss, p = 0.625**. Two questions on 45 calls is not a purchase, it
is a coin landing the way it was already pointing, and the arm is strictly worse than the free rule that
reuses the answer the run had already paid for — 391 for zero calls against 389 for 45.

The mechanism is visible in the 45 bought cases: the paid call was correct on **10** of them, and the
recorded selector answer was correct on **12**. Buying a third opinion where two groups tie bought a
*worse* opinion than the one on file, which is the one reading that would have stopped the arm from being
dispatched if the earlier pool had shown it. It did not, because the earlier pool's tie set was itself
polluted: the bug put empty statements into groups, empty groups into ties, and the gate's +13 was
measured on 46 questions of which some were ties only because two statements had answered nothing.

**What ships is the free rule.** `vote` at 387 with zero calls beats the four-call selector at 379 by 8,
and the gate cannot buy the remaining gap: the 17 cases between 387 and 404 are questions where the pool
holds the answer and the vote's group does not, which is a routing problem and not a spending one. Two
levers were priced this round and both were refused on their own numbers — the shape rule (−4 on one pool,
+1 on this one, net nothing) and the tie gate (−2 against a free policy that already held the answer).
`select-cross-pooled-tie` stays in `ON_DEMAND_ARMS` as the arm that holds the refutation, and `gate: 'tie'`
stays configurable because a config with no arm is observable and a deleted enum is not.

### Where each of the four absent rows would have to go

**WikiSQL** is nearly saturated (SeaD + execution-guided decoding 93.0% test EX, X-SQL + EG 91.8%,
SQLova 89.6% against a crowd-worker baseline of 88.3%) and it is the benchmark this pipeline is least
shaped for: every question is single-table and single-condition, so the schema card, the join graph
and the linker — the three mechanisms this repository has priced — have nothing to do. A number here
would measure a capability the product does not sell.

**Spider 1.0** is the opposite problem: it needs EM as well as EX, and this repository has only the
execution judge. `arms[].exactMatchRate` is a normalised string match over generated statements, not
Spider's component-wise clause match, so quoting it as Spider EM would be the coordinate error this
file spends thousands of lines refusing. The dev leaderboard runs 82.8% EX (DIN-SQL and DAIL-SQL with
GPT-4) to 93.52% EX (MA-SToR-SQL V5, as its authors report it), with dev EM in the 58–77% band
(LGESQL + ELECTRA 58.4, RESDSQL-3B + NatSQL 63.1, DAIL-SQL + GPT-4 66.5, Graphix-T5-3B + PICARD 77.1).

**nvBench 2.0** is the only absent row that is a *method* gap rather than a corpus gap. One query maps
to a set of valid visualizations, so the reading is F1 over that set; the mark vocabulary is Vega-Lite
specifications rather than this repository's eleven-mark contract. Step-NL2VIS (trained on the
benchmark) reads 81.50 F1@3 against GPT-4o prompting 22.54pp lower; a system that answers one chart
per question — which is what this product does — cannot be scored on a metric that asks for a set.

**VisCodeBench** ships through a leaderboard precisely so the corpus stays out of training data, so it
cannot be vendored the way BIRD and Text2Vis are. Its contract is also different: the system writes
Python into a marked region of a notebook and the reading intercepts the plotting calls. Best
displayed-data similarity is 0.81 (0.69 on the hardest subset) with latency 39–78s per request.

**Text2Vis** is the one corpus where this repository is ahead of the evidence rather than behind it:
no external system publishes an accuracy on its 1,470 scored rows, so the table above carries four of
the nine rows and none of the comparisons. That is a fact about the field, not about the product, and
it is the reason the Text2Viz section of this file quotes its own arms rather than a leaderboard.

### The rows are checked, and the checker is an argument

The gate has four rules, and each exists because a table like this has failed in that way somewhere:
a citation that no longer resolves, an absence with no reason, a percentage that is a count (1,418
rendered figures were called "1,418 percent" in the first draft), and a required leaderboard that has
quietly disappeared from the manifest. `REQUIRED` is the list of nine; deleting a row fails the build
rather than shrinking the table.

## Three calls, one opinion, and the third call's real job

Every selection reading in this file has been a reading *over* a fixed pool. `pool-replay` priced
seven policies on one candidate set, the gate priced when to pay for an eighth opinion, and the shape
rule priced what a result's width says — all of them holding the pool constant. The bill was never
part of the question, and it should have been: on `44905985381`'s pool, 417 of 600 cases return
**one** distinct result across three candidates. Three generations bought one opinion on 70% of the
questions, and no policy over one opinion can be better than that opinion.

`pool-replay --compositions` prices every non-empty subset of the pool's sources on the same rows.
Same cases, same judge, same call accounting: a source generates once, so a subset's `calls` is its
size, and the columns are comparable across rows.

| calls | candidate set | vote | ceiling | one opinion | tied |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | `inline+evidence@second` | 365 / 598 | 365 | 598 | 0 |
| 1 | `metadata+evidence` | **371** / 595 | 371 | 595 | 0 |
| 1 | `values` | 370 / 595 | 370 | 595 | 0 |
| 2 | second + metadata | 368 / 600 | 410 | 445 | **141** |
| 2 | second + values | 369 / 600 | 401 | 469 | 117 |
| 2 | metadata + values | **374** / 599 | 401 | 482 | 105 |
| 3 | all three | **387** / 600 | **421** | 417 | 45 |

Two readings come out of it, and only one of them was expected.

**The third call is worth 13 questions over the best pair and 16 over the best single.** It is not
free — it is 50% more generation — but it is now a price rather than a habit: 371 for one call, 374
for two, 387 for three, against a ceiling of 421. A product that wants 64.50% pays three calls; one
that wants 61.83% pays one.

**Parity, not information, is most of what the third call buys.** A two-candidate pool turns every
disagreement into a tie, and the vote settles a tie by generation order — the defect this file
already named when the tie gate was priced. The best pair ties on **141** of 600 cases; the triple
ties on 45. That is why `metadata+values` (374) sits three questions above a single call (371) while
its ceiling is thirty above it (401): the second call raised what the pool *could* answer by 30 and
what the pool *did* answer by 3, because 141 questions became coin flips. An odd candidate count is
not an aesthetic; a majority needs an odd number of members, and a pool without one is decided by
arrival order on a quarter of the questions.

### The router the pool cannot see

The 34 questions where the vote is wrong and the pool holds the answer are the whole remaining prize;
`vote` 387 against the pool's ceiling 421. Splitting them against the arm that pays for an opinion:

| | selector right | selector wrong |
|---|---:|---:|
| **vote right** | 362 | 25 |
| **vote wrong** | **17** | 196 |

`trustOf` reports the four cells and the exact sign test: 17 up, 25 down, p = 0.2800. The selector is
not significantly better than the count and it loses eight net — which is the reading that made the
free vote ship, now expressed as a 2×2 rather than as two rates.

The 196 in the bottom-right cell are questions no selection policy can reach: no member is correct.
The 17 in the bottom-left are the only ones a router could win, and a router has to find them among
42 disagreements without paying the 25. Every feature the pool itself carries was scored on those 42:

| feature | AUC |
|---|---:|
| the modal answer uses `DISTINCT` | 0.646 |
| the modal group is tied | 0.627 |
| distinct results in the pool | 0.598 |
| the modal answer aggregates | 0.594 |
| columns in the modal answer | 0.546 |
| empty results in the pool | 0.529 |
| rows in the modal answer | 0.484 |
| size of the modal group | 0.373 |

The best of them reads 0.646, and 42 pairs cannot distinguish 0.646 from a coin (a 4,000-resample
bootstrap over the 17 × 25 grid spans 0.518 to 0.774). The bar this repository set for spending a
dispatch on a router is **AUC at least 0.70**; nothing here reaches it.

**The reason is not that the features are weak, it is that the features are the wrong side.** A
router that decides "this question wants rows, that one wants a number" reads the *question*, and no
artifact this repository has ever written carried one: `cases[]` held `id`, `sql`, `gold` and the
pool, and `bench:bird:route` priced a question-side family over an artifact that could not hold the
question. That is why the answer above is a table of seven pool features and not the family the
literature builds — not a decision to look only at the pool, but the only list that could be
computed.

### The record now carries the question

`caseRows` writes `asked: { db, difficulty, question, evidence }` on every case, capped at 400
characters a field with `truncated: true` when the cap fired. It is the same join as `gold` — the
artifact records what ran, the questions file supplies what was asked — and it costs about 250 KB on
a 600-question, four-arm run.

The cap is a truncation and says so, because a reader who fits a feature to a cut question would be
reading half a document as a whole one. `db` and `difficulty` travel with it for the same reason the
question does: `bench:bird:route` groups its thresholds by database so a rule cannot memorise a
corpus's corners, and until this round the grouping key was not in the artifact either.

This is the third time a missing field cost a dispatch — `rows`/`columns` cost the shape rule a run,
`chosen` cost every policy comparison one, and the question cost the router family its only testable
form. The pattern is uniform: **a field that is not recorded is an analysis that is not possible**,
and it reads in the report as an analysis that was not worth doing.

### The dispatch it earns: what the third call should be

If the third call is a copy on 70% of questions, the question is what it should be instead. On this
pool `values` is byte-identical to `metadata+evidence` on **474 of 591** cases — the block is built
from the literals a question names and 60.9% of questions name none — so the third vote restates a
vote already cast on almost three quarters of the split. Its sole contribution is 11 cases: the
ceiling without it is 410, with it 421.

`select-cross-diverse` swaps that slot for `decompose`, the one generator here that answers by a
different method rather than different wording. It is a **swap, not a purchase**: three generations,
one selector, four calls, identical to `select-cross` except for what the third call is asked to do.
It also keeps the pool odd, which is the property the pair table above says matters — the arm that
bought a fourth candidate (`select-cross-pooled-dissent`) made the pool even, and its conversion fell
to 89.62% on a ceiling that had risen 27 cases.

Registered before the dispatch, on the incumbent's own metric:

- **coverage** (cases where any member is right) **at least 421 of 600** — the ceiling `select-cross`
  reaches with `values` in the third slot. A swap that costs the same and lowers the ceiling is a
  loss, and it has to be visible as one.
- **the third slot is solely right on at least 11 cases** — what `values` is solely right on
  (421 − 410). This is the number the swap is actually about: an opinion, not an index.
- **the free vote over the new pool at least 387 of 600**, from `select-cross-diverse-pooled-vote` in
  the same run. A slot that raises coverage without raising the count is information the vote cannot
  reach, and that is a different finding from a slot that carries no information at all.
- **`--verify-vote` 600 of 600** on the new artifact, and `asked` present on 600 of 600 cases.

If coverage rises and the vote does not, the third slot is information the decision cannot use and
the next lever is the decision, not the generator. If coverage falls, the third call was buying the
index and the diversity line closes here rather than paying for a fourth prompt.

### The reading (`44917562527`): the swap is neutral, and the reason is the decision

Four arms on 600 questions, code `105abba2`, second model `deepseek-reasoner`:

| arm | calls a case | correct | accuracy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `select-cross` (selector) | 4 | 379 | 63.17% |
| `select-cross-pooled-vote` | 0 | **390** | 65.00% |
| `select-cross-diverse` (selector) | 4 | 371 | 61.83% |
| `select-cross-diverse-pooled-vote` | 0 | **386** | 64.33% |

Against the three pre-registered criteria:

| criterion | bar | reading | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| coverage | ≥ 421 of 600 | **432** | pass (and equal to the incumbent's 432) |
| the third slot solely right | ≥ 11 | **16** (`values` 16, `decompose` 16) | pass, exactly tied |
| the free vote | ≥ 387 | **386** | fail by 1 |
| `--verify-vote` / `asked` | 600 of 600 | 600 of 600 / 2,400 of 2,400 | pass |

Read against its own run instead of against the other run's arm, the third criterion is not a
one-question miss: the control moved too. `select-cross-pooled-vote` read **390** here and 387 on
`44905985381` — the same arm on a re-drawn pool, which is the pool displacement this file has
measured before at 1.3–3.3pp. So the honest pairing is 386 against 390 on the same 600 questions:
**21 gains, 25 losses, p = 0.6587**. The swap is a wash.

The mechanism is the parity reading, one level deeper. `decompose` is not a weaker opinion than
`values` — it is exactly as informative, which the tied sole-correct count says in the sharpest form
available (16 and 16) and the identical ceiling says again (432 both). What it is, is *more
disagreeable*: the diverse pool returns **401** one-opinion cases against the incumbent's 409, and
ties on **47** against 41. Every one of those conversions moves a question out of a majority and into
a coin flip, and a three-way vote settles a coin flip by generation order. **More information the
decision cannot use is strictly worse than less information it can.** The diverse pool's ceiling is
the same and its answer is 4 lower; the 8 questions it gained in disagreement, it lost in ties.
