The selectors in the same run say the same thing from the other side. On the cross pool the selector
is 27 down and 16 up against the count (p = 0.1263); on the diverse pool it is **39 down and 20 up**
(p = 0.0183). Same judge, same prompt, same four calls — the only difference is that the second pool
carries more disagreement, and the judge's deficit roughly doubles where the statements genuinely
differ. **The more informative the pool, the worse the judge.** That is not a paradox: a judge handed
three statements that are all different has to adjudicate, and this one adjudicates worse than the
count it was supposed to beat.

So the diversity line closes here, and it closes with a reason rather than with a null: the pool is
not short of information, the decision is short of a way to use it. `decompose` stays in the
catalogue as a source — it is the best single candidate in that pool (369 of 593, above the second
model's 366) — but swapping it into the third slot buys nothing, and buying it as a fourth would
make the pool even, which the composition table above prices as a loss.

What that leaves, on this pool: 168 of 600 questions where **no candidate is right** — coverage, not
decision — and 42 where the answer is in the pool and the count misses it. The first needs a
generator or a retrieval this pipeline does not have; the second needs a judge that beats a count,
and two selectors, a shape rule, a gate and a tie-break ordering have now all failed to be one.

### The 168 have a shape, and it is not the shape the next purchase was aimed at

The reading above leaves two numbers, and the two candidate levers were aimed at them:

- **coverage** — 168 of 600 questions where no candidate in the pool is right;
- **decision** — 42 where one is and the count does not take it.

Before spending a call on either, this round asked what the 168 *are*. Two instruments, both
reading the artifact `44917562527` already wrote, both costing nothing:

| instrument | question | result |
|---|---|---|
| `bench:bird:gap` | what shape is the failure | 121 `values` (72.0%), 47 `column-count` (28.0%), 0 `engine-refused` |
| `bench:bird:values` | of the `values`, which fix does it ask for | 120 of 121 classified |

The second table is the one that decides the next iteration, so it is worth printing in full:

| bucket | cases | share of 121 | what it asks for |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `filter-wide` | 28 | 23.1% | a join multiplied the rows, or a predicate is too weak |
| `predicate` | 21 | 17.4% | the filter names the wrong column or the wrong comparison |
| `tables` | 20 | 16.5% | the statement reads a different relation |
| `filter-narrow` | 18 | 14.9% | the predicate matched nothing |
| `literal-missing` | **14** | **11.6%** | a value the gold compares against is not in the column |
| `aggregate` | 11 | 9.1% | the wrong level of aggregation |
| `projection` | 5 | 4.1% | the wrong columns |
| `grain` | 2 | 1.7% | grouped by the wrong thing |
| `literal-case` | 1 | 0.8% | one stored value differs only in case |
| `unclassified` | 1 | 0.8% | — |

**Value retrieval is worth 2.3pp at most.** Fourteen of six hundred cases name a value the column
does not hold, and `literal-case` adds one more. The plan carried an offline embedding pass for
value retrieval as a parallel item; the census says it can win fourteen questions, which is less
than the noise floor of a 600-question A/A pair. It stays in the catalogue as a repair and stops
being a route to coverage.

**Sixty-nine of the 121 are relational**: `filter-wide` (28), `predicate` (21) and `tables` (20) all
describe a statement built on the wrong relation or the wrong key. That is a generator problem in
the precise sense — more candidates from the same prompt will not reach it, because the prompt
already contains the schema and the evidence and the model still joined the wrong table. It is also
the bucket a decomposition arm is designed for, which is why the next dispatch aims there.

### Can the purchase be aimed? No — the question does not say which cases need it

A fourth call on every case is priced and does not pay (the diversity line above). The remaining
hope was to buy it only where the pool is empty: 168 cases at one call each is 28% of the corpus for
the 28% that need it. That is a routing question, and `bench:bird:route` had already answered its
shape for cards — one feature, one threshold, leave-one-database-out. `bench:bird:coverage-route`
asks the same question of the 168, reading `asked` and `candidateRecall` from the artifact and
nothing else, so it can be re-run on any future artifact for free.

| arm | best feature | AUC | held-out vs majority | gain | share it would buy |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `select-cross` | `chars` | **0.632** | 73.00% vs 72.00% | +1.00pp | 3.7% |
| `select-cross-diverse-pooled-vote` | `chars` | **0.618** | 72.67% vs 72.00% | +0.67pp | 3.7% |

The criterion was written before the run: **AUC ≥ 0.70, ≥ 3pp out of fold, buying at most 80%**.
Two independent arms, two readings, both far below it. And the failure is worse than the AUC
suggests: the fitted rule fires on 3.7% of the corpus, because BIRD's questions are short — the
median is **79 characters**, the 90th percentile is 122, and only 3.3% of questions reach the 150
the fold chose — so a length feature has almost no resolution, and every per-database fold lands on
the same cut at the top of its range. The longest questions are the ones with
literal-heavy evidence, and those are exactly the ones the model *can* answer.

That is the second time this repository has measured a question-side router and found nothing
(0.646 on seven pool features, 0.632 here on nineteen question features), and the two readings agree
on the cause: **the features are not weak, they are absent.** Nothing in the text of a BIRD question
says whether the schema join the model will choose is the right one.

So the purchase cannot be aimed, and the next iteration does not buy a call. It changes what the
call is for.

### Pre-registered: what the next dispatch must show, and why a fourth vote is not it

The 69 relational failures are the only stratum left that a call can reach. `decompose` is the best
single candidate in this pool (369 of 593, above the second model's 366) and was diluted by the vote
rather than beaten by it, so the next arm gives it a path of its own — its own repair turn, its own
judgement — and compares that path with the three-vote pool as a paired reading on the same 600
questions.

| criterion | bar | why this number |
|---|---:|---|
| paired net gain | ≥ +8 of 600 with exact sign test p < 0.05 | the noise floor of a 600-case pair is 1.3–3.3pp; +8 is its lower edge |
| on the 69 relational cases | ≥ +4 | the hypothesis is about the relational stratum, not about the average |
| cost | ≤ 4.6 calls a case | today is 4.0; +0.6 is the budget for one extra turn on part of the corpus |
| record | `asked` and `candidateRecall` on 600 of 600 | so the reading after this one costs nothing again |

Two things are excluded by construction, and both were measured rather than assumed:

- **A fourth vote is not a candidate.** Four candidates make the pool even, and §"Three calls, one
  opinion" prices the even pool as a loss — the tie rate doubles and the vote settles ties by
  generation order.
- **Buying everywhere is priced and does not pay.** The diversity arm bought 3.6pp of ceiling for
  2.8pp of answer on `44917562527`, and the router that would have aimed the purchase separates the
  cases at AUC 0.632. There is no version of "one more call on every case" that this repository has
  not already measured as neutral or worse.

### The last purchasable lever cannot be aimed, and the best source cannot be consumed alone

Two hypotheses were left standing after the 168 were priced, and both were written into the plan as
the next two dispatches: buy the audit only where a condition is missing (`AH.2`), and stop diluting
`decompose` by voting it against two prompts (`AH.2`'s "single consumption"). Neither was dispatched,
because both can be priced against an artifact that already exists, and one of them prices to a loss.

**Hypothesis one: the condition audit can be aimed.** The population is real — `bench:bird:conditions`
reads 128 of 600 cases whose statement names no column of a gold condition (21.3%) — and the audit
that fires on every case has already lost (1,507 of 1,532 fired, 30 named a condition, 43 rewrote,
and the arm scored below its parent for twice the calls). So `bench:bird:condition-gate` prices six
gates over what exists *before* the call: the question, the statement the arm already wrote, and the
schema. The label it is scored against is `missingConditions(gold, sql)`, which no gate can read —
the inputs the tool hands a gate do not carry it, and a test pins that.

| gate | fires | hit | precision | recall | worst database | calls/case |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `no-where` | 24 | 6 | 25.0% | 4.7% | 0.0% | 0.04 |
| `cue` | 125 | 37 | 29.6% | 28.9% | 0.0% | 0.21 |
| `named` | 398 | 87 | 21.9% | 68.0% | 7.7% | 0.66 |
| `cue-and-named` | 83 | 23 | 27.7% | 18.0% | 0.0% | 0.14 |
| `no-where-or-cue` | 146 | 42 | 28.8% | 32.8% | 0.0% | 0.24 |
| `no-where-or-named` | 410 | 89 | 21.7% | 69.5% | 7.7% | 0.68 |

The bars were registered before the run: **precision ≥ 0.50, recall ≥ 0.40, fires on ≤ 25%**. No gate
clears all three, and the shape of the failure is the sharp one: **every gate's precision is within
eight points of the 21.3% base rate**. `cue`, the best of them, is 29.6% — a lift of 1.39× on a
budget of 0.21 calls a case, and it reaches a quarter of the population. A gate whose precision is a
few points above the base rate is not a gate; it is the base rate with a smaller bill.

The reason is in the second line of the report, and it is the finding worth keeping:

> **Of the 128 cases whose statement dropped a condition, only 37 (28.9%) state a comparison word.**

The other 91 imply the filter through domain language the question never spells as a comparison —
"high schools", "female students", "the same county" — and 79 of the 83 `cue-and-named` fires are
questions whose cue word belongs to a clause the statement already wrote. A lexical gate cannot
reach a filter that is carried by the evidence note's semantics rather than by its words, and the
evidence note is exactly what the generator already has.

**Hypothesis two: `decompose` is diluted by the vote.** `--compositions` priced the subsets and put
`decompose` at 369 of 593 — the second-best single member — so the story was that a vote against two
prompts of the same model buries the one generator that answers by a different method. `--consume
decompose` reads the members instead of the subsets:

| reading | value |
|---|---|
| `decompose` consumed alone | **369/593 = 62.23%** |
| the vote on the same 593 | **381** |
| disagreements with the modal group | 95 |
| — `decompose` right, vote wrong | **16** |
| — vote right, `decompose` wrong | **28** |
| — both right / neither | 0 / 51 |
| a perfect judge over the pair | **397** (+16 over the vote) |

16 wins against 28 losses. The dilution story is falsified in the direction that matters: it is not
being outvoted, it is being **outvoted correctly**. The ceiling a judge could reach is +16 of 600
(2.7pp), the judge would cost 0.158 calls a case, and this repository has now failed to move a
decision with a judge four times — the selector, the shape rule, the tie gate and the agreement
marks. A 2.7pp ceiling behind a mechanism with a measured negative track record is not a dispatch.

### What is left, now that every cheap thing has been priced

The measurement that keeps surviving is the one about *where* the missing statements are, and this
round adds a third instrument agreeing with it. On the same 600 cases:

| lever | price it was given | reading |
|---|---|---|
| a fourth candidate on every case | +0.745 calls | ceiling +3.6pp, answer −2.8pp (`44917562527`) |
| a fourth candidate only where the pool is empty | routing, AUC ≥ 0.70 required | **AUC 0.632 / 0.618**, buys 3.7% |
| an audit on every case | +1.00 calls | named 30 of 1,507, scored below its parent |
| an audit only where a condition is missing | gate, precision ≥ 0.50 required | **precision 21.9–29.6%**, base rate 21.3% |
| `decompose` consumed alone | 0 extra calls, 1 candidate instead of 3 | 369 against the vote's 381; 16 wins / 28 losses |
| a plan before the statement | 0 extra calls | **−7.2pp** (63/27, p = 0.0002), measured earlier |

Nothing in that table is about instructions or calls. Every row is a *shape* of generation, and every
one of them is neutral or negative. That leaves two things that are not shapes: **what the prompt
knows** and **what writes it** — and both have a reading here too. The synthesized definition block
carries the profile (`packages/ai/src/definitions.ts` renders observed values, ranges and distinct
counts into it), it costs one call per database rather than per question, and it measured a tie with
`inline` (18 vs 17). The reasoning model is in the pool as `@second` and reads **366** against the
chat model's 371.

Which is what MAC-SQL's 4.90pp on dev (p = 3.4 × 10⁻⁶, 1,532 questions, one endpoint) has been
saying since it was measured: **the gap is their template and their examples, not their architecture.**
Their card rule, applied here, loses 3.43pp to its parent (261 against 278, p = 0.0241); their `decompose`-everywhere is already a source here;
their refiner fires on 6.7% of dev. What has never been run beside ours is their *prompt* — the
`decompose_template_bird` template in `core/const.py` (`agents.py` only formats it), pinned at
`31a9df5`, with our card and our endpoint.

That is the next dispatch, and the bar is registered here before it exists:

| criterion | bar | why this number |
|---|---:|---|
| one-candidate accuracy | ≥ 12 cases over `inline+evidence` **in the same run** (2.0pp), paired exact McNemar p < 0.05 | 2.0pp is the lower edge of a 600-case pair's resolution, and the template would be adopted as a *source*, not as an arm — it has to beat the prompt it would replace. The row first read "`inline+evidence`'s 371 + 12"; 371 is `metadata+evidence` on 595 questions, so the anchor was a mis-attribution before it was ever compared against — the correction is in the section below |
| calls a case | 1.00 | a template copies at zero marginal cost; a template that needs a second call is a pipeline, and pipelines have been losing here |
| the three-candidate pool | ≥ 387 with the template in the third slot | the pool is the product; a source that wins alone and loses in the pool is a source that restates what the others say |
| record | `asked` on 600 of 600, `candidateRecall` on every case | so the reading after it costs nothing again |

## The ninth shape is not a shape: the prompt itself, re-authored, and the reader it broke

Every arm on this page is a lever on one skeleton — `buildSqlPrompt`'s rules, card, blocks and
`Question:` line — so the fifteen of them can price a rule and none of them can price the skeleton.
That is the gap the last section named and this round built the instrument for: `PromptOptions.template`.

### What the instrument sends

`packages/ai/src/template.ts` renders MAC-SQL's BIRD prompt on our card and our evidence. Three
things separate it from every other arm: a five-rule constraint list stated before the schema, two
worked examples (a BIRD question over `frpm`/`satscores` and a Spider question over
`account`/`client`/`district`, each answered as a sequence of sub-questions), and an output shape
where the model writes `Sub question <n>:` lines with one fenced statement each and the answer is
the **last** fence.

Three differences from what they run are deliberate, and each is a thing this project would not
ship — so an arm that carried them would be measuring a self-inflicted wound rather than their
prompt:

| difference | why |
|---|---|
| the card keeps the column **type** | their list format is `(name, description. Value examples: …)` and states no type; a prompt that hides it would lose to a card this project already sends |
| the **value examples are not compiled** | profiling every column is `samples-wide` here, measured at +2.02pp for +74.9% of the prompt — a separate lever, so it stays off inside the template |
| **no selector** | their pipeline prunes the card with a model call before this prompt; that rule is `card.ts` here and it lost 3.43pp, so the template runs on the full card |

The text is ours, the information is theirs: MAC-SQL carries no licence file, so nothing is copied
verbatim — the constraints are restated in this project's voice, the two examples are public corpus
data, and the section markers are kept because the examples and the input block have to share one
format for the examples to teach anything. What that costs is resolution: if the arm loses, its
reading cannot separate their **wording** from their **information**, and that limit is recorded
here rather than discovered later.

### The declaration refuses to be two changes

A template is the whole prompt, so `definitions`, `demonstrations`, `values`, `rowSamples`, `plan`,
`interpretation`, `decompose`, `reasoning` and `notes` have no slot in it — and a non-SQLite
`dialect` contradicts both its instruction and its examples. `assertTemplateCarries` throws on each
rather than dropping it, at the arm declaration *and* at the prompt builder, because an option a
caller believes is on and nothing reads is the defect this repository has paid for twice
(`emptyRetry` wired to a hook that never fired, `values` read by the harness and never passed down).

The arm is therefore `macsql-prompt`, one field from `inline+evidence-nolink` — a test pins that,
including the one field that cannot reach the prompt (`definitions: 'inline'`, which is how its
parent gets the dataset's descriptions onto its card; `promptFor` gives a template arm the same
descriptions through its own switch and the template refuses the block). The third arm in the
dispatch is `inline+evidence`, so the run reads two questions at once: what their prompt is worth
against ours as shipped, and what it is worth against ours with the hint removed.

### The reader the template exposed, and the arm it had already been costing

Their output shape is a sequence, so the answer is the last fence — and the harness had two readers
that disagreed about that. `parseDecomposed` takes the last block; `extractSql` takes the first, and
`eval/bird/run.ts`'s reconcile turn called `extractSql` **under a comment that said it took the
last**. The reply that prompt asks for is one line per result group followed by the statement, and a
model that fences each group's statement — several do — had its correction read off group one, which
is a candidate's own statement: the turn then looks like a restatement, the funnel counts it as one,
and the adoption policy hands back the vote's decision. That is not a hypothetical: `reconcile` is
the mechanism that is *supposed* to be worth its call, and the reading it was judged on could only
see the corrections a model wrote in the first fence.

The fix is one function, not two call sites: `readStatement(text, { template, decompose, last })`
decides which block is the answer from the prompt that asked for it, and every caller in the harness
now passes the prompt it sent. `extractSql` keeps its first-block default and gained a `last` option,
because the default is correct for the fifteen one-statement arms and changing it would re-read every
artifact this project has published.

Two consequences are recorded rather than repaired. The reconcile arms measured before this round
were read with the wrong block, so their readings are a **floor** for the mechanism, not an estimate
of it; and the empty-result rewrite now follows the source arm's template for the same reason.

### The first dispatch (`44974188185`): 0/600 in zero seconds, and the two things it caught

| arm | reading | calls a case |
|---|---|---|
| `inline+evidence` | **384/600 = 64.0%** | 1.00 |
| `inline+evidence-nolink` | 378/600 = 63.0% | 1.00 |
| `macsql-prompt` | **0/600 in 0.0 s a case** | **0.00** |

The template arm spent no calls. That is the signature of a prompt that never reached the model, and
the cause was in this round's own guard: `buildAskMessages` sets `decompose` on **every** call
(`input.decompose === true || input.prompt?.decompose === true`), so a template prompt arrives
carrying `decompose: false` — and `assertTemplateCarries` read `false` as "a block is set". Every
case threw inside `promptFor` before the first call; the table recorded 600 rows of `0.0%`.

Two defects, and both are the kind this repository writes down:

1. **The test went through the wrong door.** `buildSqlPrompt(…, { template })` was covered; the
   message builder, which is the path the harness takes, was not. The guard's unit test called the
   function directly and its `decompose` was `undefined` there — the only value that passes. The
   fix treats a boolean lever set to `false` as off, and the test now goes through
   `buildAskMessages`, with a second test that a real `decompose: true` is still refused.
2. **A whole arm failing inside the harness was published as an accuracy.** `assertArmProducedResults`
   refused two states: every case refused by the provider (`llm`) and every case cut at the budget
   (`truncated`). Every case failing in *our* code matched neither, so 600 zero-second rows went
   through the funnel and the refusal came from `assertReportComplete`, two layers away, naming the
   symptom (`its row carries no format profile`). The guard now refuses a table whose every row is a
   harness failure and prints the first error, which in this case was one sentence long and named
   the fix.

The bar's anchor was wrong twice over, and both errors are worth recording because they are the two
ways a pre-registered threshold goes bad.

**The number belonged to another arm.** The row said "`inline+evidence`'s 371"; 371 is
`metadata+evidence` on 595 questions, and `inline+evidence` has never had a 600-case reading in this
document — its readings are 60.5–61.3% on the 1,532-question split. The anchor was mis-attributed at
registration, before any run could compare against it.

**The parent moves, and here it moved more than the bar.** `inline+evidence` read **384 of 600** on
the same questions with the same pinned weights (`170d0beaa768594b`, unchanged before and after the
run). A 2.2pp move on an unchanged prompt at temperature zero is a draw, not a capability, and it is
larger than the 2.0pp the bar was set to detect. An absolute bar on a paired experiment therefore
measures the parent's draw as much as the candidate's, which is why the criterion is restated before
the next run as a **paired difference**: the template must win **12 or more of the 600 cases** against
`inline+evidence` in the same run, exact McNemar p < 0.05. No absolute number survives in the
criterion; 371 stays in this document as a reading of a different arm.

The same run also prices the hint, which no arm had ever measured: **384 against 378**, +6 cases at
1.00 calls each. The second run reads **380 against 379** — one case the other way. Two runs, +6 and
−1: the `Likely columns` line is worth nothing measurable on this split, and the honest statement is
that its 30%-precise list is neither the reason the prompt works nor the reason it loses.

### The second dispatch (`44976101168`): +20 cases, and a card four times the size

| arm | reading | calls | prompt chars | prompt tokens | cached | completion |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `inline+evidence` | 380/600 = 63.33% | 1.00 | 2,604 | 685 | 494 | 48 |
| `inline+evidence-nolink` | 379/600 = 63.17% | 1.00 | 2,604 | 653 | 460 | 46 |
| `macsql-prompt` | **400/600 = 66.67%** | 1.00 | **12,668** | 3,705 | 3,315 | 136 |

Paired, exact McNemar on the same 600 questions:

| pair | wins / losses | delta | p |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| `macsql-prompt` vs `inline+evidence` | **61 / 41** | **+3.33pp** | **0.0594** |
| `macsql-prompt` vs `inline+evidence-nolink` | **56 / 35** | **+3.50pp** | **0.0355** |
| `inline+evidence-nolink` vs `inline+evidence` | 20 / 19 | −0.17pp | 1.00 |

Every count bar was cleared — 20 cases over the parent against a registered 12 — and one of the two
p-values was not: **0.0594** against the shipped prompt, 0.0355 against the arm without the hint. On
the registered criterion as written ("≥12 cases **and** p < 0.05 against `inline+evidence`") the
template passes the count and misses the significance, by about a fifth of a standard error.

**And the price column is theirs too.** The template's prompt is **12,668 characters against the
parent's 2,604** — 4.9×, and it is not a truncation artefact: `BIRD_SCHEMA_LINES` is 400, both arms
render every column of every table, and the difference is the layout (`# Table: x` + one bracketed
line per column against one compact line per table). That layout is part of the template — a card the
examples are written in has to be the card the question arrives on — so the reading is *their prompt
and their card against ours*, which is the object the pre-registration named. It is also why the
arm's first reading was briefly believed to be confounded: `schemaLines` reached `buildSqlPrompt` and
`renderMacSqlCard` ignored it, which is the same defect class as an option a caller sets and nothing
reads. That was fixed (`limit`, one line per column, continued across tables; three tests), and the
fix changed nothing on this arm because the budget it was given is 400 — the honest version of the
story is that the defect was real and inert here, and the 4.9× is the template's own price rather
than an accident.

### The third dispatch (`44978468988`): the same three arms, a clean reading

| arm | reading | calls | prompt chars | tokens | cached | completion |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `inline+evidence` | **386**/600 = 64.33% | 1.00 | 2,604 | 685 | 494 | 47 |
| `inline+evidence-nolink` | 381/600 = 63.50% | 1.00 | 2,604 | 653 | 460 | 47 |
| `macsql-prompt` | **401**/600 = 66.83% | 1.00 | 12,668 | 3,705 | 3,522 | 129 |

| pair | wins / losses | delta | p |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| `macsql-prompt` vs `inline+evidence` | **50 / 35** | **+2.50pp** | **0.1284** |
| `macsql-prompt` vs `inline+evidence-nolink` | **50 / 30** | **+3.33pp** | **0.0330** |
| `inline+evidence-nolink` vs `inline+evidence` | 20 / 25 | −0.83pp | 0.5515 |

The count bar is cleared again (+15 against a registered 12) and the significance bar against the
shipped prompt is missed again, further out (0.1284 against 0.0594 in the previous run). Against the
arm that carries the same inputs and no hint, the template is **+3.33pp at p = 0.0330 for the second
time in two runs** (0.0355 before). Three runs now exist for the parent on identical prompts and
identical weights: **384, 380, 386** — a 6-case spread, which is the resolution everything here has
to be read against.

So the reading is: **the template is better than our prompt by about three points, and that is the
same size as what our own hint is worth** — the hint reads +6, −1 and −5 cases across the three
runs, which is noise. The template is not adopted on this evidence: the criterion registered before
the first dispatch required p < 0.05 against the shipped prompt, and two runs at n = 600 have not
delivered it. What the next dispatch has to buy is sample, not another mechanism: the discordance is
85 of 600 (14.2%), and at that rate separating 2.5pp at 80% power takes **1,775 questions** — more
than the dev split's 1,534, which resolves **2.69pp** at the same power and 14.2% discordance. The
full split is therefore the biggest single purchase available, it is the only one that could move
this from *a reading* to *a verdict*, and it buys 2.7pp of resolution for a 2.5pp effect — which is
the honest statement of how thin this is.

### The dev dispatch (`44981690629`): the bar is cleared, and so is the control's

The tenth shape was registered with three conditions, and the first two are decidable on the split
the leaderboard reports. 1,532 of 1,534 questions (gold refused on 518 and 701), one call a case,
same endpoint, same weights (`170d0beaa768594b` before and after):

| arm | reading | strict match | prompt chars | tokens | cached | completion |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `inline+evidence` | 947/1,532 = **61.81%** | 876 | 2,781 | 676 | 484 | 49 |
| `inline+evidence-nolink` | 931/1,532 = 60.77% | 864 | 2,672 | 646 | 448 | 49 |
| `macsql-prompt` | **1,004/1,532 = 65.54%** | 914 | 12,728 | 3,694 | 3,480 | 138 |
| `inline+evidence#2` (A/A) | 930/1,532 = 60.70% | 862 | 2,781 | 676 | 484 | 49 |

| pair | wins / losses | delta | 95% CI (Newcombe, paired) | exact McNemar p |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|
| template vs `inline+evidence` | **134 / 77** | **+3.72pp** | **[+1.87, +5.57]** | **0.0001** |
| template vs `inline+evidence-nolink` | 147 / 74 | +4.77pp | [+2.88, +6.65] | 1.0e-6 |
| `nolink` vs `inline+evidence` | 47 / 63 | −1.04pp | [−2.38, +0.30] | 0.1523 |
| **`inline+evidence` vs its `#2`** | **13 / 30** | **−1.11pp** | **[−1.95, −0.27]** | **0.0137** |

The registered criteria — at least 12 cases over `inline+evidence` in one run with exact McNemar
p < 0.05, and 1.00 calls a case — are **met**: +57 cases at p = 0.0001, one call. The strict string
match moves the same way (+38), so this is not an artefact of the execution judge's tolerance.

**The last row is the finding, and it is about the criterion rather than the template.** The A/A
copy carries the same prompt, the same weights and the same 676-token request — the artifact's
`tokens` lines for the two are identical down to the 484 cached — and the two draws differ by
1.11pp with a confidence interval that excludes zero. The harness printed it itself:

```
A/A inline+evidence: -1.1pp (30/13, p=0.014, 95% CI [-1.9, -0.3]pp, resolves 1.2pp) — the harness's own noise
```

So on 1,532 questions **a criterion of p < 0.05 is satisfied by a re-run of nothing.** This is the
third time a criterion here has needed a coordinate it did not carry: `4pp` was measured at n = 239
and applied to 1,532 (v6.71), the absolute anchor 371 belonged to `metadata+evidence` (§ the ninth
shape), and now the p-value itself belongs to a spread. The disposition is not to tighten the bar —
it stays exactly as registered — but to require the control beside it: any sentence that cites this
criterion has to print the A/A line and state the ratio. Here it is **57 / 17 = 3.35**.

### The same 600 questions are not a smaller dev, and they understate the effect

The three earlier dispatches ran 600 questions and read 386 / 381 / 401. Restricted to those same
600 ids inside the dev artifact:

| question set | `inline+evidence` | `nolink` | `macsql-prompt` | template vs parent |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| all 1,532 | 947 (61.81%) | 931 | 1,004 (65.54%) | 134:77 = **+3.72pp** |
| the 600 ids | 383 (63.83%) | 374 | 392 (65.33%) | 50:41 = **+1.50pp** |
| the other 932 | 564 (60.52%) | 557 | 612 (65.67%) | 84:36 = **+5.15pp** |

Three facts, and the third is the expensive one. The subset is **2.02pp easier** for the same arm,
even though its difficulty mix is the split's (363/181/56 against 925/463/144 — 60.4/30.2/9.4%
both). Two runs on the same ids differ by 0.5–1.5pp, which is the n = 600 re-run spread that had
only ever been inferred from 384/380/386. And the subset **compresses the effect from +3.72pp to
+1.50pp** — so the previous round's "criterion not met" was not merely noisy, it was biased in the
direction that rejects a real mechanism.

The mechanism's shape is visible in the corpus's own difficulty bands (paired, same run):

| difficulty | questions | `inline+evidence` | `macsql-prompt` | wins / losses | delta | p |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|
| simple | 925 | 67.2% | 70.9% | 75 / 41 | +3.68pp | 0.0020 |
| moderate | 463 | 54.2% | 56.4% | 41 / 31 | +2.16pp | 0.2888 |
| challenging | 144 | 51.4% | **60.4%** | **18 / 5** | **+9.03pp** | 0.0106 |

13 of the 57 cases are in the 144 hardest questions, which is why an easier subset reads a smaller
effect. The prediction this licenses: on a corpus aimed at hard questions the template's relative
value is larger, not smaller.

### The pool (`44985557283`): the ceiling moves and the rule spends it

The third registered condition is the pool, with the template in the third slot — `values` out,
`macsql-prompt` in, same draw count, same free rule, same judge (`select-mixed-rule-template`, one
field's worth of sources). 600 questions, run beside the shipped arm and an A/A of it:

| arm | selected | ceiling | conversion | prompt tokens | cached | completion |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `select-mixed-rule` | 388 (64.67%) | 415 (69.17%) | 93.5% | 3,164 | 2,587 | 143 |
| `select-mixed-rule-template` | **395 (65.83%)** | **437 (72.83%)** | **90.4%** | 6,176 | 5,608 | 225 |
| `select-mixed-rule#2` | 380 (63.33%) | 413 (68.83%) | 92.0% | 3,164 | 2,587 | 141 |

| pair | wins / losses | delta | p |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| selected | 28 / 21 | +1.17pp | 0.3916 |
| **ceiling** | **31 / 9** | **+3.67pp** | **0.0007** |
| baseline vs its `#2` | 19 / 27 | −1.33pp | 0.3020 |

The bar is cleared literally — 395 against 387, with the baseline reading 388 in the same run, so
this is not a collapsed control. And the score difference is inside the A/A's own spread (+7 against
8), while the ceiling difference is not (31:9, p = 0.0007). `shortest` spends 15 of the 22 new cases:
`selectionLoss` goes 27 → 42 and conversion 93.5% → 90.4%.

**So the template buys ceiling, not score**, which is the same shape the deep pools already showed —
except the pool's width did not change and its *source* did. The next lever is therefore a chooser,
not another prompt, and its criterion is registered here: recover `selectionLoss` from 42 to at most
28, i.e. `437 × 0.935 = 409` selected.

**And the price is not the token ratio.** 1.95× tokens, **1.32× money**: the template is a fixed
prefix, 90.8% of it served from the provider's cache, and the 568 tokens that missed cost almost
exactly what the baseline's 577 did. A large fixed prompt is cheap at the margin; what is expensive
is the part that changes with the question. Any price table that multiplies tokens is wrong in the
direction that rejects this kind of mechanism.

### Where the ninth shape lands

| condition (registered before the first dispatch) | bar | reading | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| one-candidate accuracy | ≥ 12 cases, p < 0.05 | +57, 134:77, p = 0.0001 | **met** |
| calls a case | 1.00 | 1.00 | **met** |
| three-candidate pool | ≥ 387 | **395** | **met** |
| ceiling (not registered, read anyway) | — | 415 → 437, 31:9, p = 0.0007 | significant |
| pool score (not registered) | — | +7, 28:21, p = 0.39 | inside the control |

Adopted as a **candidate source**; not adopted into the shipped configuration. All three registered
conditions are met and the ceiling moves, so the prompt has earned its place in the catalogue — the
ninth lever, and the first prompt that leaves a mark inside the pool. But the pool's score does not
move beyond the control's own spread, and the money is 32% higher; buying that before a chooser
exists is buying a hypothesis. Ceiling is a hypothesis; the product is the selected statement.

### The free-rule space is closed on this pool, and the bar it was given is not reachable

The tenth shape's third condition left one question and one bar: recover `selectionLoss` from 42 to
at most 28, i.e. 409 of 600 selected. That bar carries an assumption — that some chooser which
spends no call can reach it — and the assumption had never been tested, because testing it by
dispatch costs a run per rule.

It does not have to. The pool's artifact records, per case, each candidate's source, statement,
row count, column count, a fingerprint of its result and the judge's verdict, which is everything
`chooseCandidateByRule` reads except the rows themselves. `bench:bird:rules` replayed twenty
strategies over `44985557283` for nothing:

| strategy | kept | share | vs `shortest` (won:lost) | p |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| `shortest` (shipped) | 395 | 65.83% | — | — |
| **`first:macsql>metadata>inline`** | **401** | **66.83%** | 30 : 24 | 0.4966 |
| `chars-no-alias` | 400 | 66.67% | 9 : 4 | 0.2668 |
| `first:macsql>inline>metadata` | 400 | 66.67% | 29 : 24 | 0.5831 |
| `nonspace` | 398 | 66.33% | 3 : 0 | 0.2500 |
| `modal-then-shortest` | 396 | 66.00% | 15 : 14 | 1.0000 |
| `modal` | 392 | 65.33% | — | — |
| `wider` | 391 | 65.17% | 16 : 20 | 0.6177 |
| `first` (recorded order) | 380 | 63.33% | 11 : 26 | 0.0201 |

The candidate set held an answer on 437. The family's ceiling is **401**. Twenty comparisons put
the Bonferroni bound at p < 0.0025 and no member clears it — nor the uncorrected 0.05, where the
best is 0.2668.

**And the reason is countable rather than mysterious.** Of the 36 cases the best strategy loses,
**24 have candidates whose result shapes are identical** (row count and column count equal for
every member), and **18 of those are three `1r1c` results** — one row, one column, three different
numbers. That is not an accident of those 36: **485 of the pool's 600 questions (80.8%) have every
candidate shaped the same**, which is why the one rule that reads shape (`wider`) has no input on
four questions in five and reads 391 here.

So the registered bar stays exactly as written and the reading is that **no zero-call chooser in
the catalogue can meet it.** A criterion no member of a family can satisfy is not a failed
criterion; it is a criterion that prices the next mechanism, and its price is now stated: **eight
cases above 401**.

### Two things the harness could not express, and one defect that adding them exposed

`wider` was in the library and not in the variant list, so the rule that motivated the pool had
never been priced against it. It is a port, and the port is held to the library by an invariant
rather than by a comment: on the same rows and the same arrangements, this file and
`chooseCandidateByRule('wider', …)` must keep the same candidate. A second implementation of
"wider" is a second opinion about which candidate is wider.

The other is the pool's *arrangement*. `first` reads arrival order and nothing else, so an ordering
of the sources is a lever that costs nothing and had never been priced — and the shipped trio names
`inline+evidence` first while the template was the source that answered most often. Every ordering
of the sources an arm recorded is now generated per arm (six for three sources, twenty-four for
four, and no more: an arrangement is a preference among prompts, and a nine-source pool offers no
preference a reader could act on). One of the six reproduces the recorded order and is kept rather
than filtered, because it is the control that says the family costs nothing when it says nothing.

Adding them broke the correction, and the reader that caught it was the harness's own sentence. It
compared every lead against `0.05 / 14` — the static list's unshipped count — while printing that a
lead had to clear the bound "for 20 variants". Six arrangements were walking through a door the
correction had shut. `correctedThreshold` now takes the number of comparisons and `verdict` and the
per-arm line both take it from `reading.against.length`; a test holds ten wins and no losses to
p = 0.00195, **past the bound for twenty and short of the one for fourteen**.

### What the pool is worth before a chooser exists (`44985557283`, 600 questions)

| configuration | kept | calls a case | prompt tokens | cached | CNY a case |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| template alone (replayed inside the pool's own artifact) | **400 (66.67%)** | 1.00 | 3,694 | 3,480 | 0.00167 |
| template pool + `shortest` | 395 (65.83%) | 3.00 | 6,176 | 5,608 | 0.00316 |
| shipped pool (`inline+meta+values`) | 388 (64.67%) | 3.00 | 3,164 | 2,587 | 0.00240 |

| pair | wins / losses | delta | p |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| template alone vs template pool | 29 / 24 | +0.83pp | 0.5831 |
| template alone vs shipped pool | 45 / 33 | +2.00pp | 0.2127 |

The pool and the single source are **indistinguishable**, and the pool costs 47% more and spends
two more calls. Against the shipped pool the single source's +2.00pp sits at p = 0.21, inside the
2.5pp this split resolves — so it is not "a better pool", it is **a cheaper configuration that is
at least as good**, which is what a price table has to be read for.

**Verdict: the shipped configuration is the template alone.** The pool is postponed, not rejected:
its ceiling (437) really is higher, but nobody can cash it before a chooser that reads SQL exists,
and the two extra calls are on the bill every time. **Ceiling is a hypothesis; the product is the
selected statement.**

### The dev dispatch settles it: the single source, at 40% of the money (`44991167518`)

The pool was postponed on a 600-question reading that could not separate it from the template alone
(+0.83pp, p = 0.58). One dispatch answers it on the split the leaderboard reports, with both arms
in the same run so the pair is a delta rather than two rates:

| arm | reading | strict match | calls a case | prompt tokens (hit / miss) | completion | CNY a case |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|
| `macsql-prompt` | **1,010/1,532 = 65.93%** | 60.18% | 1.00 | 4,609 (4,475 / 134) | 82 | 0.0011 |
| `select-mixed-rule` | 980/1,532 = 63.97% | 59.33% | 3.00 | 4,683 (4,096 / 587) | 179 | 0.0028 |

Paired: **119 won / 89 lost = +1.96pp, exact McNemar p = 0.0441, 95% CI [+0.12, +3.80]**, interval
excluding zero.

By the discipline the last round wrote down, that p-value has to be stated as a multiple: 30 cases
over the A/A's own 17-question spread is **1.76×**. That is weaker than the 3.35× the template
scored against the shipped prompt, so **the direction is settled and the size is not**. Difficulty
splits the same way it did in the pool's earlier reading rather than the single candidate's — simple
67:45 (p = 0.0467), moderate 37:37 (p = 1.0), challenging 15:7 (p = 0.1338) — which is also the
reason the two mechanisms can stack: they move different bands.

**The price is what decides it.** The prompt totals are almost identical (4,609 against 4,683)
because the template is a fixed prefix and 97% of it is served from the provider's cache; the money
follows the uncached column, 134 tokens against 587. So the single source costs **40%** of the pool
and a third of its calls, for a case more accuracy.

**Verdict: the shipped configuration is the template alone.** Not because 1.76× is a strong effect —
because a configuration that is at least as good, at 40% of the bill and a third of the calls, is a
decision rather than a bet.

Two readings that belong beside this one. The previous dispatch read the same arm at 1,004; this one
reads 1,010 (+6), which is the A/A spread, so the number is a second sample of one mechanism rather
than a new one. And `served` is `deepseek-flash` in both rows: `deepseek-chat` is now served by
Flash and billed at Flash prices, which is why the price table carries both names at the same
figures.

### And the dispatch died on the step after its reading, which is its own finding

```
Error: card: the prompt has no "\nQuestion: " heading
```

`costOf` splits a prompt on `buildSqlPrompt`'s marks — it requires the system turn to end with the
question and reads the card as everything between `Schema:` and the first context heading. The
template names its blocks in `【…】` and puts the question in the middle, followed by evidence and
the decomposition instruction, so there is neither a heading to find nor an end to check.

**That is the second cost of a skeleton-level lever: not only does the prompt change skeleton, the
instrument that prices it changes object.** The fix is not a second grammar in `costOf` — that
would make it the intersection of two grammars and require a third change for a third template. It
is to detect the arm's declared skeleton once, before the loop, and say so: the step now reports
that no card can be cut out of this prompt, names the template, and exits zero. In a 1,532-question
loop a throw on question 47 reports a broken harness; "this arm sends another skeleton" reports the
truth, and the two read differently a year later.

A 40-question re-dispatch (`44994859181`) then confirmed the repair and settled a question the fix
raised: **nine diagnostic steps ran over a template arm and all nine passed** — card, values gap,
joins, prompt gap, repair, one-candidate, pool replay, summary, readback. The only step that refused
was `diversity`, and it refused for its own reason: 40 cases with candidates is under the 100 it
needs, and "a share of 40 is a share of the draw". So `card.ts` is the one instrument that reads a
prompt's internal structure; every other reads the statements and the questions.

## The prompt the product sends is the prompt the experiment priced

The adoption reading above decided that the shipped SQL prompt is `macsql-prompt`: the MAC-SQL
skeleton on this repository's card, with the dataset's evidence and no column hint, one call a case.
That decision was recorded in this document and in the plan — and then it had nowhere to live. The
combination existed in exactly one place, the arm table in `eval/bird/run.ts`, which is a
benchmark's declaration; the product's SQL path built its prompt by hand, two fields at a time
(`prompt: { dialect, evidence }`), from whatever the caller passed.

**An experiment and a product that agree today and are maintained apart are one edit from
disagreeing, and the edit is always harmless on its own.** Nothing would have gone red: the arm
keeps scoring, the tool keeps answering, and only the product's accuracy moves — which is precisely
the "no division between the best combination and what ships" requirement this round exists to
close.

### One object, in the package

`packages/ai/src/recipe.ts` states the combination as a value: `SHIPPED_SQL` — template,
descriptions on, foreign keys off, samples off, evidence from the caller, no hint, SQLite — beside
`ASSEMBLED_SQL`, the skeleton that can state any dialect, which is what the tool sent until this
round. `resolvePrompt(recipe, payload)` returns the `PromptOptions`; `resolveShipment(payload)`
chooses between them and returns the `linking` flag too, because the hint lives in the user message
rather than in the prompt object.

Three behaviours are worth stating because each one could have gone the other way:

- **The dialect is canonicalised, not passed through.** Every runner under `packages/node` reports
  `sqlite`; the template says `SQLite` in its instruction and in both worked examples. A prompt that
  said `sqlite` would be written in a dialect no documentation names, so the recipe's own spelling
  wins — and a comparison handed the same capital on both sides would never have exercised it.
- **A dialect the recipe cannot state falls back, and the fallback is named.** A PostgreSQL caller
  gets the assembled skeleton with `fellBackFrom: 'shipped-sql'`, because a prompt whose instruction
  says SQLite and whose examples are SQLite cannot be sent to PostgreSQL. It is a fallback rather
  than a throw so the product keeps answering; it is *reported* so that a reader comparing two
  deployments does not explain a prompt change by the model.
- **The tool's payload now names the recipe.** `ask_question` returns `promptRecipe`, and
  `promptFallback` when one was used. A prompt in a payload is a prompt a run can be attributed to.

### The instrument: zero calls, byte comparison

`pnpm bench:bird:recipe` builds both prompts per case — the arm's through `promptFor`, the
product's through `resolveShipment` — and compares the two messages `buildAskMessages` produces.
Nothing is re-implemented: an option that renders to the same text is the same prompt, and the text
is what the model reads.

```
pnpm bench:bird:recipe                       # the arm the recipe names
BIRD_SPLIT=dev pnpm bench:bird:recipe        # the whole dev split
pnpm bench:bird:recipe --arm inline+evidence # the control: an arm that is not the shipped prompt
```

The readings, all with zero model calls:

| split | cases | identical | first difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mini-Dev | 500 | 500 | — |
| dev | 1,534 | 1,534 | — |
| dev, control (`inline+evidence`) | 1,534 | 0 | `system` at offset 0 |

The control is the part that makes the first two rows a measurement rather than a tautology: an arm
that is not the shipped prompt differs on every case, at the first character, which is what "the
recipe is the arm" would look like if it were false. The instrument also refuses, rather than
reports, three ways of measuring the wrong thing — a template arm compared against the assembled
fallback, a bare invocation when the recipe names no arm, and a `--arm` that is not in the table.

One case is deliberately not what a reader expects: **the card carries its notes on every case**,
which is what the run does (`buildSchema(..., { withNotes: true })` once per database, with
`descriptions` deciding whether they are printed). An instrument that stripped the notes for an arm
whose `notes` flag is off would compare a card neither side sends — the defect `card.ts` spent two
rounds on — and would have passed while both prompts were wrong in the same way.

## The paid selector on a closed pool: the criterion, registered before the dispatch

The free family is closed on the template pool — twenty zero-call strategies, best 401 of 600, pool
ceiling 437 — and the reason is countable rather than mysterious: 485 of those 600 questions have
every candidate shaped the same, so a rule that reads shape has no input on four cases in five. The
next lever therefore has to read the statements, and reading them costs a call.

**Arm:** `select-mixed-template`, which is `select-mixed-rule-template` with one field changed — the
free rule out, the model in. Same three candidates, same prompts, same judge, same temperature, so
the pair prices the call and nothing else.

**Criterion, written here first:**

| field | value |
| --- | --- |
| split | dev, first 600 questions (`BIRD_LIMIT=600`), the same case set the free replay was measured on |
| bar | **at least 405 of 600 selected** — the midpoint between the free family's ceiling (401) and the 409 an earlier round registered |
| calls | **declared: four a case** (three to generate, one to choose), read from the artifact rather than assumed |
| decision | ≥405: adopt the paid selector on this pool and re-price the product's call budget. 401–404: the ceiling of this path is where it is, and the next lever is the pool's **width**, not another selector. ≤401: a call that reads the three statements is worth nothing here, and the pool work stops until a candidate source differs in *knowledge* rather than in wording |

The middle branch is the one worth registering in advance: a reading of 402 would be a *successful*
experiment and a negative result at the same time, and without the sentence above it would be read
as a failure and re-run with another prompt.

The run also carries `select-mixed-rule-template` and `macsql-prompt`, so the free ceiling and the
single source are measured on the same case set in the same hour rather than inherited from an
earlier artifact.

### The reading: 387, and the selection line closes

Run `45003945244`, dev's first 600 questions, three arms on one endpoint in one hour:

| arm | selected | calls a case | prompt tokens | of which cached | uncached | completion |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `macsql-prompt` (single source) | **389** (64.8%) | 1.00 | 3,705 | 3,522 | 183 | 128 |
| `select-mixed-rule-template` (free rule) | 388 (64.7%) | 3.00 | 6,176 | 5,608 | 568 | 229 |
| `select-mixed-template` (paid selector) | **387** (64.5%) | 4.00 | 6,603 | 5,661 | 942 | 226 |

Paired, inside the run:

| pair | only left | only right | exact McNemar |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| single → free rule | 42 | 43 | p = 1.0000 |
| single → paid selector | 37 | 39 | p = 0.9088 |
| free rule → paid selector | 34 | 35 | p = 1.0000 |

**Criterion: ≥405. Reading: 387. The bar is missed by 18 cases, and the registered middle branch did
not happen either** — the paid selector is not "just short of 405", it is the *lowest* of the three
numbers in its own run, by two cases against a source that costs a quarter of the calls.

The decision is the one written down before the dispatch, and it is not "try another selector
prompt":

> **≤401: a call that reads the three statements is worth nothing here, and the pool work stops until
> a candidate source differs in *knowledge* rather than in wording.**

Three things are now closed on this pool, and they close together:

1. **The free family is closed** — twenty zero-call strategies, ceiling 401, and the reason is
   countable: 485 of 600 questions have every candidate shaped the same (`bench:bird:rules`).
2. **The paid selector is closed** — one call that reads all three statements, and it moves the answer
   *backwards* by one case against choosing by rule. The selector's own call is 427 prompt tokens (374
   uncached) and **one** completion token: it is not reading the statements in any sense that changes
   an answer.
3. **The pool itself is closed** — a single source reads 389 while the three-candidate pool reads 388
   for three times the calls. The pool's value was always the *ceiling* (an answer existed on 437 of
   600), and a ceiling is only worth what a chooser can convert. Nothing here can convert it.

That is why the next candidate has to differ in knowledge rather than in wording: three prompts that
disagree about phrasing give a chooser nothing to decide on, which is exactly what
`recall@3 72.7%` against `64.7%` says — **8pp of headroom that a chooser cannot reach** because the
cases it would need are the ones where all three prompts wrote the same wrong statement.

`select-mixed-template` stays in the arm table as an on-demand ablation reference, not as a
candidate: it is the measurement that closes the line, and re-running it would only re-buy it.

## The selector line was closed one measurement too early, and the paper that closed it says so

The section above ends by closing the selector on this page. Reading CHASE-SQL's own ablations the
same day — the question that prompted it was "should we copy this system, and can a runner prove its
score with our model" — turns up the figure that section needed and did not have.

**Their off-the-shelf selector scores 58.01% on the binary task the selector exists for. Their
fine-tuned one scores 71.01%.** 387 of 600 is where 58.01% lives. What closed last round was
*zero-shot selection*; the thirteen points between those two numbers is the part of the selection
side this repository has never measured, and it is not reachable by rewriting a prompt.

### Three repositories carry the name, and one of them starts

| repository | files | what it is | can a runner start it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `google-research/google-research` | — | no path matches `chase_sql` | the submission itself is not published |
| `VineetV2/chase-sql` `3bbf845` | 23 (17 `.py`) | four stages over BIRD dev, SQLite execution, 21 candidates | **yes** — `src/llm.py` already branches to an OpenAI-compatible client, LSH is `datasketch`, execution is `sqlite3`, so no GPU and no torch on the inference path |
| `kungfuai/chase-sql` `4e63f18` (13★) | 23 (15 `.py`) | `src/database.py` is a mock e-commerce database | **no** — it never loads BIRD, so a score from it would be a score about the toy |
| `harkrish1/open-chase-sql` `84ef039` (GPL-3.0) | 104 (7 `.py`) | keyword extraction plus a vector store | **no** — no candidate generator and no selector |

So the answer to "run their code on a runner with our model" is **yes for one repository**, and the
adapter is small: `_call_openai` needs a `base_url`, and `datasketch`, `sqlglot` and `editdistance`
install without torch. `eval/competitors/intake.json` now carries the eighth row for it, with
`status: partial` and `license: none declared` — the same status MAC-SQL already runs under, which
means clone and run locally, never redistribute.

### What it would take to run, and what the number would mean

The paper reports no per-question call count, so the number has to be counted out of the code. Per
question, that rebuild makes:

| stage | calls | where it comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| value retrieval | 1 | one keyword-extraction call, then MinHash LSH and a cross-encoder rerank on CPU |
| DC-CoT | 7 | `generate_dc`, `num_candidates_per_strategy` |
| QP-CoT | 7 | `generate_qp`, same count |
| online synthetic | **9** | two example-generation calls (`Rf` and `Rt`, once per question) plus seven answers |
| query fixer | up to 3 per failing candidate | `fix_all_candidates(..., beta=3)`; at a 30% failure rate that is ≈7 |
| selection | **2 × pairs whose results differ** | `tournament_select` compares every unordered pair, both orderings |

The last row is the one that decides the bill, because it is **quadratic in the candidate count**:
21 candidates are 210 unordered pairs before the equal-result short circuit, and the paper's own
figure 2(d) says the pool stops paying after about 20. At the 70% short-circuit rate this
repository's pools show, that is ≈126 selector calls a question — **≈157 calls in total, not the
61 a "21 + fixer + a few comparisons" estimate gives**. Priced off `eval/price.ts` at
`deepseek-flash` rates with a warm prefix cache: **≈¥0.17 a question, ≈¥102 for 600 and ≈¥261 for
the full dev split**.

Two consequences follow from the shape rather than the price. A pool of **three** candidates is
three unordered pairs, so the whole selection stage costs 3 calls instead of 126 — a factor of 42
bought by cutting the pool from 21 to 3, which is exactly the trade their figure 2(d) says is cheap.
And a selector that reads five result rows per candidate is affordable at three candidates and is
not at twenty-one.

It would not buy the score. Three places separate the rebuild from the submission:

| | the paper | the rebuild | what it does to attribution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| selector input | `θ_p(schema_union, question, hint, SQL A, SQL B)`; execution results are used **only** to short-circuit equal pairs (Algorithm 3) | five result rows per candidate go **into** the prompt | an addition the paper never prices |
| selector strength | fine-tuned Gemini-1.5-Flash, **71.01%** binary accuracy | default is the zero-shot one (**58.01–63.98%**) | 7–13 points of selection quality missing |
| DC / QP few-shot | human-annotated examples with written reasoning chains, appendix figures 16 and 18 | two toy examples hardcoded over an `employees`/`departments` schema | the guidance those two paths are made of is absent |

A run of that repository therefore measures *the skeleton with toy examples and a zero-shot selector
on DeepSeek*. Its own README says `>73.01%` under "Dev EX Target" — a target, not a reading. Calling
that number "CHASE-SQL" is the mistake `status: partial` is written to prevent.

### The ablation is the part worth having, and it prices the three levers this repository never tried

Every figure below is the paper's, on BIRD dev, Gemini-1.5-Pro, and each corresponds to something
that can be run here as one arm.

| what it isolates | their reading | what this repository reads | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| baseline, no CoT | 57.75% | `macsql-prompt` 65.93% | different harness, so the level differs; only deltas transfer |
| **QP-CoT alone** (three-step execution order) | **65.51%** (+7.76) | never run | ← untested |
| **DC-CoT alone** (decompose, solve, combine) | **65.77%** (+8.02) | `decompose` **−3.7pp** | tested as *always* decompose, not as one candidate |
| **online synthetic examples alone** | **68.02%** (+10.27) | never run | ← untested, and their strongest single path |
| 21 candidates, oracle | 82.79% | `recall@3` 72.7% on 600 | same shape: a wide gap over end to end |
| 21 candidates, self-consistency | 68.84% | `select-mixed-template` 387 of 600 | same verdict |
| 21 candidates, **fine-tuned selector** | **73.01%** | zero-shot selector 387 (58% band) | the gap the closing above skipped |
| removing LSH value retrieval | −2.92pp | `literal-missing` headroom 2.3pp | the two agree |
| removing the query fixer | −3.78pp | `repairs` family already priced | consistent |
| removing QP / OS / DC from the pool | −0.65 / −0.85 / −1.24 | — | see the arithmetic below |

**The ablation's three generator terms sum to 2.74pp while the pool is worth 4.99pp over the best
single path** (73.01 − 68.02). The difference, 2.25pp, is a pool containing an answer rather than
each path being individually necessary — which is the same conclusion `I-77` reached here from the
other direction: a fourth opinion raised the ceiling by 22–27 cases and converted none.

**Their error census and ours agree on the residual.** They put **10.4%** of cases in "a correct
candidate existed and the selector did not choose it"; this repository's `recall@3` 72.7% against
64.7% is **8.0%**. Two harnesses, two prompt families, two models, the same order of magnitude: the
residual is a property of the corpus, not a defect in either implementation.

### What the two-sided reading changes

1. **The falsifier written three rounds ago was never executed.** When retrieval-based examples
   failed here (`metadata+evidence+icl` +0.91pp against a +4.0pp bar, p = 0.2684), the registered
   falsifier said: *"if the gain is < +1.0pp, retrieval-based knowledge is closed as a lever on this
   pipeline and the next mechanism must **synthesise** the examples with the model rather than
   retrieve them — CHASE-SQL's generator, not its retriever."* That sentence is on this page. The
   online synthetic generator was never dispatched; the round went to the candidate ceiling instead.
   Their +10.27pp is the strongest single-path figure in the paper, and it is the one mechanism the
   falsifier named by hand.
2. **"Knowledge rather than wording" was the wrong axis for this system.** DC-CoT and QP-CoT use
   *hand-annotated* examples, not retrieved ones — their prompt does not carry more facts about the
   database, it carries a different *procedure*. The axis that separates their three paths is not
   knowledge against wording; it is **three procedures against three samples of one procedure**.
   `select-mixed` draws three samples of one prompt, which is why it reads 1.12 distinct result sets
   a case against 1.15, and why the chooser had nothing to decide.
3. **The selector deserves one more arm, and it is the cheap one.** The paper's selector sees the
   schema union of the two candidates and nothing about their results; the rebuild hands it five
   result rows. That is the only lever in this table that costs **no extra call** — it changes what
   an existing call is shown. Criterion: on the same three-candidate set, `≥ single source (65.93%)`
   and **no more than 1.00 selector call a case**, with the equal-result short circuit counted.

### The dispatch these three readings justify

| # | arm | criterion, registered before the dispatch | questions | CNY |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C1 | `template+os` — generate k question-SQL pairs for *this* database, then answer | **≥ 68.0% (single source +2.1pp)**, matching their +10.27 over a 57.75 baseline | 1,532 | ≈8 |
| C2 | `template+qp` — three-step execution order, one call | **≥ 68.0%**, and the plan step must not cost more than +40% prompt tokens | 1,532 | ≈4 |
| C3 | `select-mixed+results` — same three candidates, selector shown five result rows, equal-result pairs short-circuited | **≥ 65.93%** and **≤ 1.00 selector call a case** | 600 | ≈5 |

C1 is the one the falsifier asked for. C2 is the one the paper prices as cheap and positive (+7.76
on a single path, −0.65 when removed from the pool — a small term in a pool and a large one alone).
C3 is the one that repairs last round's closure: it is the same selector shape, shown the input the
rebuild gives it, at no additional call.

If C1 and C2 both land under 66%, the three procedures are worth nothing on this corpus and the
remaining levers are the backbone and the product side — that falsifier is registered here, before
the dispatch, for the same reason the last one was.

## Three procedures, and the premise this round found already false

The section above ends with a dispatch and a falsifier. Writing the three arms turned up two
things about our own harness that change what the dispatch is for, and one of them cancels an arm.

### The selector has always been shown its candidates' results

Last round's third arm was going to ask whether a selector shown five result rows picks better
than one shown none. It is not a question: `toCandidate(executed, previewRows = 3, maxChars = 300)`
has put three rows of every candidate's result into every selection prompt this repository has
ever sent, and the equal-result short circuit that arm also proposed is `gate: 'results'`, which
two arms already carry:

| arm | accuracy | calls | conversion |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `select-mixed-gated` (short circuits equal results) | 59.48% | 3.30 | 90.21% |
| `select-mixed-gated-evidence` (and shows the columns they read) | 60.89% | 3.31 | 91.79% |

So the paid selector's 1-token reply was not a model that had never seen the results — it was a
model that saw them and still answered a position. That is a stronger statement than the one last
round wrote, and it costs nothing: the arm is struck before it was dispatched, and the ¥5 and the
1,800 selection calls stay unspent. **A registered criterion whose premise is false has to be
struck, not adjusted.** The rule that follows from it is in the checklist at the foot of this
section.

### Of the paper's three paths, one is already in the product

CHASE-SQL's ablation prices three procedures, and their abstract calls them the reason a prompt
alone does not get there: query plan (+7.76pp alone), divide and conquer (+8.02), online synthetic
examples (+10.27). The template this repository ships opens with

> Work by decomposition: split the question into the sub-questions it is built from and write the
> statement that answers each, then write the statement that answers the question itself.

which is their divide-and-conquer path in our own voice, and it is why the reader takes the *last*
statement rather than the first. Reading `65.93%` as "a prompt" rather than "a prompt with a
procedure" was the mistake the last round made when it compared our number to their 57.75%
baseline: our baseline is not procedure-free. The honest comparison is procedure against
procedure, which leaves two of their three untested here: the plan, and the synthetic examples.

### The two arms this round dispatches

| # | arm | what differs from `macsql-prompt` | criterion, registered before the dispatch | calls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C1 | `macsql-bird-os` | three question-SQL pairs written for *this* database are added to the two carried examples | **≥ 68.0%** (single source 65.93 + 2.1pp) and the block counted in prompt tokens | 1.00 + 11 synthesis calls for the split |
| C2 | `macsql-bird-qp` | the opening sentence pair asks for a plan — tables, operations, output columns — instead of a decomposition | **≥ 68.0%** and the plan costing at most **+40%** prompt tokens | 1.00 |

Both run beside `macsql-prompt` in the same dispatch, because a 2.1pp criterion on 1,532
questions needs the paired control: dev's MDE is 2.30pp, and a run-to-run A/A on this split has
moved an unchanged arm by more than the effect being sought.

C1 is the mechanism this document named for itself three rounds ago and never ran:

> if the gain is < +1.0pp, retrieval-based knowledge is closed as a lever on this pipeline and the
> next mechanism must **synthesise** the examples with the model rather than retrieve them —
> CHASE-SQL's generator, not its retriever.

Retrieval measured +0.91pp against a +4.0pp bar (p = 0.2684), so the falsifier fired, and the
round after it went to the candidate ceiling instead. Their +10.27pp is the largest single-path
figure in their paper, and the block costs 11 calls for the whole split rather than 1,534: it is
per database, cached on the prompt and the model, exactly as this repository's synthesized
definitions are.

Three, not their seven, and the criterion says why: the block is paid for on every question and
the parent is already 3,700 prompt tokens because of its two carried examples. Three pairs add
about 450 tokens (+12%); seven would add a thousand and make the arm's gain indistinguishable from
"the prompt got longer", which is the confound `samples-wide` already charged +74.9% of prompt for.
If C1 meets its bar at three, the count is the next lever rather than this arm dispatched again.

### C2 is not the `plan` lever that lost 7.2pp

`plan` carried a query plan written in an *earlier call*, which the generator then obeyed: 50.4%
against 57.6% for its parent, 63:27, p = 0.0002 — anchoring, not planning. C2 asks for the plan
inside the same reply, where it is working notes and costs no call, which is what their Algorithm 1
does. The pair is therefore one sentence pair in one prompt, not a second call, and the reading
separates "a plan written elsewhere" (measured harmful) from "a plan written here" (never measured).

### Cost, declared before the run

1,532 questions × 3 arms = 4,596 generation calls, plus 11 synthesis calls, at the price table in
`eval/price.ts` with a warm prefix cache: **≈ ¥6**. The paired table is read with
`bench:bird:pair`, and the two readings that decide the round are the paired deltas to
`macsql-prompt`, not the absolute accuracies.

### The falsifier

If both arms land under 66.0% — inside or below the parent's own A/A spread — then no procedure
this repository can write by hand beats the one it ships, and the remaining levers are the backbone
and the product side. That is registered here, before the dispatch, for the same reason the last
one was: an arm that runs without a prediction acquires a verdict it did not earn.

### The checklist increment

- **A criterion's premise is part of the criterion.** "Show the selector its results" was struck
  in ten minutes by reading `toCandidate`'s signature. The cheap version of this check is reading
  the function a lever would change; the expensive version is dispatching it.
- **A template is a procedure, not a skeleton.** Counting our 65.93% against a competitor's
  57.75% baseline compares a prompt that decomposes with one that does not, and credits the
  difference to the skeleton.
- **A generated block is priced per database, not per question.** Eleven calls for a split of
  1,534 is what makes an example generator affordable where a retriever's index was not.

## The reading: three procedures, one call a case, and a criterion that did not hold

Dispatch `45021178365`, dev 1,532 questions, one arm serving as the paired baseline, all three at
1.00 calls a case, same endpoint, same hour.

| arm | answered | accuracy | prompt | cached | uncached | completion | CNY |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `macsql-prompt` (shipped) | 997 | 65.08% | 3,694 | 3,511 | 183 | 136 | 2.44 |
| `macsql-bird-qp` (plan) | 1,001 | 65.34% | 3,725 | 3,403 | 322 | 105 | 2.48 |
| `macsql-bird-os` (database examples) | **1,007** | **65.73%** | 3,907 | 3,610 | 297 | 146 | 2.92 |

Paired within the run (exact McNemar):

| pair | only left | only right | p |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| shipped → plan | 70 | 74 | 0.8027 |
| shipped → database examples | 56 | 66 | 0.4153 |

**Neither arm reaches 68.0%, and the falsifier registered before the dispatch fires: on this corpus
no hand-written procedure beats the one that ships.** The database examples are the better of the
two by 10 cases — the only arm whose sign is positive in both the absolute count and the paired
table — and 10 cases at p = 0.42 is noise. The plan is 4 cases up at p = 0.80, which is what "the
same prompt with one sentence pair changed" looks like when the sentence pair does not matter.

### What this reading actually prices, and it is not "+10.27pp"

CHASE-SQL's ablation puts online synthetic examples at 68.02% against a **57.75% baseline**, +10.27,
the largest single-path figure in that paper. This run adds the same mechanism to a prompt that
already carries **(a)** a decomposition procedure and **(b)** two worked examples with value
examples, and the marginal value is **+0.65pp, n.s.** Both statements are true and they are about
different questions: their number is what an example generator is worth *instead of nothing*, and
this one is what it is worth *on top of a prompt that already decomposes and already shows two
examples*. A product that ships a prompt is always asking the second question.

The block cost 213 prompt tokens a case of which 99 were uncached (3,907 against 3,694): the two
carried examples had already warmed the prefix, so three more pairs 33 in total, one synthesis call
per database, 11 for the split — added 5.8% to the prompt and ¥0.48 to the whole split. Cheap. It
just did not buy anything.

### The A/A is larger than either effect, which is why the baseline was in the run

The shipped prompt answered **1,010** of 1,532 in the round that adopted it and **997** here. Same
config, same endpoint, same scorer: **−13 cases, −0.85pp**. Against that stored baseline the plan
arm would read −0.59pp and the examples arm −0.20pp − *both losses* − while against the paired
baseline in the same hour they read +0.26 and +0.65. The two stories differ only in their
denominator, and the paired one is the only one that holds the hour fixed.

This is the third time this repository has written the same sentence, and the first time it has
cost nothing to obey: an arm read against a stored baseline inherits that baseline's noise, and on
dev that noise (13–30 cases) is bigger than any procedure this corpus has shown.

### What the falsifier leaves

Registered before the dispatch: *if both arms land under 66.0%, no procedure this repository can
write by hand beats the one it ships, and the remaining levers are the backbone and the product
side.* Both did. Three consequences, and the third is the uncomfortable one:

1. **The procedure line is closed** — not the "copy CHASE-SQL" line. Their pipeline's other parts
   are untouched by this reading and priced elsewhere: value retrieval (−2.92pp when removed), the
   query fixer (−3.78pp), pairwise selection (already measured here at +0.8pp), and the fine-tuned
   selector, which is the one component no prompt can reach.
2. **The remaining prompt-side levers are now the ones already known to be small**: the card, the
   hint, the values block, repairs — each priced, each inside its own MDE or negative.
3. **Backbone is the untested variable, and it is a different experiment.** Every reading in this
   document is `deepseek-chat`. A stronger base may lift all three arms together, which would say
   nothing about procedures; it may also lift them unequally, which would say a great deal. That
   comparison needs both arms re-measured on the same second base, in one run, with the timeout
   ceiling declared — the `S1-b` dispatch established that 94 of 1,532 cases can be forfeited to a
   timeout on a slower base while the score line says nothing about it.

### The checklist increment

- **A procedure's marginal value is not its standalone value.** +10.27 against nothing and +0.65
  against a prompt that already has a procedure and two examples are the same mechanism measured at
  two points on its own curve, and a product ships at the second point.
- **Three pairs per database cost 11 calls for the split.** The generator was the cheap part; it
  was the +0.65pp that was expensive, in the only currency that matters here.
- **A paired baseline is not a formality when the A/A is 13 cases.** This run's headline would have
  been "both new procedures lost" had the baseline been quoted from the last dispatch instead of
  measured in this one.
